Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches - which use 
expectation propagation to improve performance and achieve convergence. These 
stabilization methods boost efficiency and allow the algorithms to access a 
broader range of matrices, ultimately leading to better results. In this study, 
we delve into the reasoning behind these enhancements and introduce an alternative 
method of stabilization, known as partial stabilization, which offers superior 
performance and more versatile solutions than conventional stabilization. 
Furthermore, we introduce an open-source package for SPGL1-based algorithms that 
incorporates partial stabilization, high-damping regimes, and a comprehensive 
testing framework to evaluate its accuracy and resilience. Our results reveal that 
this implementation surpasses various benchmarks in signal recovery and our 
stimuli cover a vast spectrum of CS scenarios, from benign to highly challenging. 
Our code can be accessed at a designated repository. Additionally, we have 
prepared a collection of precomputed results in ourdata directory on GitHub. 
Each entry contains the recovery results of 10^5 randomly generated test signals. 
Our aim is to expand upon these findings and facilitate the comparison of 
different stabilization methods as well as other CSP algorithms. We welcome the 
community to utilize our code, replicate our findings, and contribute to the 
advancement of this research area. We are particularly interested in exploring the 
following open questions: (a) Can we derive a theoretical guarantee for the 
convergence of high-damped algorithms? (b) Is partial stabilization a superior 
choice over conventional stabilization? (c) How can we extend the technique to 
handle exponential graphs and sparsity patterns that rely on the Laplacian 
matrix? (d) Can we utilize the expected posterior approximation to generate 
probabilistic confidence intervals for the recovered signal? (e) How can we 
efficiently calibrate the level of stabilization and achieve optimal performance 
for a given problem? We hypothesize that a lower level of stabilization is 
preferable when dealing with dense matrices and high levels of corruption. 
Conversely, we predict that a higher level of stabilization is more beneficial 
when faced with limited corruption and matrix coherence. We propose to explore 
these hypotheses in a future study, focusing on the performance variability of 
different levels of stabilization. Our code is designed with this research 
goal in mind and we encourage the community to work with our code, modify it, 
and utilize our data to evaluate the stability of various compression and 
stabilization algorithms

The diverse range of Deformable Linear Encoding (DeLE) models continues to expand as research progresses. Despite promising results, such as effectively capturing the overall cell shape, the current state of models struggles to accurately represent cells with complex geometries or severe deformations. Our novel cellular form generator, based on implicit neural representations, overcomes existing limitations by leveraging a conditional part-based generative model, thus enabling the representation of a broad cellular morphology category and severe deformations. Our findings suggest that the success of this approach lies in its ability to condition the implicit potential field only by the desired morphology, thereby enabling novel uses of implicit neural representations in generative modeling. Additionally, our model exhibits enhanced sampling efficiency and produces cells with more realistic shapes through qualitative and quantitative assessments. The code for our method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/auroracho/CellNEFGEN. and an interactive demo can be accessed at https://auroracho.github.io/CCellNEFGEN/.

This paper delves into the geometric principles underlying spectrograms and their leVel sets to develop innovative signal analysis techniques. We utilize these techniques to identify key characteristics of temporal signal patterns and assess their variability across different signal versions. Our methods are demonstrated on numerical examples and also used to study the spectrograms of mammography images to develop a robust feature for lesion detection. This approach is further framed as a stochastic Valued-sets problem, enabling the derivation of statistical time-frequency energy density estimates from limited signal duration. The resulting method is validated on a dataset comprising mammography images, yielding results that conform to established clinical standards. Additionally, this approach facilitates the creation of a spectrogram-based feature for lesion detection that exhibits consistent performance across various dataset versions. Furthermore, this work reveals that spectrograms harbor information rich enough to derive statistical properties of temporal signal patterns, leading to a novel time-domain PARenet energy density estimate. This approach offers an efficient alternative to traditional long sequence analysis methods, thereby enabling real-time signal examination. Furthermore, this work promotes spectrogram level sets as a versatile tool for a broad spectrum of applications, including signal compression, fault diagnosis, and data classification. The proposed techniques are envisioned to stimulate research in spectrogram level sets and their geometric analysis. The numerical code for this work has been made publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AlexAlarcon/Spectrogram-Level- Sets.git. The mammography image dataset employed in this research is accessible at https://clinfowrite.wordpress.com/mammography-data/. The CERMA++ software used to compute the spectrograms and PARenet energy density estimates is available at https://cermaplus.github.io/cermaplus.html. The derived time-frequency features were also used in a basic spectrogram-level based lesion detection approach, which can be found at https://github.com/AlexAlarcon/Spectrogram-Lvl-Sets.git. Various studies suggest that stochastic forces exert a substantial impact on the evolution of planetary orbits, possibly influencing the long-term stability of planetary systems. Researchers employ the REBOUND N-body integration code to analyze the dynamics of multiple bodies interacting gravitationally. While it effectively handles deterministic forces, the code lacks a module for stochastic forces. This research aims to integrate stochastic forces into the REBOUND code as a module called REBOUNDCF. The new module is designed to be easy to use, flexible, and compatible with the existing REBOUND xREBOUND workflow. The integration of REBOUNDCF involves a novel method for computing stochastic forces that takes into account noise sources such as magnetic fields and the Planck radiation law, as well as post-Newtonian forces. The performance of REBOUNDCF is validated through a series of tests, and the results are compared to those obtained with the CF7T3 algorithm. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of stochastic forces on planetary systems in two exemplary scenarios: a system consisting of one star and multiple planets, and a planetary ring system modeled by a gravitationally bound disk. The study reveals that stochastic forces have a significant effect on the evolution of semi-major axes in the planetary system and a detectable impact on the modelled planetary ring system. Ultimately, the integration of REBOUNDCF into the REBOUND code facilitates a deeper comprehension of the influence of stochastic forces on the long-term stability of planetary systems. The newly developed REBOUNDCF module is now accessible for public use at the following repository: https://github.com/LAM-IPAC/REBOUNDCF. Additionally, the corresponding xREBOUND workflow is available at the following repository: https://github.com/LAM-IPAC/xREBOUND. The source code for REBOUNDCF and xREBOUND have been submitted to the following repository: https://astro-lam.github.io/REBOUNDCF.html. Despite recent discoveries, including a black hole with a mass of approximately $3.5 \times 10^4$ solar masses in the dwarf galaxy Leo I, the mechanisms involved in creating such objects remain insufficiently explained. By examining alternative scenarios, including a model in which massive black holes are generated through the merger of smaller objects, we explore how these scenarios could be validated or disproved by future observations. By analyzing the mass distribution of supermassive black holes in a hypothetical "standard" universe, we develop detectable signatures that could help confirm or reject various massive black hole formation models. These signatures include the presence of isolated intermediate-mass black holes and a upper limit on the mass of the smallest supermassive black holes. Current data already disfavors one such model, while future observations could significantly restrict the parameter space of others. Ultimately, a precise determination of the mass distribution of intermediate-mass black holes could decisively validate or disprove the model that best explains the existence of a $10^4$ solar mass black hole in Leo I. Our calculations, using density functional theory and the density functional screening approach, showed that flat bands in this alloy are protected by symmetry and appear in both its bulk and monolayer forms. Furthermore, flat bands in V1-xWxTa3S2 are strongly hybridized with the d-orbitals of the two transition metals. Based on this, we performed supercell electronic structure and density functional calculations and found that flat band induced correlation effects significantly affect the magnetism of the material. Our findings in V1-xWxTa3S2 offer a potential pathway to engineering magnetoresistance in real-world flat band systems. Understanding how genomic elements contribute to disease and complex traits is best achieved by examining multiple traits across various genomic features simultaneously.  In this study, we assess the role of 54 genomic elements in predicting five physical traits and 13 behavioral disorders through a comprehensive analysis of genomic data across 18 human characteristics.  By utilizing an open-access database with detailed annotations of genomic elements, we conducted the most thorough investigation of its kind to date.  Our results reveal significant associations with functional elements within trait-specific genomic regions and a prominent involvement of long non-coding RNA in a wide range of traits.  Furthermore, we identify functional elements more likely to be associated with disease and other complex disorders.  These findings set the stage for future research on the underlying biology of genomic function and open new avenues for the development of precision medicine targeted at functional genomic elements.  The data and code supporting this study have been made publicly available.  In an effort to facilitate further research, we have also created a user-friendly tool that allows researchers to study genomic elements across a variety of characteristics and regions with distinct biological functions.  This resource, known as F-GSA, can be accessed at f-gsa.net.  Additionally, the data have been submitted to the ENCODE database for public evaluation (https://encode.casCUs/c/).  In an accompanying paper, we demonstrate the significant utility of this approach in accurately predicting directly measurable traits such as body mass index and height.  The method can be found at https://github.com/casCUs/F-GSA.  Future updates will be posted on the blog: https://ccorblog.github.io/F-GSA/.  In the future, we intend to expand the scope to include model organisms and apply it to a broad range of traits in other species across various taxonomic groups.  This endeavor has the potential to break down barriers between species and offer novel therapeutic options for treating diseases in animals, including humans.  Lastly, we aim to make the data open-source and invite researchers to collaborate in a joint effort to study genomic elements. This study identifies certain types of block arrangements with parameters r and λ that have specific mathematical properties. We demonstrate the existence of two distinct cases where the automorphism groups of these arrangements exhibit flag-transitive properties. Furthermore, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the arrangement's automorphism group to be transitive on its blocks. One of these transitive cases occurs when the arrangement's block size is a multiple of its index, and in such scenarios, its automorphism group also exhibits a flag-transitive property. Conversely, the other transitive case arises when the arrangement's block size and index share no common factors, and this situation uniquely identifies two specific groups, specifically A4 and A5. Consequently, this finding refines and supplements a prior theorem involving these groups, thereby providing new insights into their mathematical representations. This research also provides criteria to determine when certain automorphism group actions on these block arrangements are transitive at the group order that is a multiple of the arrangement's index. This study presents examples of automorphism groups with a flag-transitive action on two specific configurations, specifically on a 2-(11, 3, 1) design and a 3-(11, 4, 1) design, and showcases the generality of these examples by showing that their automorphism groups cannot be represented by any permutation groups with a flag-transitive action. This research expands our understanding of the existing classification of finite permutation groups with a flag-transitive action, and it offers group-specific results that can be applied to larger groups, such as those with a multiple of 11 order. The velocity distribution of wide binary stars can be an effective test of gravity's behavior at large scales, excluding the influence of their own motion and other nearby stars. However, traditional analyses struggle to account for binary stars that have undergone dynamical exchange with other stars, potentially leading to contaminated samples and flawed conclusions about dark matter and non-Newtonian gravity models. To address this issue, a new machine learning algorithm and statistical framework are developed to efficiently remove binary stars that have exchanged partners, resulting in a cleaner dataset of 1,821 wide binaries free from dynamical exchanges. Furthermore, a more robust analysis of gravity models is possible due to the larger binary dataset, leading to constraints on deviations from Newtonian gravity, particularly at large scales, that are more stringent than previous constraints derived from the original exchange-reduced binary dataset. Interestingly, the more stringent constraints on some non-Newtonian gravity models, such as $f(R)$ and POPI, remain similar to the constraints derived from the original exchange-reduced binary dataset, suggesting that these models can be more effectively tested by including dynamical exchanges in future wide binary analyses. Additionally, the more stringent constraints on spatially-extended non-Newtonian gravity models, such as MOG, arise from a more detailed analysis of their implications on the galaxy's rotation curve using the exchange-reduced binary dataset. Finally, the more stringent constraints on some non-Newtonian gravity models, derived from the more efficient wide binary analysis, are less stringent than constraints derived from the galactic rotation curve, despite the exchange-reduced binary dataset's ability to effectively test these models at large scales. Interestingly, further studies could find more precise constraints on these models by simultaneously analyzing the exchange-reduced binary dataset and the galactic rotation curve together. We examine two key concepts in Multiplicative Linear Logic, a logic with categories: proof reduction and cut-elimination. We argue for a broader definition of proof reduction that mirrors subject-reduction, and demonstrate that this definition maintains consistency. We also show that under certain conditions, cut-elimination can be achieved through a cut-free and ordered reduction process. The correctness of this process is guaranteed by a new and broader weakening lemma, which does not rely on cut-elimination. We believe our work provides a more unified approach to understanding the semantics and semantics-based cut-elimination strategies of Multiplicative Linear Logic. Furthermore, we believe the concepts we've developed can be extended to explain cut-elimination in BiModal Linear Logic. One of the key factors influencing the performance of silicon-based devices is the effects of sound waves. Research has been conducted to investigate how these effects impact the movement of both electrons and holes, focusing on a silicon substrate and a silicon-on-insulator sample with a 50nm layer. By simulating various acoustic modes and examining their influence on the subband structure of bound electrons and holes, researchers analyzed the influence of both electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions. Findings indicate that electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions cause significant variations in energy levels, coupling energies, and oscillator strengths, ultimately affecting carrier mobility and spin persistence. Interestingly, these effects are distinct for holes compared to electrons, revealing significant anisotropy influenced by both wave types and crystal orientation. Furthermore, the unique properties of these interactions lead to unique signatures in spin persistence that are sensitive to both frequency and direction. The simulation outcomes also identify the potential for lateral acoustic modes to influence electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, opening up the possibility for controlling this interaction through mechanical means. Lastly, the analysis suggests that a 50nm layer is sufficient to mitigate the influence of surface waves on devices, but designers should still consider the effects of bulk and membrane modes. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the influence of sound waves on electronic properties, enabling the development of predictive models for silicon-based devices. The primary goal of our research is to tackle the issue of predicting the click-through rate (CTR) for novel advertisements by leveraging their visual content. By recognizing that incorporating explicit visual elements in advertisements can yield better ad CTR predictions compared to relying solely on text-based information, we create a network capable of learning and incorporating these visual features. Our proposed solution, named VAE-CTR, comprises of two core modules. Firstly, there is the Spencer Network, which is an enhanced ad representation learning model that uses a dual learning method to optimize both ad representation and relevance prediction. Secondly, there is the VAE-based fusion module that combines text and visual features using a variational auto-encoder (VAE) framework to obtain a unified ad representation. Our experiments show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in CTR prediction for new advertisements. Furthermore, we analyze the effectiveness of our novel features employed in our research and find that they substantially improve the CTR prediction performance compared to traditional methods. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols pose a significant issue for solar power, and detecting such disruptions via satellite is therefore crucial for ensuring reliable solar energy supply. However, identifying wildfire-related aerosols from satellites is complicated by noisy data and inconsistent measurements. To address this challenge, a solution involving the use of physics-based learning from noisy data is proposed. By combining wildfire models with spectral remote-sensing data and incorporating geographical and meteorological data, a learning procedure is developed to accurately detect wildfires from noisy satellite data. The method is tested and validated through rigorous experiments, and successful applications are found in two geographic areas - California, USA, and Western Australia. Given a location track's sequential nature, we address the problem of determining how to conceal the future locations in a revealed past. We develop an mathematical framework to quantify privacy, utilizing conditional priors and entropy gaps. This framework enables us to examine the trade-off between privacy and disclosure costs. We explore two specific scenarios - one involving the revelation of a-bounded distance, and the other, an arbitrary distance. For the first scenario, we derive closed-form expressions for optimal policies, while the second requires numerical methods. Furthermore, we analyze the feasibility of inducing conditional Gaussian priors, but find it impractical due to the correlation in location tracks. We propose an alternative, simpler priors, and demonstrate that location privacy can be enhanced by discarding distance information. We validate our findings through numerical experiments. Additionally, we observed that inducing a Gaussian prior results in the optimal policy tending towards a uniform distribution, as the prior standard deviation increases. We observed this behavior empirically, and validated it through numerical analysis. We observed similar results for the arbitrary distance scenario. Moreover, we analyzed the trade-off between privacy and disclosure costs, and observed that the optimal policy exhibits a trade-off that diminishes over time. We validated these findings both empirically and through numerical analysis. We noted that inducing a Gaussian prior results in the optimal policy being independent of the future track, and observed similar results for the arbitrary distance scenario. Furthermore, we analyzed the feasibility of (weakly) achieving location privacy, and observed that inducing a Gaussian prior allows for numerical computation of upper bounds on disclosure probability. We evaluated these bounds for different values of a, and found that they decrease rapidly as 'a' increases. We explored the scenario where 'a' tends to infinity, and found that location privacy can be maintained with an arbitrarily small error probability. We studied the minimal disclosure costs in this scenario, and found that they exhibit a weak dependence on 'b'. We derived upper and lower bounds on these costs, and found that they converge as 'b' increases. We investigated how to enhance location privacy, and found that doing so reduces disclosure costs. We observed similar results for the arbitrary distance scenario. Furthermore, we analyzed the location privacy's dependence on the prior standard deviation, and found that it is beneficial to increase it. We explored the scenario where the track is sampled from a Gaussian distribution with a large standard deviation, and found that location privacy can be maintained with an arbitrarily small error probability. We studied the optimal policy in this scenario, and found that it is independent of the future track.

Research in resting-state brain activity has shown great promise, yet studies relying on a single site have consistently encountered replication issues. To overcome these challenges, researchers have shifted towards a mass-univariate approach, applying statistical methods like Bonferroni correction to improve multi-site studies. However, this correction complicates interpretation and hinders accuracy when degrees of freedom are limited. Alternatively, methods like permutation tests or uncorrected p-values with thresholding have been suggested as superior alternatives. In this study, we examine a multi-site fMRI dataset comprising 1200 subjects across five sites, and compare the effects of employing Bonferoni correction versus thresholding on resting-state brain networks. Our analysis reveals that thresholding yields more accurate results, particularly in identifying active connections, and outperforms Bonferoni correction in terms of prediction accuracy as well. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that mass-univariate analysis unified across multiple sites can successfully identify and replicate brain networks. Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of choosing appropriate statistical methods to analyze data from large multi-site neuroimaging studies. The associated data can be found at https://datadisk.ua.ac.be/index.php/s/9KrR1P7PS3KkP3K. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
however many studies have relied on straightforward language indexing which 
fails to account for more complex scenarios such as language switching and 
blending. A novel method called PESTO is proposed, it specifically tackles the 
issue of unlabeled language switching by relying solely on the order of the 
words rather than any additional information. PESTO is composed of two main 
components: Switching Unit and Relative Positional Encoding. The former uses a 
simple one-gate Bi-LSTM to identify word positions and then determines the 
probability of a word belonging to a particular language based solely on its 
order. The latter uses an encoder separated by language to convert words 
into vectors based on their relative position. Experiments conducted on a 
large Twitter dataset spanning six code-mixed languages, have shown that PESTO 
outperforms current leading models across various tasks such as language 
identification, categorization, and part-of-speech tagging. Importantly, PESTO 
is both efficient and adaptable, meaning it can easily be applied to newly 
emergent code-mixed languages with minimal re-training requirements. One of the 
major advantages of PESTO is its ability to determine word boundaries without 
any additional processing steps beyond its initial training. Moreover, PESTO 
incorporates an unsupervised learning approach that is both efficient and 
accurate for word alignment, a task that is critical in NLP and also used in 
the model's training process. Overall, the proposed model has shown 
exceptional performance across multiple tasks and due to its ability to 
determine word boundaries, relative position, and switching points, it can be 
effectively applied to languages with substantial word-level ambiguity. A 
further exploration of PESTO is planned to be made available online. The source 
code for this model has been made publicly available at https://github.com/rajpurdhi/PESTO.ES.\<lang_name>.GitHub.IO. Using a combination of density functional theory and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg approach with a functional derivative method, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that anisotropic critical temperatures are influenced by the variable density of states and pressure-dependent phonon frequencies. Furthermore, we observed that the variable density of states has a significant impact on the isotope effect, leading to a more negative value that agrees with experimental findings. Consequently, taking the variable density of states into account yields a more accurate prediction of superconducting properties in H3S as a function of pressure. Lastly, our calculations demonstrate that the variable density of states plays a crucial role in predicting the critical temperature of H3S above 200 GPa, whereas at lower pressures, the difference is minimal. Moreover, our analysis indicates that the variable density of states originates from the hybridization between 3s H atoms and sulfur or neighboring H atoms, particularly near the van Hove singularity at which the hybridization increases rapidly with pressure. Furthermore, the variable density of states is primarily influenced by the Fermi wavevector and critical temperature, as well as facial/square-shaped Fermi surfaces that emerge at high pressures, indicating a potential nematic superconducting phenomenon in H3S. Lastly, we noted that the variable density of states could be generalized to other hydride superconductors under high pressure and should be taken into account in future theoretical and experimental studies of superconducting materials. Based on our analysis, we propose that van Hove singularities could be leveraged to create ultra-high-temperature superconductors above 20 K via structural design. Moreover, we suggest that nematic superconductivity could be realized by adjusting the pressure at which the variable density of states emerges, thereby facilitating the development of novel functional superconducting materials. Finally, our study indicates that van Hove singularities hold significant potential for expanding our understanding of superconductivity and electron-phonon coupling, thereby opening up new avenues for designing ultra-high-temperature superconductors and functional materials. Lastly, we acknowledge that our results can be extended to (H$_{2}$S)$$_{n}$ hydrides as the variable density of states is primarily governed by the sulfur atom. Fisher developed the fundamental concept averaging the size of genetic mutations to understand the stability of the genetic material. However, the underlying mathematics of this approach is suspect because it relies on an ill-defined statistical average. In statistics, this type of average is only legitimate in linear models, which requires the satisfaction of three distinct criteria. First, the parameter in question must be linear in the data. Second, the parameter must be unaffected by the specific measurements used. Third, the parameter must be consistent across different datasets. Fisher's average, known as the cross-reactivity parameter, fails to meet these criteria as it varies significantly with different types of mutations, even those closely related. Ultimately, our study refutes the reliability of Fisher's approach and provides an alternative metric that overcomes these limitations in both the traditional and modern models of molecular biology. This new metric draws upon the fundamental principles of Cramer-Rao variance, which estimates the overall accuracy of the protein target binding. Our work also extends to quantitative analysis, where the average effect can be utilized as a novel metric in assessing the overall linear relationship between the chemical activity of the ligand and the target protein. This linear relationship can further be applied to predictions in both retrospective and prospective scenarios. Our work offers a mathematical explanation for the apparent scale independence observed in molecular biology and provides an alternative metric that amplifies the significance of Fisher's original idea. Additionally, our findings bridge the gap between statistical mathematics and the underlying biology, where the average effect appears as a straightforward scale transformation that reflects both the accuracy and information content in the data. This view of the average effect also opens the door for novel applications in biochemistry and pharmacology. Finally, our work provides a unified mathematical understanding of the critical role played by scale in both statistical analysis and the molecular biology context. Our study demonstrates that Fisher's original idea, though flawed, holds a profound truth that reflects both the underlying biology and the statistical mathematics that were influenced by it. Our work offers a mathematical explanation for this phenomenon. Our study provides an objective mathematical interpretation of the apparent symbiotic relationship observed between statistical mathematics and molecular biology. Our work also offers a pathway for future researchers to utilize this insight in understanding the co-evolution of statistical mathematics and molecular biology. This post presents recent developments in our research on using modular robotic legs for space exploration. We have updated our leg design with improved actuation and control systems, modeled after a human ankle, and are utilizing these legs in a space-rover platform. Through simulated walking sessions, we have demonstrated the capability to walk using only one leg per step and have achieved successful field tests on a Quanser moving platform. Furthermore, we have successfully integrated a set of compact thrusters onto the rover, which have enhanced our walking patterns and allowed us to walk down slopes and adjust the rover's orientation. We are currently refining its control system. We anticipate that with further advancements, this configuration will enable efficient and robust motion on uneven and gradient surfaces. We believe the data collected in this project will be instrumental in the future development of autonomous space exploration. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel maps. A straightforward approach involving surfel feature matching and global optimization is combined with a machine-learning-based method for improved performance. A key challenge of visual relocalization is accurately determining the relative pose by minimizing both feature mismatch and geometric discrepancy. By generating surfel descriptors through a point-based neural network, we leverage both 2D-3D and 3D-3D relational cues to support localization. Furthermore, global optimization is applied to resample and refine feature tracks, incorporating a geometric error term to refine the estimation. Moreover, our method capitalizes on the existing 3D map for localization, and by generating a few frames ahead, it achieves more accurate results. Experimental findings on three datasets (Dataset1, Dataset2, and Dataset3) demonstrate our method's superiority over state-of-the-art approaches without additional 3D geometric information. Additionally, our method is robust against corrupted input and can localize even with a single RGBD frame as supplementary information. When personalization and semi-supervised learning techniques are combined with a federated approach to collaborative machine learning, differences in local datasets and parameters can produce significant model ambiguity after global parameter aggregation. This complexity makes it difficult for downstream tasks and can be an advantage for malicious users who can manipulate model ambiguity to interfere with the learning process. Addressing this issue, we introduce a novel measure of model ambiguity and propose a framework called Federated Semi-Supervised Learning with High Confidence Averaging (FSSLA). It guarantees both the minimization of model ambiguity and the protection of user privacy through the adoption of high-confidence averaging on local updates. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed approach, which outperforms existing baselines and is resilient to attacks. Additionally, the code for our methodology is available on GitHub at https://github.com/guipaul/FSML. Our study provides a framework for addressing ambiguity and attack-related issues in various federated learning applications. Moreover, it opens up the possibility of using similar attack-resistance techniques in other FL scenarios where model poisoning is a concern. Our findings suggest that high-confidence averaging can be a versatile tool for maintaining the reliability of FL systems. Extensive experiments have been conducted to validate the performance of the proposed approach using real-world FL environments such as computer vision and NLP. Our study is grounded in a theoretical analysis and is expected to contribute to the development of efficient and resilient FL systems. Furthermore, it paves the way for further research into using local trust metrics for distinguishing legitimate and malicious users in FL. Our work has potential applications in various FL domains beyond the ones used in this study. It could also be employed in scenarios involving data heterogeneity and distribution differences. For instance, it can be utilized in the federated learning process of multiple applications operating on mobile devices. Our findings are general and can be applied to scenarios with or without a central server. Additionally, our approach is adaptable to various FL use cases and can be easily integrated into existing FL systems as a layer on top. It generates local update confidence scores, which are then used for secure averaging at a trusted third-party server. Our study provides a framework for using confidence scores in FL to increase the reliability of the learning process. It opens up the possibility of employing other high-confidence averaging techniques in FL to enhance model robustness. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/guipaul/FSML. Our study has potential applications in various FL environments such as computer vision, NLP

The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing substantial mass outflow compared to the initial neutron star mass.  The generic behavior includes a high-entropy envelope formation around the black hole due to magnetic and non-magnetic mass outflows; this envelope's mass is highly sensitive to the neutron star's initial magnetic field strength.  The existence of a common understanding for the post-merger system can be identified only when the accretion rate exceeds a certain threshold; subsequently, a common trend of disk mass shrinkage along with thermal relaxation and disk cooling begins to emerge, influenced by a neutron star's initial mass and black hole mass.  The generic characteristics of a binary system in an equilibrium state include a radius for the accretion disk's inner boundary and a luminosity due to viscosity, electromagnetic forces, and particle annihilation; this equilibrium state remains unaffected by variations in configuration, but becomes evident only after a sufficiently long numerical simulation time.  The influence of a neutron star's initial magnetic field strength on disk mass and luminosity can be understood by considering the competition between magnetic mass outflow and disk cooling processes. For a compact Riemann surface $X$ of genus $g \geq 1$, we demonstrate that its Jacobian variety $J(X)$ possesses a twisted attribute, namely that the twisted form of an open subscheme $U \subset J(X)$, where the twisted form is denoted by $U^{(\lambda)}$, exhibits $3g-2$ connected components rather than the anticipated $1$ when the genus $g$ is greater than or equal to $4$. This phenomenon is valid for any divisor $\lambda$ of sufficiently large height on an even genus $g$ and for any divisor $\lambda$ on a odd genus $g \geq 1$ where the genus is not less than or equal to the square root of $8|\lambda|$. This discovery confirms conjectures put forth by Feigin and Scheithauer. Furthermore, we identify the necessary and sufficient condition for the connectedness of $U^{(\lambda)}$, establish a relationship with the Hecke algebra, demonstrate that the twisted form of an abelian variety is not isomorphic to the twisted form of its image under the map to its associated line bundle, and show that the general hybrid pure Eynard-Grassmannn nanopower does not possess the property of connectedness. Additionally, we show that the conditions of being non-separable, separable but not purely non-separable, and purely non-separable are all equivalent to the condition where the twisted form of an open subscheme $U \subset J(X)$ is isomorphic to the whole variety for a divisor $\lambda$ on a genus $g \geq 1$ where the genus is not less than or equal to the square root of $8|\lambda|$. This confirms another conjecture by Feigin and Scheithauer. Lastly, we show that the signature of the action of the 2-body Hecke algebra on the homology of the twisted form of a smooth curve of genus $g$ where the genus is not less than or equal to the square root of $8|\lambda|$ sign changes precisely $6g+1$ times. This discovery confirms another conjecture by Feigin and Scheithauer. This work is motivated by a question in the 2004 summer research announcement of the MIT PRISM Center for Geometry and Symmetry. This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near a graphene layer. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, we computed the optical force acting on each particle and derived equations to assess the influence of graphene's surface plasmons. Our findings demonstrate that the graphene's surface plasmons can trap particles at terahertz frequencies. Additionally, we found that the force holding the dimer together originates primarily from the radiation pressure generated by the particles' oscillations. Our research also demonstrates that the optical binding effect can be achieved using terahertz frequencies and identifies an optimal condition for this phenomenon: when the particles have matching natural frequencies. Furthermore, we found that the binding effect can be either attractive or repulsive, depending on the particles' relative positions. Lastly, we found that our theoretical model can be experimentally realized using a substrate with a hole and an appropriate terahertz source. Our research lays the groundwork for exploring the optical binding effect at terahertz frequencies. Moreover, our study identifies potential applications for graphene in trapping particles. Lastly, our research paves the way for further investigation into the optical binding effect at even higher frequencies. Motivated by the importance of predicting ambulance arrival times to optimize emergency department operations, we've developed average reaction curves for treatment durations in the emergency department. By averaging the time it takes for each patient to be treated after arriving at the emergency department, we've created a dynamic model that accounts for evolving arrival patterns. Our proposed model utilizes a linear quadratic recurrent equation to represent the average treatment time, and we've also derived a convergence condition based on the sufficient condition for the optimal policy found in Li et al. (2021). By applying the average treatment time model, we've developed a dynamic programming solution that considers a finite number of arrival groups, and we've further extended our approach to a special case of a Poisson arrival process. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed solution, and we've used empirical data from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to calibrate and evaluate our average reaction curves. Specifically, we've calculated the optimal policy for the UCLA emergency department based on historical data, and we've compared its performance with and without our proposed solution. Our findings show that using our average reaction curves improves the emergency department's performance compared to not utilizing them. In cooperative systems, performing multiple tasks simultaneously is crucial for efficient execution, and implementing it strategically can significantly impact performance. This study explores the concept of multi-task synchronization, introducing a protocol that allows independent agents to synchronize their strategies through minimal interaction. These agents have restricted capabilities for processing and communicating information, such as robots on a grid network, and the proposed protocol is proven to be globally applicable and computationally efficient. The issue of scheduling a multi-point robotic manipulator over time is a combinatorial optimization problem with vast potential applications in simulation and real-world scenarios, primarily in domains like e-commerce automation and industrial processes. Given the exponential growth of the problem's solution space, conventional techniques such as sequence optimization and reinforcement learning struggle to tackle it effectively. To improve outcomes, we propose a novel greedy grouping method that leverages domain expertise and heuristics to break down the problem into more manageable parts. The proposed algorithm outperforms benchmark solutions using comprehensive numerical case studies. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of our solution through successful experimentation using a three-ARM manipulator in an autonomous e-commerce warehouse setting. Our findings show that the greedy grouping approach significantly enhances solution quality while reducing computational complexity compared to existing high-fidelity methods. The worst-case computational complexity of our greedy grouping method is on the order of $O(NN^2/\log N)$ and is comparable to some of the existing high-fidelity methods on the order of $O(N^{3/2}}$ for large values of $N$. The performance of the interface between semiconductors and barriers is a crucial factor in producing consistent, high-quality quantum dots essential for reliable quantum information processing. This research investigates the characteristics of undoped Si substrates by measuring the Hall mobility of SiMOSFETs manufactured using a standard 300mm CMOS process. A detailed analysis is conducted to identify the dominant sources of resistance at various temperatures and explore ways to enhance the Hall mobility. Additionally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy is used to examine the composition of the SiMOSFET surface, and a correlation is found between surface contamination and Hall mobility as measured by four-point probe techniques. A significant improvement in Hall mobility has been observed after a light chemical clean and a dry etch to remove a 300nm thick SiO2 layer and 10nm of the upper Si surface, respectively. Ultimately, Hall mobility values of up to 14,600 cm^2/Vs have been achieved, exceeding previously reported results by a factor of twofold. When working in a group on a task, such as solving a math problem, individuals with different backgrounds may have varying understandings of key terms. Despite these differences, which can lead to conflicting working groups, research has shown that in many cases, individuals with disparate expertise can productively interact. We have discovered that the effectiveness of group interactions is influenced not only by their previous experience working together, but also by the nature of within-group connections among team members. Within the context of a teacher-mediated classroom, where students with shared knowledge goals occasionally experience communication issues due to their varying knowledge, we have observed two primary student connection types: "bridging" (connecting students with related knowledge) and "harmonious" (linking students with similar levels of knowledge). Findings have revealed that in many cases, within-group harmony can greatly impact group performance, often outweighing the benefits gained from interactions with externally diverse groups. Ultimately, we have learned that the success of group learning environments depends on a combination of effective connections both within and outside of the group. These findings have been further visualized using a network representation of student interactions in an 8th-grade math class. Video search platforms struggle with variety bias, a problem where search results fail to include sufficient diversity due to the biases of users and systems. Our research tackles this issue by exploring the phenomenon through the eyes of users, particularly those from different genders. We've found that, similar to existing biases, gender influences the type of video search outcomes, leading to a shortage of non-binary, trans, and lesbian content. To address this challenge, we've developed a method that assesses variety bias from a user perspective, incorporating an auditing technique which utilizes virtual user agents to gauge the disparity in video search results between diverse groups. This approach enables the calculation of a fairness metric, specifically the Group Similarity Ratio (GSR), which reflects the similarity in search outcomes between user groups, ultimately guiding the system to uncover its underlying biases. In experiments, our proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting variety bias under both real-world and synthetic settings, and reveals that the bias can also be found in results that meet traditional relevance standards. Moreover, our method enables the system to generate unbiased results comparable to those found by actual users with similar preferences. The findings of our study open up new avenues for research in information retrieval, specifically in the area of diversity and fairness. Additionally, the variety bias affects not only video search but any application that displays results, potentially influencing users' perceptions and the overall user experience. The results of our audit can also be found on a publicly available website: https://variedaudits.github.io/. Finally, the GSR metric has been incorporated into the IR-benchmark repository as a pre-built auditor. The repository can be accessed at https://github.com/UsmanMohamed/IR-benchmark. This research introduces a novel resource allocation scheme, known as OBD, to optimize information and power transfer in multi-service SWIPT networks with multiple users and modes of operation. The proposed scheme is designed to maximize the network sum-throughput by allocating optimal power and modes to users under constraints, including limited power for receivers, power beamforming, and fast and slow time division multiple access. In strongly repulsive Fermi gases with at least two components, generalized theories fail to accurately predict the behavior in the large-N limit.  In the large-N limit, generalized theories break down due to an intractable fermion cloud in the vicinity of a single high-density quark. Because the thickness of this cloud is on the order of N, it cannot be ignored. In order to improve upon existing theories, a novel method utilizing a self-consistent potential derived from a quantum field model is presented. Multivariate data that change over space or time can be analyzed using Gaussian processes, and graph-based models help identify dependencies within this data. We examine two specific models - graphical Gaussian processes and functional Gaussian graphical models - that enable the representation of functional data using graphs. The latter model uses a prescribed function space, whereas the former relies on a stochastic process whose realizations form a Gaussian distribution. Our findings reveal that the functional Gaussian graphical model reduces to a graphical Gaussian process only under certain conditions. Furthermore, we develop methods to estimate the model parameters through likelihood maximization and demonstrate the performance of these methods in a simulation study. Our approach also provides a novel method for time-series data imputation. The proposed methods will be incorporated into the R package fieldGaussianGraphicalModels.

Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize quantum programs to match the hardware's capabilities. These optimized
programs are typically based on a sequence of repeated gate patterns that suit
the processor's gate cycle. Currently, the best method to generate such patterns
involves heuristic search techniques which don't guarantee the optimal solution.
This study introduces two new methods to efficiently compile quantum programs with
repeated gate patterns in scalable quantum processors. These methods guarantee the
best possible outcome. The first method identifies the most suitable pattern in a
given program and applies it uniformly across the circuit. The second method
combines smaller, uniformly arranged patterns to cover the entire program.
Both methods consider the costs of the patterns and ensure they match the hardware
cycle. The introduction of these algorithms enables optimal program compilation in
a scalable quantum processor without the need for approximate methods. The new
algorithms perform well even with a large number of gates and provide significant
improvements in program compilation time. The source code for these algorithms is
also available on the MIT Quantum Development group's GitHub repository. At this
point, we haven't performed experiments with real quantum data but have instead
used random programs with a specified number of gates to evaluate our algorithms.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves multiple techniques working in tandem.  While "preconditioned conjugate gradient" (PCG) is typically used for this purpose, research suggests that a post-iteration residual check could indicate whether the iterative process has reached its optimal point of termination.  Specifically, if the residual magnitude is reduced to a value less than a user-specified tolerance ($\mathtt{TOL}$) within each IPM inner iteration, the linear solver can be halted and the solution considered sufficient.  This study demonstrates that, under certain conditions, such an early termination condition (ETC) is both necessary and sufficient for ensuring optimal IPM performance.  Our findings also reveal that standard ETC practices in conjunction with PCG often result in suboptimal performance.  PCG is typically used in an ad-hoc manner with respect to ET, with many codes simply employing a fixed tolerance or "small but non-zero" residual criterion.  In order to take full advantage of Krylov solvers, a better understanding of their interplay with solvers and halting conditions is required.  Two new solvers have been developed, with the first based on an iterative refinement loop combining Krylov solvers and outer Bunch-Parlett updates.  The second combines an ET-conforming polynomial iterative refinement (PIR) approach with the BQP algorithm.  The proposed solvers have been successfully tested within an IPM framework and against robust commercial software solvers, with the performance enhanced by a significant reduction in overall computational operations.  Our numerical experiments further indicate that early termination, coupled with inexact linear equation solving within inner iterations, can even outperform the conventional benchmark in interior point methods (IPM) and also excel against robust commercial software solvers.  The enhanced algorithms were also found to extend the domain of convergence for certain problems.  The research provides a theoretical justification for prematurely terminating iterative solvers within inner iterations of interior point methods (IPMs) based on early termination conditions, which is hypothesized to be particularly beneficial in iterative precision methods.  The study introduces two refined algorithms: an inexact variant of the outside-inside Bunch Parlett algorithm and an inexact variant of the inside-outside Bunch Parlett algorithm, with these algorithms indicating that interior point methods (IPMs) based on early termination conditions can be more robust than their conventional counterparts and also outperform commercial software solvers.

The practical application of the Renormalization Group (RG) to complex problems like Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) faces difficulties due to its abstract nature.  A new, more tangible approach is proposed that maintains the core principles of RG, but presents it in a format similar to Gradient Descent (GD).  This framework is based on a novel loss function and its associated flows, which are driven by artificial neural networks.  By utilizing this concept, the traditional RG equations can be replaced with a straightforward optimization process.  Furthermore, this approach is adaptable to various RG strategies and can be used to solve problems beyond DNN training.  Its effectiveness is demonstrated through an experimental evaluation of the RG's application to DNNs.  Unlike conventional RG methods, this framework is accessible to researchers who are new to the subject and offers a more collaborative approach to addressing complex problems.  Importantly, it facilitates the exploration of the RG's application to DNNs.  The proposed approach is called RGFlow.  Additionally, a complementary method called RGForce, which is inspired by the Optimizer's acceleration techniques, is presented as an alternative strategy to further accelerate the optimization process.  The proposed methods are dubbed Flow and Force.  The theoretical framework consists of three key components:  The RGFlows, which are driven by artificial neural networks to define the loss function and its associated flows;  The Acceleration, which provides a means to adapt these flows and accelerate the optimization process;  and The Optimality Conditions, which provide a means to revert to the optimal RGflows.  The proposed framework consists of three key components:  The Flow Optimality Theorem, which establishes the relationship between the optimality conditions and the acceleration;  and The RGFlow and RGForce algorithms, which are grounded on the theoretical framework.  The proposed framework consists of three key components:  The Formulation, which is based on the theoretical framework;  The Experimental Evaluation, where the efficacy of the RGFlow algorithm is tested through numerous experiments;  and The Analysis, where the results of the experiments are examined and the findings are discussed.  The key components of the theoretical framework are:  The RGFlows, which are driven by artificial neural networks to define the loss function and its associated flows;  The RGFlow algorithm, which is based on the theoretical framework;  and The RGForce algorithm, which is inspired by the Optimizer's acceleration techniques and provides a means to adapt these flows and accelerate the optimization process. This research paper focuses on observing the behavior of process descriptions generated from pairs of Petri net models, one for each normal and exceptional scenario. The primary goal is to identify violations that may arise when an exceptional situation occurs normally. To accomplish this, we develop a method for expressing the interplay between these two Petri net models as a single, composite model. Then, we create a monitoring automaton for this new model, which enables us to detect potential conflicts and anomalies during process execution. The proposed approach is evaluated through a practical case study related to business process modeling. The study demonstrates the monitoring automaton's capability to express the monitored strategy and identify conflicts and anomalies, with an analytic method available to verify the effectiveness of the monitoring automaton and the complexity of the resulting algebraic expression. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm to solve anomalies in hybrid process models and illustrate its application in a practical example. The results of this research are substantiated by a theoretical comparison with existing methods. The proposed methodology is validated by an experimental evaluation involving the BPMN 2.0 Process Model. The findings of this research are presented at the BPM 2022 conference. This research offers an innovative monitoring approach with the potential to manage conflicts and anomalies during process execution, providing an effective monitoring strategy and verifying the validity of the monitoring automaton, solving anomalies, and demonstrating better results compared to existing methods through a practical comparison. The primary tool used to support this research is the ProMoA tool, which allows us to generate a monitoring automaton for a given process model and monitor conflicts and anomalies, with an alternative method available through the analysis of the Petri net structure. The proposed approach is compatible with process algebra languages, such as YAWL and BPEL, and the BPMN 2.0 Process Model used in the practical evaluation. The source code for this research is available on GitHub. The proposed methodology contributes to process analytics by introducing an innovative monitoring approach with the potential to manage conflicts and anomalies during process execution. The core idea of this research can be applied to other areas, including (but not limited to) process mining and declarative process automation. The proposed approach is compatible with existing process modeling languages and can be extended with additional monitoring techniques. The source code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. The following specifications define the semantics of Quipner, the C version, and Netner, the.NET version, by translating their respective abstract machines into a standard quantum circuit model. Due to the inherent machine-specific details, a direct and straightforward translation was not possible. Consequently, we introduced 'proto-quipper-m' as a higher-level language, eliminating the machine-specific code by incorporating type classes for circuit gates, states, and superpositions. Subsequently, we defined the abstract machines for the two languages as well as the quantum circuit model by interpreting the 'proto-quipper-m' type system. Ultimately, we demonstrated that the machines are correct by showing their equivalence to the standard quantum circuit model, specifically by using a 'proto-quipper-m' compiler for the domain-specific language 'quipper'. The work described in this paper has been successfully implemented and tested using NetGener, a tool that generates the machine code for a given quantum circuit. Lastly, the research drew on existing knowledge of quantum circuit logic and Haskell-type functional programming. We suggest creating bosonic pairs using large numbers of optical photons interacting with ensemble of dipoles with long-lived moments, employing a cavity. This approach, headquartered in Linblad master equation, uses the thermodynamic weak coupling limit and relies on two parameters: a pure loss rate for the cavity and a two-body cooperative decay rate for the dipoles. By optimizing this parameter setup, we demonstrate the production of bosonic pairs at the optimal point for detecting macroscopic light states and observe the generation of entangled states with sinusoidal patterns. Furthermore, we propose an experiment-based framework for the implementation and analysis of this idea, incorporating a setup with dipoles, a driver laser, and detection systems, and outline a method for extracting key components of the state through squeeze-root and square-root operations. This technique enables the characterization of the ensemble's state and allows for its application in enhanced optical phase measurements. We estimate that in an experimental setup with 10^5 to 10^6 dipoles, we can achieve enhanced precision in optical phase measurements compared to current record holders by two orders of magnitude with 80% efficiency. This design has the advantage of lower driver power and fast data readout for detecting macroscopic states. In particular, we demonstrate the potential for our design to outperform current ensemble-based interferometers by making a predictive calculation of experimental outcomes under realistic conditions. This procedure could also serve as a starting point for future development of precision measurements in a wide array of ensemble-based quantum information applications. Following this, we discuss the relevant time scales for the state preparation and show the prospects for the extension of our scheme to numerous other quantum information applications. Lastly, we outline the significant benefits and potential pathways for enhancing the efficiency and performance of this design as well as other ensemble-based interferometers through the use of nearly coherent two-photon states. This could involve hybridization of traditional linear interferometry with the novel features of bound photon states, perhaps with the aid of a mirror. This has the potential to enlarge the currently existing separation between coherent states and number states, thereby expanding the range within which states are sufficiently coherent to enable precise phase measurements. This could lead to major advancements in future research on ensemble-based quantum information applications. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to create continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are concatenated to produce the complete genome, achieving up to 80% efficiency across 128 nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and speed, paving the way for the efficient assembly of large genomes. Parameters such as genome size, number of nodes, and sequence length were extensively examined to analyze the performance variability. Additionally, the code has been evaluated for its responsiveness, readability, and maintainability using the Metrics for Evaluating Scientific Software standard to ensure high-quality code and effective utilization of computational resources. Our solution to this problem involves proposing a new depth measure that combines the idea of isometric log-ratio with the characteristics of multivariate data. This method extends the concept of depth to functional data, allowing us to recognize that the structure of multivariate data like spike train, network data, or galaxy distributions inherently contains information about the multivariate data's depth. Through our Isometric Log-Ratio adaptation, the multivariate data can be transformed into a univariate representation, making it possible to apply the concept of depth to multivariate data. Our technique achieves this by applying the bivariate extension of depth to individual elements within the multivariate data. These examples showcase our depth measure's ability to effectively analyze various types of multivariate data and extract meaningful insights from the resulting data universes. We've developed a hybrid quantum machine based on superconducting quantum circuits that's similar to the Lincoln-Paulus box game. In this setup, two classical operators and two quantum operators work together to move information around. By optimizing performance using feedback from real-world experiments, we've refined the machine's components and demonstrated the efficient creation of entangled qubits. This hybrid device now serves as an ideal model for understanding how measurement outcomes are influenced by past decisions, particularly in quantum systems. Moreover, we've successfully applied this hybrid model in a task known as quantum learning. Furthermore, we've observed that the dynamics of this hybrid device can be effectively described using the 'quantum process tensor' technique, which enables the precise quantification of entanglement and other quantum processes throughout the device's entire chain. This allows for the precise quantification of entanglement and other quantum processes throughout the entire device. Finally, we've explored the boundaries of the hybrid device by examining the entanglement of multiple qubits as they pass through it and found that their entanglement actually increases as they move through it. This is unusual because we typically expect entanglement to decrease or remain the same as information becomes less organized. This unexpected behavior was observed consistently across various experiments and holds significant theoretical importance. These breakthroughs open up the door for further research into the underlying mechanics of quantum information and its potential applications. Radioactive beam experiments were conducted at RIKEN for the production of $^{58,62}$Ge isotopes through the transfer of neutrons from a $^{76}$Ge beam at an energy of 230 MeV.  The nuclear properties of these isotopes as evidenced by their yields, reaction cross sections, and excitation functions, suggest that $^{62}$Ge has an unusual dipole band at 2023 keV, indicating a unique structural feature.  The rotational characteristics of $^{62}$Ge were found to be similar to that of $^{44}$Ca, implying a soft $N$ = 40 core.  The angular distribution of direct neutron transfer reactions revealed that $^{62}$Ge has a positive two-neutron halo configuration, whereas $^{58}$Ge was found to have a stable core and minor two-neutron halo feature.  Various theoretical models were employed to explain the experimental results and the underlying nuclear interactions.  The study of these even-even isotopes provides valuable insight into the symmetry and deformation properties of nuclear matter near the $N$ = 40 subshell closure.  The research also sheds light on the unusual structural features exhibited by $^{62}$Ge and the diverse range of nuclear properties demonstrated by the germanium isotopes.  The investigation further underscores the significance of focusing on the region around $N$ = 40 in exploring novel quantum phase transitions in nuclear matter.  The study also opened up opportunities for conducting similar experiments in other nuclear systems using the RIB facility at RIKEN.  The research will be utilized to develop new theoretical frameworks to explain the diverse range of nuclear properties and the unique structural features exhibited by the region around $N$ = 40.  The investigation provides a valuable connection between the research in exotic nuclei and the existing studies of stable nuclear systems. The Tevatron Run II has already commenced, where the Fermilab Collider will generate a large dataset consisting of $p\bar{p}$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV. In the context of heavy particle production, top quark creation is of particular interest due to its relevance in two scales - the large mass of the top quark and the soft interaction components of the final state. As a new step in hadronic particle collisions, the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus encounters represents a significant area of investigation. This article will provide a theoretical examination of detecting top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions, focusing on the observable characteristics and cross-sectional values for the processes $p+A \to t+\bar{t} + X$ and $p+A \to t+j+X$. The analysis will also consider the influence of non-collisional effects on the $t$-quark transverse momentum spectrum. It is anticipated that the $t$-quark will be identified through the identification of its leptonic decay products, namely the charged lepton and the truncated $b$-jet, where the $b$-quark is stopped in the detector's rear end. The determination of the $t$-quark $p_T$ will be crucial in assessing the role of non-collisional effects, particularly if the $t$-quark is identified when it is completely outside the detector's range. The calculation of the $t$-quark $p_T$ distribution in proton-nucleus collisions will be performed using the next-to-leading order parton matrix elements via the CTEQ5M parton distribution functions and the inclusion of nuclear effects in the parton densities, where the impact of non-collisional effects will be evaluated for various nuclear parameters and scales. Furthermore, the influence of non-collisional effects on top quark production will be compared with their impact on dijet production, where top quark production can be identified through the $b$-jet richness of the selected events. Ultimately, the detection of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions will provide a new standard for testing the concepts of nuclear parton distribution functions and non-collisional effects at high-energy particle colliders. The outcome of this research will offer a fresh perspective on the non-Abelian gluon contribution to heavy quark production and will provide a valuable benchmark to compare with the experimental outcomes of the LHC Collider system

The auxiliary task drives codebook learning and enhances model performance through cross-domain reinforcement learning. Experimental results demonstrate that our auxiliary task significantly improves the translation performance, surpassing codebook-based models. Moreover, our end-to-end model exhibits superior robustness and adaptability in various cross-domain translations, outperforming previous models. Notably, our auxiliary task allows the model to generalize better to unseen database queries. To validate our model's effectiveness, we employed a diverse set of Google Spanner database schemas in our experiments. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to nondifferentiability. Building on the successful application of adaptive sieving in the Lasso problem, we propose an adaptive-sieving-based algorithm, ASP-SDL, for solving the HDR Lasso. The proposed method incorporates a novel sparsity-enforcing heuristic that takes into account the nonconvex nature of the problem, resulting in substantial performance improvements over existing methods, as evidenced by our numerical experiments using real-world and simulated datasets. Additionally, the ASP-SDL algorithm has been rigorously tested and validated in various applications, including gene selection using microarray data and signal classification. Notably, the results obtained are comparable to those of state-of-the-art algorithms such as SPG and COCONUT, while outperforming them in certain instances. The proposed algorithm is comprised of two primary components: adaptive sieving and a modified loss function that leverages the properties of Wilcoxon scores, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in computational complexity and a more efficient solution to the HDR Lasso problem. The code for this project has been publicly released on GitHub for the benefit of other researchers and practitioners. Furthermore, our findings are complemented by an extensive tutorial that demonstrates how to classify synthetic data using the HDR Lasso. Specifically, the tutorial employs the ASP-SDL algorithm to resolve a signal classification problem within the context of the Berkeley Growth Study. The associated data can be downloaded from the Open Access Server. Lastly, we provide a detailed response to address inquiries about our work. Key details include an explanation of how the inner problem is formulated, why the outer loop requires nondifferentiable optimization, and how the choice of Wilcoxon scores in the loss function aids method performance. Additionally, we outline the general approach to formulating modified loss functions for various score functions. The proposed HDR Lasso algorithm utilizes adaptive sieving and demonstrates superior performance compared to other methods, ultimately providing an efficient solution to the HDR Lasso problem. There are two primary approaches to analyzing the thermodynamic consequences of a system's initial state and its rapid transformation. The first method relies on the asymptotic entropy change formula, which determines the ultimate boundary of a system's entropy variation following a rapid change. This formula validates the second law of thermodynamics under such scenarios but fails to provide information about the system's transitional path or its temporal entropy generation rate. In contrast, our research focuses on developing a detailed, temporally-dependent approach for calculating entropy generation in systems undergoing rapid transformations. This method is based on the thermodynamic system's infinitesimal geometric characteristics and yields a convex entropy generation rate for systems with this property. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the relationship between the asymptotic entropy change formula and the system's infinitesimal geometric characteristics. This relationship confirms that the asymptotic entropy change formula represents the minimum entropy variation boundary and that the system's convex entropy generation rate is directly related to its public resource cost. Finally, our research showcases the convolution theorem-based temporal entropy generation rate formula for optimal free energy extraction, thereby substantiating the optimality of maximum work principles. This research is anticipated to facilitate a deeper understanding of the thermodynamic consequences of rapid transformations and to develop novel methods for calculating entropy generation and optimal work potential. Additionally, our research may be generalized to describe the thermodynamic behavior of small systems by incorporating dispersion into our approach. This generalized research is expected to be a crucial component in the development of future thermodynamic theories for small systems. Those interested in this topic can find a detailed discussion in Section 7 of the paper. This discussion reveals how our research aligns with the fundamental principles of quantum thermodynamics and reveals new perspectives on entropy change asymptotics, public resource cost, and optimal work potential. These perspectives are rooted in the infinitesimal geometric characteristics of quantum states and transitions. This research is expected to provide fresh insights into the world of quantum thermodynamics. Please see our related work in arXiv:2106.11384 and arXiv:1808.11233 for more information.
