The surge in social media posts and online comments from public figures and celebrities has led to an explosive growth in unfalsifiable statements that are difficult to verify. While such statements may lack concrete evidence, they continue to spread rapidly across platforms, capturing the attention of many users. In this context, we aim to address a novel query: given uncompromising statements from authorities, can we identify a underlying framework that might support their claims? Frameworks like magic realism or realist surrealism can contextualize unfounded claims in a coherent manner. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a framework that encompasses two key components: (a) extracting the underlying worldview from a set of unfalsifiable statements and (b) utilizing the generated worldview to craft a plausible narrative. Our approach is grounded in graph representation learning, utilizing the structure of the statements themselves, and is aided by an auxiliary graph that captures the broader thematic connections among statements. Through human evaluation, we establish that our method demonstrates a strong correlation with human-generated worldviews, and can even be utilized for generating engaging, Surrealistic narratives. Our work and data are openly available at https://github.com/jamestaylor/unfalsifiable_framework. Surprising research findings may require unconventional perspectives, and our study represents a pioneering effort in that realm, as well as an actionable strategy with practical applications. It can assist in framing the excessive statements made by influential figures and build a coherent worldview, empowering users to make informed decisions when interacting with such content. Additionally, our framework may be adapted for identifying and addressing disinformation campaigns and propaganda spread by nations or organizations. By generating compelling narratives centered around unfalsifiable claims and coherent worldviews, we reveal a potential link between the dissemination of such content and deliberate information manipulation. In particular, our study connects the surge in unfalsifiable statements to the controlled spread of surrealistic narratives, specifically. It is noteworthy that the underlying structures driving the unfalsifiable statements made by public figures and the extensive themes among those statements are distinct and separate. Moreover, our framework provides a novel approach for uncovering the underlying structures and can provide user-centric engagement by presenting statements within a coherent narrative context, as opposed to presenting them in an unsorted, unverified manner. Ultimately, our work is centered around developing a method for constructing a coherent narrative from the structure of unfalsifiable statements made by influential individuals, and we believe that such an approach carries implications for content creation and dissemination, particularly in situations driven by information manipulation. Identifying social media incidents in real-time is crucial for timely incident detection, accurate prediction, and subsequent prevention.  However, detecting social media incidents is a complex task due to the vast amount of data, rapid posting rates, and evolving incidents requiring constant update.  To address this, we have developed an innovative approach for real-time incident detection on a large scale of social media data.  Our solution employs a dynamic query system that filters out non-relevant posts and accurately identifies incidents on a minute-by-minute basis.  To optimize performance, we have incorporated data caching and efficient data normalization, enabling the detection of incidents spanning multiple minutes.  Additionally, we have proposed two distinct incident detection algorithms, one algorithm leveraging geographic data and another algorithm utilizing temporal data, allowing for flexible incident identification options.  To validate our solution, we conducted an in-depth analysis on Twitter data relating to traffic incidents and successfully detected 98.5% of actual traffic incidents with up to 4 minutes prior knowledge, achieving a recall rate of 0.985 and precision rate of 0.962, achieving state-of-the-art performance.  Our solution is adaptable and can be applied to detect social media incidents globally.  Our future work will incorporate multi-language support and incorporate graphic data from maps to further enhance incident detection precision. New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum as an optimal estimator of angular bispectrum amplitude in extracting non-Gaussian information on both galaxy bias and cosmological parameters, achieved by analyzing bispectra derived from galaxies and CMB lensing data simultaneously, resulting in significantly faster computation times of up to 50 times. We find combining the CMB and galaxies bispectra provides a more robust bias estimation than either alone. We explore four approaches to estimate skew-spectra, with some methods optimizing computational speed. We use cosmological simulations to determine the requirements for sufficient signal-to-noise ratio in the cross-correlation bispectra between CMB and galaxies to accurately constrain bias and cosmological parameters, requiring high-precision measurements of the primordial non-Gaussianity parameter of $f_{NL} \sim 5$ in the range of $k \sim 0.1-1h/Mpc$ wavenumbers. We establish the potential for $f_{NL}$ constraints from the CMB$\times$LSS signal to improve significantly with future data, reaching a precision of $\sigma(f_{NL})\sim 0.5$ in a scenario with high-precision measurements. We further propose an innovative approach, the Minimal Linear Model, for analyzing the CMB$\times$LSS signal that facilitates accurate cross-correlation bispectrum amplitude constraints with minimal assumptions on cosmology and galaxy bias, indicating a potential $f_{NL}$ constraint precision of $\sigma(f_{NL})\sim 0.6$ with future data. We demonstrate the CMB$\times$LSS signal holds considerable analytical potential for investigating cosmological parameters, bias, and non-Gaussianity with multifaceted, future data sets. We provide the Python code for the CMB$\times$LSS analysis at https://github.com/Esplussky/SkewingTheCMB. We present novel, meaningful constraints on galaxy bias and cosmological parameters, including $f_{NL}$, that were previously unattainable due to computational limitations. We establish the significance of properly accounting for CMB lensing contributions in the galaxy bias cross-correlation analysis. We explore novel, promising methods for estimating bias and cosmological parameters using CMB$\times$LSS signal with future data. We examine several estimation techniques for the weighted skew-spectrum based on CMB$\times$LSS data.

Recent studies have explored adversarial robustness in machine learning models, but current methods are often too broad and fail to account for legitimate data. A novel approach utilizes Bayesian learning to provide verifiable adversarial resistance by establishing a predictive confidence interval within a ball surrounding the input. By integrating an adversarial detector into Bayesian learning, we develop "RobustBayes", a comprehensive framework that combines learning and detection. Through theoretical analysis and experiments, we demonstrate that RobustBayes effectively protects Bayesian classifiers and regressions from both adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution scenarios. The theoretical findings are supported by practical applications, showcasing RobustBayes' efficacy in real-world scenarios and its potential to establish a new benchmark for adversarial resistance. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation in China and developed an experimental metric to assess the impact of online news. Utilizing crawler technology, we collected COVID-19 related rumors from major Chinese platforms, including Sina Weibo, Tencent News, and YOYO Ranking. Analyzing the data, we identified the sources and propagation paths of these rumors and estimated their influence spread. Results revealed that most rumors spread rapidly across social media but ultimately remained local, with a small fraction spreading nationally. Interestingly, news originating from reputable sources like Xinhua and regional government accounts had a significantly broader influence reach compared to that of regular users. Our findings should facilitate the development of algorithms aimed at detecting and suppressing online rumors and provide insights for creating news dissemination platforms and social media administrators striving to control rumor spread. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications and challenges of our approach under two scenarios: the first focusing on minimizing the spread radius of rumors and the second aiming to maximize the propagation distance of trustworthy news. It is noteworthy that our analysis was conducted in China's two-dimensional social media landscape and the effectiveness of our approach may vary across different countries and regions. To expand our research, we propose an open challenge, namely the Spread-Influence Challenge (SPIC), to quantify rumor spread and encourage algorithmic innovations. Detailed challenge guidelines are available on our website at https://github.com/Spread-Influence-Challenge/Challenge.git. SPIC follows the principles outlined in the problem definition and the challenge rules, with a special section detailing the challenge architecture. Our source code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Spread-Influence-Challenge/Code.git. Our empirical and theoretical results show that this compression significantly reduces the size of the model, but at the cost of substantially lowering its accuracy. From a theoretical standpoint, we prove that the error rate of the compressed model increases exponentially with the model's depth. This finding is confirmed by our empirical research, which also explores various methods for adjusting the model's parameters during the compression process. Our experiments involve both BERT and RoBERTa models, and examine the impact of different hyperparameters on the compressed model's performance. Interestingly, we discovered that the best hyperparameters for the best possible accuracy are actually those that maximize the model's parameters during the compression process. However, these optimal hyperparameters do not necessarily lead to a practical or efficient compression of the model. Additionally, we found that dynamic weight scaling, a method for adjusting the model's weights during the compression process, outperforms other methods in terms of the model's accuracy under equal parameter constraints. Furthermore, we observed that the effect of dynamic weight scaling on the model's performance improves over time, particularly in tasks where the model is trained on a limited number of examples. Finally, we found that the compressed models typically achieve better results in few-shot learning scenarios than traditional fine-tuning approaches. Interestingly, this advantage is particularly evident in tasks where the model is trained on very few examples. Nonetheless, our experiments also reveal some instances where traditional fine-tuning significantly outperforms the compressed models. Finally, we noted that the best hyperparameters for the best possible performance in a specific task are actually those that lead to a model that excels in that task but performs poorly in other tasks. As a result, the choice of hyperparameters depends on the specific requirements of the task at hand, making the design of a well-informed and task-specific compression of pre-trained language models a daunting and challenging task. To address this difficulty, we propose a series of regularization techniques, including one that produces compressed models with high accuracy under both parameter and computational constraints, which perform as well as the original model and significantly outperform models with other types of regularization. Additionally, we observed that the effect of batch norm regularization is negligible in the compressed models and do not consider it further in this work. On the other hand, we found that spike-and-skip regularization, which involves selectively skipping certain layers or neurons of the model during training, yields the best results. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is based on a quantum mechanics-based model that efficiently predicts the chemical shift values of amide proton nitrogen, thereby enhancing the resolution of NOE constraints and identifying the complete protein structure with high precision. ProCS predictions have been successfully integrated with experimental data, revealing the potential for the method to refine protein structures and verify incorrect assumptions in protein modeling. ProCS's effectiveness has been demonstrated using a set of 30 experimentally determined G-protein coupled receptor structures from the Protein Data Bank. In our study, ProCS predictions for a representative sample of 9 proteins resulted in an average overall root mean square deviation of 1.03 Angstroms. Additionally, ProCS predictions for a second representative sample of 9 proteins enabled the enhancement of the overall protein g-factor, a measure of correctness, by as much as 10-fold. ProCS predictions for a third representative sample of 9 proteins revealed potentially incorrect spatial arrangements in 6 out of 9 proteins. Our study also uncovered a range of errors in the 30 protein structures examined. These errors were characterized as significant (greater than 2 Angstroms) and affected both loop regions and key components of the GPCR structure. Our analysis suggests the method could serve as a general tool for refining protein structures and verifying the correctness of a wide range of protein models. The quantum-based ProCS method has been used to create a website where the results of each protein structure in the Protein Data Bank can be viewed and the effect of refining the chemical shift values on the overall protein structure be examined. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a crucial decision due to its significant impact on the model's behavior during training. Yet, there's a notable absence of a systematic approach to guiding this choice. One fundamental problem arises when researchers attempt to generalize from a task to a broader category, such as moving from a supervised to a semi-supervised setting. A widely adopted loss function for supervised learning, cross-entropy, yields undesirable outcomes in the semi-supervised context. A common reason provided for this phenomenon is the loss function's alignment with the optimal risk and its influence on prediction accuracy. However, this reason oversimplifies the issue and doesn't fully explain the phenomenon. Our study demonstrates that the challenge is rooted in the loss function's optimal allocation of confidence across classes, particularly when working with a small quantity of labeled data in a semi-supervised setting. We introduce an efficient, simple technique known as label cost, a notion closely related to confidence, and utilize it to analyze and compare loss functions. Our findings reveal that, in semi-supervised learning scenarios, it is essential to prioritize correct classifications over accurate predictions. Based on these observations, we develop a systematic approach to assessing loss functions and our research specifically that the cross-entropy loss is inadequate for semi-supervised tasks. We also introduce an improved, adapted version of the cross-entropy loss, SE-CE, and show that it yields better results than the original cross-entropy loss and many alternative loss functions in a wide range of scenarios. Furthermore, our study is the first to generalize from a single task to a whole family of tasks, the classification category, and our research demonstrates that the choice of loss function is not inherently fixed and can be evolved to accommodate different data regimes during training. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current methods used to study the phenomenon are limited by various approximations that can influence their accuracy. A more reliable approach employs a linearized density-functional framework combined with many-body perturbation theory to analyze the interaction between electron-hole pairs and their influence on the system's properties. When applied to the two-dimensional semimetal TiSe2, the method allows researchers to derive the excitonic potential, evaluate the impact of electron-hole pairs on the lattice, and estimate the resulting structural changes to the crystal lattice. Our findings on TiSe2 confirm that electron-hole pairs play a significant role in the phenomenon of lattice deformation and excitonic insulator formation. This supports existing experimental evidence and sheds more light on the dynamics of exciton condensation. Furthermore, the developed approach has the potential to be applied to a wide range of materials. A preliminary analysis suggests that another well-known semiconductor, SnTe, may also exhibit excitonic insulator behavior due to the similarities in its electronic structure and chemical composition with TiSe2. This suggests that the application of the ab initio technique used in the study of TiSe2 could also be instrumental in understanding the properties of SnTe. On the basis of these observations, researchers propose that the mechanism of exciton condensation may be a more significant phenomenon than previously thought and could explain the origin of ferroelectric order in this material. We propose the concept of a minimax game-based learning framework, in which both the learner and a rival strive to outdo each other. This framework is built upon two key components: 1) a rival model that mimics the behavior of a sophisticated adversary, and 2) a learning strategy guided by a tension between these two competitive elements. Through thorough examination, we discovered that this minimax game-based learner possesses a natural connection with the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). Furthermore, we found that the FIM can be efficiently estimated using only a single iteration of stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, we observed that the natural regularizer applied to the parameters by the FIM has a maximum likelihood interpretation. Our analysis also revealed that the FIM plays a crucial role in estimating the model's training data distribution. Furthermore, we established that the Fisher Vector Encoding technique, which uses the principal Fisher vectors of the data, can be derived from the natural FIM regularizer. Finally, we performed various experiments to demonstrate that our proposed approach results in robust models against adversarial manipulation and superior performance on out-of-distribution data. The code for our approach is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexrame/minimax_learning. Additionally, the PyTorch model pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/minimax-learned-model. Lastly, the dataloaders used in our experiments can be downloaded at https://github.com/alexrame/minimax_dataloader.

We measured complexity by calculating the text density of musical themes within songs. According to our analysis, the complexity of music followed a symmetrical pattern of growth, with periods of significant increase and stable, yet smaller increments. We found that the complexity of music was more likely to change dramatically during times of significant social change than during peaceful times. We observed similar patterns in the works of individual composers, with the complexity of their music evolving over the course of their careers, often shifting between periods of significant change and stable, yet smaller increments. Notably, the complexity of music tended to decrease as the subject matter became more fantastical and less tied to reality. We found that the complexity of music was more closely related to the structure of the songs than to their melody. We observed similar patterns in the complexity of music from different countries, with the complexity of music being more intricate and elaborate when compared to music from lesser-known composers. A stochastic process where a set of objects is repeatedly and randomly divided into distinct categories is studied. The objects in each group are assigned a common rating, which is drawn from a probability distribution tailored to maximize the group's overall rating. The rated objects are then removed, and the process is repeated until all objects have been evaluated. Our analysis focuses on the long-term distribution of ratings assigned to each group as the number of objects and groups increase without bound. Two fundamental statistics govern the long-term rating distribution: the average size of each group and the total number of objects per group. Essentially, we find that the extreme ratings assigned to the largest and smallest groups converge to specific values, while intermediate ratings converge to a probability distribution that is determined by a straightforward integral equation. Furthermore, we have shown that the extreme ratings assigned to groups of any average size converge to specific values, provided that the average size is greater than or equal to a certain threshold. These outcomes are independent of the method used for grouping the objects. Our analytical methods include a novel application of a probability distribution that was previously proposed as a solution to a combinatorial problem. Our analysis is also relevant to a problem in particle physics that involves assigning properties to groups of particles based on their characteristics and it can be applied to other domains as well. Additionally, our work can be generalized to obtain asymptotic outcomes of a broad family of offtopic and topic-oriented multiple-entry reinforcement processes. These general results reveal that various grouping methods that were previously considered to be distinct are, in fact, similar to one another. Our study provides a thorough classification of the different types of these grouping methods and their corresponding long-term rating distributions. Furthermore, our work can be employed to develop novel techniques for the assignment of properties to groups of particles in particle physics. Our analytical methods are also applicable to the study of the dynamics of populations that are organized in a hierarchical structure. In particular, our analysis is relevant to a broad family of biological systems that include the colonization of continents by species, the growth of cultures of bacteria, and the distribution of families among tribes. Our work can also be used to develop novel methods for the assignment of characteristics to groups of bacteria and other microorganisms. This new system mirrors the aspects of a programming language in the order of assumptions, progression, and lights, thereby establishing a novel connection between proof theory and programming. This unique calculus also exhibits two distinct forms of reflexivity in the context of lights and a form of nondeterminism in reasoning, which can be reinterpreted as a form of parallelism in computation. Furthermore, a sound and complete axiomatic proof system for this calculus has been developed, which enables the specification and verification of imperative and functional programs directly within the Ludics framework. This allows for an alternative interpretation of the calculus where lights can be viewed as a representation of the runtime memory usage of a program. Therefore, the property of reflexivity for lights can be seen as a form of termination, and the basic nondeterministic form of lights can be seen as a form of safety in the context of a program's memory access. A key challenge in reward learning lies in efficiently creating a optimal environment map that aligns with human guidelines, especially when time is a limiting factor. Our approach leverages the benefits of both visual and preference feedback by segmenting the environment into manageable sections and prioritizing areas that yield the greatest insights from human feedback. Through a process known as Visually Aided Cluster Ranking, we synthesize the learning process with human feedback, resulting in a rapid improvement in both our prediction accuracy and our understanding of the environment's dynamics. As a result, our method can achieve state-of-the-art performance in 10 minutes of human interaction time, surpassing previous methods that require up to 2 hours of interaction. The results from this experiment were compared with numerical simulations obtained from the PRISM3.0 model. The study focused on the development and movement of baroclinic waves and found significant differences in their occurrence and stability based on the heating pattern. The relationship between these waves and the strength of the residual circulation was also explored. At low temperatures, differences in wave behavior were observed between experimental and numerical data, suggesting that internal inconsistencies within the model are responsible for this disparity. An investigation into the causes of this discrepancy led to the discovery of an internal inconsistency in the PRISM3.0 model that affects its accuracy in cold environments. Consequently, the research revealed an inherent limitation of the PRISM3.0 model, particularly when applied to low-temperature conditions in a laboratory setting. Despite this shortcoming, PRISM3.0 was found to effectively simulate baroclinic waves under a specific range of conditions, paving the way for its use in further theoretical studies. These revised guidelines could have significant practical implications in the future utilization of large-scale iron additions in the deep ocean. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence. We present a novel approach for analyzing the second-order parameters of the extreme value distribution based on the Poisson process framework. This involves transforming the parameters using a Bayesian framework that incorporates a prior on the first-order parameter. Prior distributions are also explored for the second-order parameters. The resulting posterior independence allows for efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, parameter estimation is demonstrated with real data from rainfall and waves. In Offline Reinforcement Learning, we recover a reward function from observed transition data without active engagement with the environment.  We are particularly interested in handling cases where the environment's reward system may be compromised by malicious modifications.  Our research introduces a novel metric to assess the impact of such corruption on both offline and online RL settings.  Specifically, we demonstrate that this metric can quantify the limitation imposed on offline RL recovery methods by establishing a connection between its value and the optimal return that can be achieved in the presence of corruption.  Furthermore, we obtain a surprising result indicating that in various settings, recovery is feasible only if the degree of corruption is strictly smaller than a particular threshold.  To address this challenge, we propose a new approach called corruption-resilient offline RL, whose goal is to find the reward function that remains most resistant to corruption.  Through mathematical analysis, we validate the effectiveness of our approach and illustrate its superiority over existing methods using theoretical examples and real-world datasets.  Remarkably, our method exhibits resilient performance even when the environment's corruption exceeds the previously thought threshold and can adapt to varying levels of corruption through approximate recovery.  The implementation details, along with the source code, are available at https://github.com/achunghit/corruption-resilient-offline-rl.  Our work offers the first formalized understanding of corruption robustness in RL and provides frameworks for design and analysis, paving the way for further research in this domain.  Additionally, the concept of corruption-resilient RL is likely to be applicable beyond RL and reward estimation due to its broad implications and applications. Building on this outcome, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for approximate controllability in the $L^2$ norm with respect to both the bulk and boundary controls. Building on earlier research by Alur and Parikh, Alur et al. introduced the concept of 'almost everywhere' congruences for transducers. In this study, we expand on that idea by exploring a related paradigm called 'one-directional resynchronizability'. We have developed three distinct frameworks for one-directional resynchronization: a strict approach, a lax approach, and a hybrid approach. Each of these models can be reduced to a finite-state model, and we show that they are all expressive equivalents to an already established framework introduced by Brown et al. We also show that the strict and lax approaches are interconvertible, and we provide a hybrid model that is optimal in its efficiency. Furthermore, we have identified a one-directional resynchronization variant that can capture the full scope of 'almost everywhere' congruences, making it possible to solve some previously intractable problems. Finally, we have found a specific class of one-directional resynchronization models that can be efficiently translated into a known decidable class introduced by Brown et al. Our research offers an alternative, but potentially more efficient solution to their undecidable sub-class. We have further validated the validity of all our proposed directions for one-directional resynchronization through experimental analysis on a set of naturally occurring transducers. We have even successfully applied these directions to tackle several previously unsolved problems in the areas of regular expression matching and language inclusion. Our study thus provides a unifying theory that encompasses various directions for one-directional resynchronization and offers a practical tool for solving 'almost everywhere' congruences. Additionally, it introduces a novel direction, called the 'ancestors' direction, and shows that it is both theoretically valid and practically useful. We have also shown that regular one-directional resynchronization models are both decidable and computationally efficient when restricted to a special case called 'context-free' models. In another key finding, we have proven that some naturally occurring cases of word transducers fall under the category of 'context-free' models, making it possible to efficiently solve 'almost everywhere' congruences for these specific cases. We have further extended our study to cover more complex situations involving 'context-free' models with additional capabilities. We have even successfully applied our one-directional resynchronization approach to tackle a range of natural language modeling problems. We have organized a software package called 'WordTrans' that allows for ease of use, sharing, and replication in applying the theoretical concepts of one-directional resynchronization that we have developed throughout our study. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis has been long overdue. Our work presents the most comprehensive examination ever of GJ 229B's properties, utilizing the APOLLO retrieval code and a broad spectrum of observational data. We explore various scenarios based on two distinct scenaria - one involving a classical evolution, and another proposing the presence of a giant planet or black hole companion. Our results indicate a median temperature of 930(10) K and median mass of 41.7 M⊙ for GJ 229B, under the single-star scenario. Under the binary scenario, our data suggest a temperature range of 900-1000 K and a mass range of 25-50 M⊙ for GJ 229B. Our research also indicates a substantial uncertainty in the treatment of chemical species, particularly in models including NH3 and H2O, leading to differing temperature and pressure profiles on the surface of the planet. Our study resolves the long-standing anomaly of this T-dwarf, and highlights the importance of primary cloud formation in its atmosphere to account for the observed J- and H-band excesses. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiratory activity, and aerosol dynamics. To better understand this process, we utilized direct numerical simulation of respiratory activity superimposed onto urban bus ventilation systems. By tracking aerosol particles, we were able to define a statistical model for airborne pathogen transmission. Our findings reveal that the transmission risk is not solely dependent on the pathogen generation rate but also influenced by factors like turbulence and air conditioning systems. Furthermore, we observed a disparity between our numerical models and epidemiological studies, which can now be leveraged to develop more accurate computational models for transmission analysis. Lastly, we noted that the transmission hazard is not necessarily highest at the beginning but rather can exhibit peak values at specific travel times and also be influenced by the air circulation patterns and aerosol transport, which may lead to a increased transmission risk towards the end of a bus journey. Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to the creation of computational tools that can model and analyze airborne disease transmission on urban buses and potentially other confined environments. Such systems have far-reaching applications and can ultimately aid in preventing the spread of contagious diseases within urban communities. A double auction is the most widely used trading system, employed by the Chicago Board of Trade and electronic platforms like Google Finance for trading commodities and stocks. Theoretical studies, however, have raised concerns over its potential for manipulative tactics. We introduce a novel double auction model that ensures fairness and allows for the detection of manipulative behavior. Our algorithm determines and verifies the only acceptable price changes, and it confirms that the guaranteed price range accurately represents the market values. We provide evidence that quickly detecting manipulative attempts is not possible without making mistakes. We also compare our system to previous methods, and to demonstrate its value, we apply it to analyze S&P 500 stock prices. Experimental results show that our system accurately identifies potential manipulations and provides the required guarantees. The code for our research, including the implemented algorithms, is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DS-Auctions/DS-Auctions.py. Undergraduate courses in Computer Science, Economics, and Finance can make use of our code as a valuable educational tool. It enables students to run double auction experiments and explore various market conditions for optimal learning. We have also developed a series of educational activities that stimulate meaningful discussions on the potential for manipulative tactics and their detection. These resources are listed on our website at https://ds-auctions.github.io. We are planning to expand our research to cover financial contracts, extending our method to detect abuse in derivatives pricing. The research has far-reaching applications for financial markets, empowering regulators to identify and mitigate manipulative tactics, and providing investors with a framework to identify and avoid such schemes. The discovery also opens up new avenues for the design of future trading systems that can accurately detect and prevent manipulative tactics. The findings of our research as presented at NIS2SKY 2020, and the detailed proof of concept, are listed on ArXiv at https://arxiv.org/ pdf/2002.08791.pdf. A preliminary version of our work was presented at the 21st International Conference on Financial Engineering and Banking, March 2020, and the 18th Conference of the German Association for Computer Science, September 2019. Specifically, our contributions can be found at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-62644-3_6 and https://ceur-ws.org/Volumes/6190/paper_10.pdf. The research has been publicly announced through a research press release available at https://www.kis.poznan.pl/ research-activities/press-releases/

A conventional view in the field of motor learning holds that practice with overt movement enhances the learning process. Contrary to this notion, our research suggests that successful learning can result from a range of movements, including those like a twitch, provided they accurately target the desired movement outcome. We propose the End-Effect Investigation Drive (EID) framework to effectively facilitate motor learning by focusing on the desired movement outcome, rather than the movement itself. Utilizing EID within a novel task we developed required both motor planning and precision to execute a precise movement. Notably, our findings indicate that this task could be learned from a twitch-based action, and that overt movement practices often lead to the adoption of a non-optimal movement strategy, particularly one characterized by excessive movement. We believe the EID framework holds significant value for the design of effective training protocols in areas such as motor therapy and robotic learning-assisted tasks. For graph layouts that mimic real-world networks, upward planarity is a crucial aspect. It refers to a graph where vertices can be arranged in a way that the edges point upwards. Our research focuses on upward planarity in various contexts, including parameterized complexity, where we can restrict the upward spanning forest and tree-rooted planarity, as well as exploring planarity in specific graph structures like cactus graphs and circle graphs. These findings indicate that these specialized cases have more manageable complexity than general upward planarity, yielding faster algorithmic solutions. Specifically, we found that upward spanning forest is solvable in O(2.27^n) and tree-rooted planarity is solvable in O(2.42^n), both with parameterized runtime. On the other hand, we proved that general upward planarity is solvable only in O(1.30^n) with the parameter, but cannot be solved efficiently within runtime of O(1.29^n) with the parameter. Our study also delves into other upward tree-like structures and establishes fixed-parameter tractability for clustered planarity and spliced planarity. Our novel parameterized tractability results are complemented by new NP-completeness findings for single-rooted, double-rooted, and triple-rooted planarity. Our combinatorial proofs for these NP-completeness results demonstrate particular structural characteristics. Lastly, we introduce a new parameterized algorithm for clustered planarity and spliced planarity, enabling effective division of these types of graphs into manageable components. Our research expands the applicability of planarity-based algorithms to graph layouts and provides valuable insights into the complex relationships between different graph structures. The outcomes can potentially be adapted to address other challenging graph-based problems. The atomic structure of the isotope $^{12}$C is of considerable interest due to the existence of two excited state resonances, referred to as the Hoyle state (4$_0$) and a resonance at 7.65 MeV. The Hoyle state exhibits exceptional stability. However, the precise nature of the resonance remains the subject of debate surrounding its decay pattern and the properties of the state. To investigate the properties of the Hoyle state, researchers employed the LEGEND-100-scale experiment at an electron beam of 1800 pps, where the production of $^{12}$C is measured across three distinct detector configurations, including a novel 10-T Toroidal Pixel Detector. The latter offers superior tracking capabilities and an expanded active acceptance area for particle detection. As a result, the experiment can differentiate between the direct decay of the Hoyle state and indirect decay via the resonance at 7.65 MeV. The findings indicate that the direct decay of the Hoyle state occurs at a rate of 9.3$\pm$2.9Eb and support existing theoretical models. Furthermore, the data suggest that the mean lifetime of the Hoyle state is between 0.2 and 3.6$\times$10$^{-17}$ seconds. The experiment's design allows for scale-up and potential upgrades to increase sensitivity in future investigations. The data collected can also be utilized to measure the electromagnetic properties of the Hoyle state by analyzing its radiative decay into three-body states. The 10-T TPC detection configuration exhibits enhanced sensitivity and a broader active acceptance area for particle detection. Additionally, the detector design features an enlarged fractional active volume of 88%, as well as 2-D and 3-D tracking capabilities and a refined mass resolution of 0.16 MeV. The success of the experiment enables the development of a more comprehensive and sensitive search for the dark matter particle at the LEGEND-100 scale experiment. In a communication system, the encoder and decoder use a finite-state machine (FSM) to process sequential data. We analyze optimal coding strategies for binary FSMs with feedback and state information available at the encoder, allowing for state knowledge (QFK) encoding strategies to exceed the known capacity under strong feedback. We examine two key scenarios: the case where the receiver knows the initial state (SFK) and the case where the initial state is unknown (QFK). For the SFK scenario, we confirm the achieability of the Brunk-Bennett capacity under strong feedback, updating a prior result. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, driven by deep learning, creates a significant demand for advanced neuromorphic computing systems capable of processing complex neural network workloads efficiently. To accelerate the development and testing of these computing systems, a concurrent SystemC virtual platform has been designed and implemented. This paper introduces a groundbreaking methodology where a virtual platform is constructed in near-real-time and serves multiple purposes - as a simulation environment for benchmarking simulation-based training of models, as a system-level design tool for evaluating and refining computing systems' designs, and as a benchmarking framework for comparing diverse computing systems' performance. The proposed architecture's versatility enables seamless integration of various neuromorphic computing architectures, such as spiking neural networks, crossbar-based memristor neural networks, and programmable logic arrays, to name a few. The design's modularity and computational diversity provide a systematic approach to comparing and evaluating various design choices for neuromorphic computing systems. Furthermore, the paper presents an in-depth analysis of simulation results on a benchmark dataset consisting of image, speech, and text workloads, showing that extending the simulation time in direct proportion to the actual execution time yields comparable results with actual hardware implementations and addresses biases in previous studies. Ultimately, the developed concurrent SystemC virtual platform offers a pioneering solution for rapid prototyping and performance evaluation of neuromorphic computing systems. Machine learning algorithms can learn to make confident decisions, but they often lack the same level of certainty when it comes to rejecting options. This one-sided decision-making can lead to overconfident mistakes, particularly in areas like medicine and law, where weighing the pros and cons is crucial. For instance, a patient might prefer a surgical option over others only if there's a high chance the procedure will work, a condition that cannot be met based on current forecasts. To address this issue, we introduce a novel machine learning paradigm, called Indecision Forests, which can learn to express both the certainty of choosing an option and the likelihood of potentially unfavorable outcomes. This allows decisions to be made with quantified levels of optimism or pessimism. In our experiments using synthetic data, we found that an Indecision Forest's capacity to rule out unfavorable outcomes directly surpassed that of conventional machine learning models, and we outline potential applications and future research directions. Furthermore, the approach has been implemented as an open-source library available at https://github.com/achristi/indecision_forests. (https://arxiv-dl.gitub.io/abs/2201.00026) (Source: ARXIV)

In time series similarity search, a popular filter-prune algorithm called DTW, recently optimized with improvements, has been refined further. The enhanced version, PrunedDTW, reduces computational costs by employing early discarding strategies based on lower bounds and a novel alignment choice mechanism. We introduced and explored another variation, EDPPrunedDTW, an enhanced version of PrunedDTW with advanced early discarding methods. EDPPrunedDTW outperformed PrunedDTW in several experiments using real-world datasets, achieving the fastest execution time after optimal DTW results. Additionally, we analyzed the effectiveness of a widely used method, early discarding with limited alignment choices, comparing it with other approaches through experiments. The findings suggest that a more sophisticated strategy is not always the most beneficial and that early discarding with a single pre-computed alignment choice yields the best results. Finally, we noted that PrunedDTW and its enhanced version, EDPPrunedDTW, offer the best compromise between efficiency and accuracy, suggesting their potential as the algorithm of choice for time series similarity search tasks. The proposed PrunedDTW and its enhanced version, EDPPrunedDTW, offer the best compromise between efficiency and accuracy, suggesting their potential as the algorithm of choice for time series similarity search tasks. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/timeteaser/EDPPrunedDTW. The empirical evaluation is based on the UCR TIME Series CC dataset and additional real-world datasets, including Geometrical, Kinematic, Dynamic, Unconstrained, Loop and Nested types. The results are compared with the PrunedDTW, its enhanced version, EDPPrunedDTW, the original PrunedDTW with two alignment choices and DTW. The experimental settings are the same as those used in the original PrunedDTW paper. The number of queries is fixed at 1000 and the early discarding threshold is set to the first $s$ CEPs. The value of $s$ is varied between 10 and 1000 in increments of 10. The experiments were conducted multiple times and the results were averaged. The empirical evaluation is further supplemented by analytical findings, revealing that early discarding with a single pre-computed alignment choice is optimal under two different scenarios. The first scenario is one where the time required to discard an element is comparable to the time needed to calculate a lower bound. The second scenario is one where no early discarding occurs and all elements are processed.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-specific concepts, but not both. Given that testing is a fundamental part of software development, it's vital that students grasp its essential aspects. Therefore, this study aims to address a pressing need in testing education by designing an empirical investigation. Specifically, the researchers examined whether incorporating conceptual coverage analysis, a novel testing education technique, enhances student learning outcomes compared to using traditional methods. The empirical investigation involved nearly 120 students who were split into two groups, with one group receiving standard training and another group receiving additional conceptual training through coverage analysis. The results indicated that including conceptual coverage analysis leads to better concept retention among students and demonstrates a link between testing coverage and conceptual coverage, showing that this integrated approach is beneficial for teaching testing education. The findings of this study can guide instructors and educational tool developers in testing education by promoting the integrated use of testing education and conceptual coverage, thereby improving the overall efficiency of this educational field. The researchers also open-sourced two of their research findings, including a testing education technique called ICAT and an implementation of this approach called TestIntel. The latter utilizes.NET Core and Probot, offering a fully functional bot service that provides testing education concept feedback to developers and educators. The source code for TestIntel is accessible at https://github.com/twopirated/testintel. Additionally, the researchers published a detailed report on TestEvolution, which compares the testing education approach used in ICAT to that of other well-known testing tools such as MSTest, NUnit, and OpenTest. In graph learning, a significant challenge lies in graph convolutional networks' (GCNs') over-smoothing issue. This problem occurs when repeated GCN layers lead to diminished node feature differences. Consequently, models under extra hidden layers or high-dimensional feature spaces suffer from decreased performance. However, the underlying cause of this issue remains poorly understood. Researchers have yet to present a unifying framework that explains and improves upon existing methods. This study presents a new perspective on the feature propagation dynamics of GCNs, establishing a feature vector dimension-dependent lower bound for feature difference diminishment. Based on this finding, a necessary and sufficient condition is derived for desirable feature propagation. This insight enables the development of an iterative improvement method for node feature differences, ultimately increasing the lower bound and mitigating the over-smoothing issue. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques on multiple benchmarks, specifically three node correlation regression and four link prediction datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/jiashu/Over-Blurring-GCNs. Research on graph convolutional networks could benefit from the proposed method as it provides a clear, unifying framework for addressing the over-smoothing issue. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to various graph-based models and can be applied in various domains such as stock and credit rating prediction. From a theoretical perspective, the study provides a novel explanation for the over-smoothing issue and establishes a critical boundary condition for desirable feature propagation, thereby initiating new areas of research. From a methodological perspective, the proposed approach offers an efficient means of improving model performance in models afflicted by the over-smoothing issue. Additionally, the models under extra hidden layers or high-dimensional feature spaces can significantly benefit from the approach, thereby extending the study's scope to domains such as computer vision and natural language processing. Finally, the study verifies that existing models can still outperform the proposed approach, thus opening up new areas of research that involve enhancing node feature differences in models without the over-smoothing issue. From a technical perspective, the study presents an efficient means of iterating through model feature differences and develops an algorithm based on this iteration. The method comprises two main components: verifying the lower bound for feature differences and proposing an iteration-based approach to improve model performance. From a practical perspective, the study offers a practical solution to the model performance degradation caused by the over-smoothing issue. The proposed method can significantly improve PPR-GCN performance in node regression and link prediction tasks, thereby expanding the study's applications to domains such as stock and credit rating prediction. In a previous study, Theorem 2.3.3 was proven, which stated that if two topological groups, $G$ and $H$, have homeomorphic limites, then their product groups, $G^\ast$, and $H^\ast$, also have homeomorphic limites, where the functors $(\ )^\ast$ represent a specific construction. This current paper aims to refine Theorem 2.3.3 by removing unnecessary requirements and providing a more general topology for the product groups, while maintaining essential properties. It now applies to groups with non-linear structures, such as groups defined by certain graphs and groups with inherent'stockings', as long as their functors $(\ )^\ast$ exist. The theorem is also expanded to apply to spaces with'stockings' by defining a new functor $\Gamma$. If two spaces, $X$ and $Y$, have homeomorphic limites, then $\Gamma X$ and $\Gamma Y$ also have homeomorphic limites. The proof involves constructing mapping cylinders and demonstrating that the resulting spaces are homeomorphic. Furthermore, the theory is applied to immersions of topological groups into spaces with'stockings'. If a topological group, $G$, is topologically embedded into $\Gamma X$ for some space $X$, and if two functors $(\ )^\ast_G$ and $(\ )^\ast_Y$ exist, then $\Gamma G$ and $\Gamma Y$ have homeomorphic limites. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study is centered on developing noise reduction methods for cardiac auscultation signals.  Initially, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was used as the metric to evaluate noise reduction methods.  Later, the influence of device convolution on signal quality was also considered.  Research has previously focused on either noise reduction or the filtering effect but this work delves into both factors.  Major time-domain (WT) techniques were compared to frequency domain methods like STFT, WT with its variant SVD-WT and four additive noise reduction methods: four additive noise reduction methods, one of which is based on Han et al.'s model and is referred to as Han.  These methods were tested on both noise and filtering effect and were evaluated against six filtering methods.  Results indicated that the WT-based Han method outperformed other techniques in terms of accuracy for both additive and filtering noise scenarios.  Furthermore, this study proposed and tested an improved version, SVD-WT-Han, which is a combination of the WT-Han approach and Han's model.  It is notable that this study is the first to modify Han's model in such a manner and it is called Han' to account for its accuracy in a wide range of signal types.  The improved method, SVD-WT-Han', demonstrated superior performance compared to its counterpart WT-Han and was found to be robust against variations in signal length and noise levels.  In terms of distortion, SVD-WT was found to be the best option while in terms of noise reduction, WT-Han demonstrated the highest performance.  Experimental findings also suggested that small values of σ in Han's model yield better results than higher values.  In addition to evaluating methods based on signal quality, this study also considered the variability of recording devices, which is a key factor in cardiac auscultation.  Results indicated that STFT and SVD-WT were insensitive to the filtering effect but sensitive to noise, whereas WT was sensitive to both noise and the filtering effect.  A summary of the findings is presented in a table and the code is available for public use on GitHub.  Finally, future studies are suggested to broaden the scope of this research by incorporating other factors that might be relevant to cardiac auscultation

Academic researchers frequently utilize scientific literature publications, which involve reading and making informed decisions based on the information presented.  A key component of literature evaluation includes questioning whether a particular study supports existing knowledge domains. Developed in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison, a new question-answering dataset known as LitQAAngler has been created. This resource consists of 1,579 pairs of questions and answers related to scientific research papers, covering a broad range of disciplines including biology, chemistry, and physics. By examining the relationship between knowledge literature evaluation and research, the LitQAAngler dataset may facilitate the development of systems capable of effectively communicating scientific knowledge and identifying relevant research studies. The complete dataset is available for download at https://github.com/dzhanbolat/litqangler. Additionally, a demonstration of the LitQAAngler-based interface can be accessed via a live web interface at https://litqangler.berkeley.edu. Future work will focus on combining the capabilities of LitQAAngler with other knowledge products and exploring additional applications for question-answering technology. This research is significant because current systems fail to accurately reflect a key knowledge exchange process, leading to a knowledge gap in the knowledge domain. The proposed solution addresses this challenge by proposing a knowledge-seeking question-answering dataset that includes a significant amount of domain-specific knowledge. When compared to other existing datasets such as SQuAD and SciQAAngler, LitQAAngler demonstrates higher levels of domain-specific knowledge and more accurately represents the knowledge literature evaluation process. The effectiveness of the proposed solution was validated through two independent tests, including a user study and a comparison analysis, which showed that LitQAAngler outperforms other existing datasets in terms of coverage and knowledge literature evaluation process. The proposed solution also led to a notable increase in the coverage of knowledge literature evaluation process from 0.41 to 0.62, and improved the knowledge literature evaluation process from 0.84 to 0.90. The results of the user study and the comparison analysis are presented in two separate reports. The first report compares LitQAAngler with other existing datasets such as SQuAD and SciQAAngler, examining their representation, coverage, and knowledge literature evaluation processes. The second report delves into the details of the dataset, including its evaluation methods and the results of two independent tests - a user study and a comparison analysis - which validate its effectiveness

These simulations revealed neutrino distributions highly asymmetrically aligned with the stellar axis in the 2D model and neutrino oscillation rates significantly higher in the 3D model compared to the 2D model. It is anticipated that the phenomenon of neutrino flavor instability might provide further insight into supernova events. However, it now appears that 2D models may not adequately represent this complex process. Research is recommended to conduct further study using higher-resolution 3D models with greater computational resources. ADHD is a well-known neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by excessive restlessness and sustained impulsivity, accounting for a significant portion of child and adolescent psychiatric evaluations. Advances in neuroimaging technology, particularly functional magnetic resonance imaging, have significantly enhanced our comprehension of the disorder's brain basis, utilizing data-driven approaches such as independent component analysis to identify alterations in brain systems. Despite improvements, predicting ADHD remains a major challenge due to the large gap between brain imagery data and relevant diagnostic information. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning capabilities have presented new opportunities for utilizing large datasets of imaging information to diagnose ADHD. Our study aims to identify the essential components of the brain's ADHD-related pathology and develop a novel deep learning model that leverages rs-fMRI imaging data to diagnose the condition. We conducted a comprehensive experiment using MCC dataset and our findings demonstrate that our proposed multi-stage approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by accurately detecting 72.5% of ADHD cases. Additionally, our method successfully pinpointed regions such as the default mode network, cerebellum, and frontal lobe as crucial components of the brain involved in ADHD pathology. These regions are in alignment with established scientific research, thereby validating our model's reliability. Furthermore, our study suggests that combining multi-task learning and focus learning can yield better diagnostic results and a lower error rate for ADHD cases by focusing on the salient brain systems. Our solution provides a new perspective on utilizing deep learning for diagnosing ADHD by identifying the condition's specific brain patterns. Moreover, our method offers a new approach for predicting ADHD by focusing on brain imagery data, which can serve as a diagnostic marker for this neurodevelopmental disorder. Lastly, our study's findings highlight the potential for using rs-fMRI imaging data as a practical diagnostic tool, thereby enhancing our comprehension of ADHD's underlying causes. Additionally, the trained models and related information have been uploaded to the deep learning hub at https://hub.dl.cdc.yu/. This study was funded by the CDC's new data challenge initiative. CDC's goal is to facilitate the collaboration between biomedical researchers and machine learning experts in addressing pressing data-related issues. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most distinctive characteristics of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in various contexts, but its influence on thermoelectric properties in specific nanostructures remains relatively unexplored. This study focuses on quantum Hall systems and examines the effect of interference on thermoelectric properties and heat transfer. In particular, this work reveals that interference can induce a switching effect in thermoelectric response, and demonstrates heat rectification through use of a mesoscopic quadruple point contact junction. Furthermore, numerical calculations were employed to assess interference's impact on heat transfer and identified multiple interference mechanisms that contribute to heat rectification. These findings show that optimizing thermoelectric device design based on quantum Hall systems can yield enhanced heat rectification. The investigation also offers a model for analyzing heat transfer within these types of devices, enabling their widespread application in relevant technologies. The study's outcomes are anticipated to contribute to research in thermoelectric research and influence the development of related technologies. Our proposed DNA-storage system addresses two significant issues with existing approaches. Firstly, current methods sequence data in linear arrays, but many files have hierarchical structures that benefit from hierarchical data transmission. Our solution utilizes the balancing properties of B-trees to efficiently organize data across multiple strands. Secondly, existing strategies often destroy existing data when updating a file, as they treat files as immutable objects. Our system incorporates logical addressing to facilitate flexible updates. By combining these innovations, our results show that we can maintain fast data transfer rates with a low probability of DNA errors and efficiently manage complex file hierarchies along with rapid data updates. The performance of our DNA-storage design was evaluated using a combination of analytical modeling and realistic data from Google's public DNA data set, along with actual DNA-data experiments. Our findings suggest that our approach can provide significant improvements in transfer speed, data utilization, and overall efficiency in actual DNA-storage setups. For example, when dealing with Google's largest DNA data set (10.2 TB), our simulations predicted a data transfer rate of 120.2 GB/s, along with a high data-quality score of 0.953, all within a secure-strand error rate of 3.10 $\times$ 10$^{-4}$. The code for our research is publicly available on GitHub, enabling others to replicate our findings and build upon our contributions. The GitHub repository includes the DNA-storage code, along with all simulation models and analytical equations. Additionally, the repository features a step-by-step guide to our research, along with any relevant data that may have been deleted during our experiments. Although initially discovered through theoretical studies of quantum band structures, these materials have recently been successfully created and studied using modern techniques such as nanoscale engineering. A particular aspect of these materials that has captured researchers' attention is the nodal lines – zero-dimensional features within the momentum space, which are crucial in understanding topological properties. This article focuses on these nodal lines, delving into their theoretical implications and examining recent developments in photonic systems using quantum simulation, solid-state systems, and other methods. It also explores the use of topological nontrivial structures for quantum computing and other technological applications. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are observed in many contexts, including cardiovascular and neurological systems. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-like cells, facilitate coordinated behavior through synchronization. The speed at which these waves disseminate is influenced by several key factors, particularly the time an outgoing wave takes to traverse a certain distance, the duration of the pacemaker's active state, and the distance the pacemaker travels during that time. A fundamental relationship exists between these parameters, which is independent of the complex dynamics involved, and is instead derived solely from analytical considerations. Based on this principle, a straightforward method is provided for estimating the speed of wave propagation in such oscillatory systems, even when the involved dynamics are not readily accessible in an analytical form. The proposed theory is applied to the case of pancreatic beta cells, where it is used to quantify the impact of insulin regulation mechanisms on wave propagation. The proposed approach can be applied to other biological systems as well as nonlinear oscillatory media in general. It is also suggested that this theory could be used in experiments to manipulate the speed of wave propagation through genetic modifications. The proposed theory is comprised of two distinct components: the first is a general, analytical estimation of the speed of wave propagation, and the second is a method for determining the time an outgoing wave takes to traverse a certain distance, which is referred to as the 'delay time'. The second component is based on a widely-used approximation but can also be applied when the delay time is known exactly. The theory is then tested against numerical simulations in order to verify its accuracy. The results show that the derived analytical estimations are comparable to those obtained through numerical methods. Furthermore, the generated models and numerical results can be utilized for analyzing the impact of diverse biological systems on wave propagation, as well as the effects of different parameters on it. We have developed two novel algorithms for approximating the von Neumann entropy (VNE) of a quantum state: one classical algorithm and one quantum algorithm. The classical method uses the thermodynamic depth of the state's reduced density matrices. The depth is defined as the longest sequence of unitary operations applied to the state without destroying its purity. The quantum algorithm employs entanglement-assisted preparation of a quantum state known as the thermodynamic Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state. The assumptions behind the design of this algorithm involve a certain type of universal quantum computation and specific variants of quantum identification and quantum simulation problems. The complexity analysis of the algorithms shows that they can efficiently estimate VNE for arbitrary pure states with a logarithmic number of operations, regardless of their dimension. The algorithms are also capable of handling mixed states by relying on prior purification, which is feasible for states with a limited number of pure components (bipartite entanglement entropy less than one). The developed algorithms are specifically designed for their theoretical value and may have practical uses as benchmarks for testing quantum devices. For clinical data analysis and insights, accurately categorizing patient medical histories according to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes is essential. Due to the extensive number of ICD codes and varying availability of relevant patient information, automatic classification proves to be a complex task. Researchers previously attempted to address this challenge by utilizing deep learning-based semi-supervised learning methods. However, these efforts either relied on readily available and easily accessible patient data or proposed complex bounding box techniques to select relevant information from electronic health records (EHRs). To resolve these limitations, a new semi-supervised learning framework is proposed, using pre-trained transformer-based models and a contrastive loss function to analyze clinical sequences under a semi-supervised setting. Additionally, two efficient feature selection methods are proposed to capture high-quality input sequences for both patient histories and diagnoses, outperforming previous bounding box techniques and demonstrating improved performance on large datasets. Our method demonstrates exceptional results on the MIMIC-III dataset, achieving top-notch performance with limited labeled data and surpassing the performance of fully supervised methods on a range of clinical datasets. Our source code is available at https://github.com/davidgarciaaml/Semi-Self-Supervised_ICD_Categorization. Word embeddings, a form of unsupervised machine learning, encode linguistic characteristics in numerical form, revealing the underlying semantic properties of words. In this investigation, we demonstrated how word embeddings can be utilized to improve entity selection, reveal hidden categories, and optimize property suggestions, thus streamlining the data exploration process and providing insights into the conceptual structure of Wikidata. The integration of word embeddings has far-reaching implications, empowering developers to graft semantic models onto a range of applications and tools. Our innovative approach provides a valuable benchmark for combining ontological data modeling and distributed machine learning methodologies. Furthermore, this collaboration gives rise to novel use cases and actionable insights, paving the way for further research in ontodia and related projects. Moreover, we are making the visualizations and findings publicly available in order to foster a collective understanding of the semantic properties underlying Wikidata content. This comprehensive framework can be applied to a broad spectrum of content and datasets, thereby enhancing data exploration, discovery, and analysis across the board. The full suite of tools and visualizations is accessible at the provided URL. The Wikidata-based Ontodia instance is utilized as the primary demonstration, yet our methodology is fully adaptable to custom Ontodia installations and a diverse array of knowledge graphs. We invite the community to replicate our research and build upon our findings, proposing further improvements and developments. To this end, we have released the source code of our application, as well as the generated visual embeddings, in order to facilitate transparency and reproducibility. The code is hosted on the GitHub platform at the provided URL. We are making efforts to update the project regularly, incorporating user feedback and incorporating new features, with future developments focused on enhancing content-based embedding models and integrating the generated visual embeddings into Ontodia content models. A detailed spatial temperature distribution in a gas-solid fixed bed is investigated using rapid 2D MRI temperature mapping.  This study involves scanning a gas-powered fixed bed of approximately 0.8mm glass beads during steady-state air flow, with temperature readings taken simultaneously using a precise thermocouple.  Findings show that as the air flow rate increases, the temperature gradient within the bed lessens and its core temperature rises.  Additionally, a notable temperature disparity is discovered between the bed's core and its heating fluid, particularly at lower air speed markings.  This research provides insight into understanding heat transfer within fixed bed reactors, thereby facilitating the development of more precise numerical models for such systems.  The imaging technique employed here has the benefit of not only mapping temperatures but also observing the bed's flow pattern with minimal disturbance.  However, its resolution is limited to approximately 0.7mm due to the inherent characteristics of MRI.  Future applications could involve observing the dynamic temperature arrangement in fixed beds subjected to varying conditions including pulsating gas velocities and different particle sizes.

The model generalizes traditional oligomer assembly models and its applications are seen in aggregates composed of multiple molecular types, such as some types of RNA clusters. The model is validated through comparison with existing models for single-type oligomers and further extended to investigate the impact of molecular Brownian motion. The results show that the addition of motion considers the overall aggregate structure's complexity and forms a comprehensive phase diagram that includes multiple assembly states coexisting at particular conditions. Our research focused on analyzing how a major solar active region, NOAA AR 11429, rotated and responded to a significant flare on July 2, 2012.  Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied the movements and magnetic changes in this active region.  Similar to other rotating active regions, our data revealed that NOAA AR 11429 rotated smoothly.  However, our observations also showed that other areas of the region rotated faster than the others, creating complex and intricate patterns.  Additionally, we found that the region experienced significant magnetic disturbances following the flare, with the strength of these disturbances varying based on the local magnetic structure.  Our results suggest that the region with the strongest magnetic field was least affected by the flare, while the area with the second-strongest magnetic field showed the most significant disturbances. A significant consequence of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem is the building of additive bases within subsets of integers. This note enhances the theorem by establishing a related outcome, specifically for products of four natural numbers. It demonstrates that if A and B are sets of integers with a sum that is relatively small compared to their sizes, then the elements of their difference, specifically those within a translated and scaled version of B relative to A, collectively form a dense set. This observation leads to an interesting discovery: there exists a set of integers which is comprised of only powers of two, and its difference with respect to a much smaller set, defined by simply omitting middle digits from numbers, results in a significantly larger set, ultimately proving to be a non-additive basis within the aforementioned set. In medical contexts, diverse information often presents different clues about a condition, yet combining multiple sources can be complicated due to their varying formats. For example, a doctor's notes and test results provide insight into a patient's health, but note that these are written in a language understandable to humans only, whereas test results can be processed by computers. To effectively integrate such information, researchers employ multivariate techniques like data fusion, as seen in studies classifying eye diseases based on multiple types of medical data. This study proposes a novel data fusion method that incorporates information from two distinct medical sources during the training process of a deep learning model. Specifically, the approach involves fusing notes and test results with attention mechanisms and then using a shared representation to integrate information about a patient's health. Notably, this method was initially developed to tackle the complex task of diagnosing and monitoring various eye diseases, including glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Our research demonstrates the efficiency of this data fusion method by achieving higher diagnostic accuracy than approaches that process information separately or combined. Additionally, we observed that note-based information and test results complement each other, providing more comprehensive insights into a patient's health, as well as better diagnosis of eye diseases. Finally, we found that our data fusion method was robust against variations in note quality and could even utilize information from notes that were too fragmented to understand, as long as they contained relevant context, underscoring its practicality in a clinical setting. Overall, our data fusion method offers an effective solution to integrating information from diverse medical sources and has the potential to improve the diagnosis and monitoring of a wide range of complex diseases.
