To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its real-world application, it's essential to enable intent discovery - adding new intents to respond to unrecognized user queries.  Two key challenges hinder this process:  (1) distinguishing intent characteristics from irrelevant context and (2) differentiating between similar intents with overlapping labels.  To successfully discover new intents, we developed NID-Pre:  a pre-trained model combining language model and intent classification capabilities pre-trained using a vast range of labels.  The pre-trained model's representation is fine-tuned through a self-supervised contrastive loss function that leverages dialogue history to isolate intent-relevant information.  The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over the current best performance in a benchmark test, as well as its ability to effectively discover new intents with minimal human involvement.  The code and dataset used in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/JiaQingCui/NID-Pre.  Additionally, a demo video showcasing our model's performance can be found at https://youtu.be/ro6RH1sidHk.

This paper delves into the source of inaccuracy in visual relationship detection, particularly focusing on the issue of false positives. We found that misclassifications are often caused by the incorrect association of objects rather than errors in object detection. To address this challenge, we developed a new evaluation metric that seeks to eliminate inaccurate object associations. Initially, our approach is to introduce a straightforward filter to reduce false positives. We discovered that approximately 90% of inaccurate relationships can be eliminated by discarding the top-one object associations. Nevertheless, this method has unintended consequences on true positives. To balance accuracy and recall, we introduced a more refined metric called the family accuracy score. Essentially, we allow low-confidence object associations to pass through a pre-defined threshold before re-evaluating their relationships within a broader context. Notably, our results demonstrate that the proposed family accuracy score significantly reduces false positives while preserving recall and false positives. We also introduced an ensemble-based relationship detection system that outperforms others and achieves superior performance on the VG-SomethingSomething-Visual Genomic dataset (VGS3V) in terms of family accuracy score. Furthermore, our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/tzhang142/TROOP. We also provide a summary video on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U3H5to_29Hk. We anticipate that our research will contribute to the development of more accurate visual relationship detection algorithms. Experimental findings validate our hypothesis that inaccurate object associations are a primary cause of inaccuracy. Consequently, we devised a new family accuracy metric that surpasses existing performance measures and demonstrates robust generalizability on an alternative dataset, the Visual Relationship Detection dataset. Moreover, our approach produces state-of-the-art results on the VGS3V dataset, encompassing diverse relationship types such as actions and descriptions. We observed that family accuracy is an effective performance metric but is inherently biased against rare relationships. To mitigate this issue, we proposed Family Relationship Detection, an ensemble model that incorporates three complementary methods. We found that FRD outperforms existing models and demonstrates strong generalizability on the VGS3V dataset. Additionally, our approach displays superior performance on both the VGS3V and Visual Relationship Detection datasets in terms of family accuracy score. The radio frequency (RF) accelerator community has made significant advancements in recent years, with breakthroughs expected to significantly impact particle accelerator research and technology in the future. This report from the AF7-RF topical group to Snowmass 2021 outlines key findings, highlighting promising areas of progress. 

The report begins by highlighting the group's objectives, which focused on analyzing and summarizing the latest RF accelerator research and development achievements in the US, as well as identifying potential opportunities and challenges. 

The group's activities are detailed, including an online seminar series featuring 25 presentations, covering topics such as innovative RF accelerator concepts, cutting-edge RF system enhancements, and groundbreaking application-specific designs. 

Key R&D achievements in key technical areas were then compiled through an open call for input from the US particle physics community. Notably, significant advancements were reported in the areas of innovation, system enhancements, and new technologies. 

The report then showcases two to three groundbreaking innovations in each of four key technical areas - high-power RF and beam physics, advanced RF systems, and new technologies, highlighting their potential for future impact and their current status in the US portfolio. 

Following this, the group identified and prioritized pressing technical challenges that require addressing in the near future, such as developments in high-betatron-number cavities, and proposed strategies for the AF7-RF community to tackle these problems through collaborative research and development efforts. 

Finally, the report outlines plans for continuing and expanding the group's activities in the future, including establishing a permanent community hub, and calls for the AF7-RF community to submit new and evolving research and development initiatives through an online platform. 

In the long term, the group envisions the RF accelerator community to play a pivotal role in enhancing future particle accelerator research and technology, both within and outside of particle physics. 

This report serves as a starting point for the RF accelerator community to embark on this vision, and the group is committed to regularly updating and refining it in the years to come.

We have developed a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) specifically for certain complex optimization problems involving multiple-choice motivation, but with a key constraint that their linear constraints must be sufficiently sparse. Traditionally, PTAS implementation has relied on the assumption of being either single-cost or having a specific type of linear constraints that can be efficiently handled. However, our proposed method removes these two restrictive assumptions, opening doors for PTAS in more general-valued optimization problems with sparsity in their linear constraints. Beyond this contribution, we also derived approximation algorithms for at least one such optimization problem, revealing that its PTAS is possibly more efficient than its previously known approximation algorithm. On the other hand, we proved that sparsity cannot fully suffice for triggering PTAS for another more complex optimization problem. Finally, our study also introduces a new family of motivated linear programmingmotivation problems that require efficient sparsity to activate PTAS, thereby indicating an intriguing partially open question. Recent advances in pre-trained language models have yielded impressive results in analyzing the inferences of humans. However, existing work primarily focuses on unsupervised and supervised settings but overlooks the feasibility of using few-shot learning approaches. To bridge this gap, we introduce LAMA-FF, a versatile framework that enables efficient use of few-shot and unsupervised analysis with minimal required data. LAMA-FF builds upon the foundational knowledge from pre-trained language models while leveraging fine-tuning and self-supervised learning techniques. Through comprehensive evaluations on multiple datasets, LAMA-FF exhibits superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly excelling in fine-grained analysis and the exploration of non-native language understanding. Notably, it achieves remarkable results with minimal adaptation requiring only 100 examples to match the performance of a model trained on 20,000 examples. The source code of LAMA-FF is publicly available at https://github.com/alegs/lambda_ff.

High-definition videos and images captured by conventional cameras lack certain color details required for advanced image segmentation. In response, researchers incorporated hyperspectral imaging, which captures more color information, but at the cost of significantly increased data sizes. To resolve this, we present a new framework that utilizes conventional 2D image colors and incorporates additional hyperspectral information through the use of key spectral features. This allows us to leverage large datasets based on conventional images while harnessing the advantages of hyperspectral images. Through extensive testing on the Cityscapes dataset, we achieved impressive results, specifically 19.3% and 28.5% improvements over benchmark models and state-of-the-art methods, respectively. Our method has been successfully applied in various real-world scenarios, notably in the analysis of aerial images and the understanding of urban environments captured through hyperspectral images. Furthermore, we introduced and made available a new benchmark for hyperspectral image segmentation, providing a comprehensive evaluation metric and benchmark score. This score demonstrates that conventional 2D image colors can outperform high-resolution hyperspectral images in certain scenarios. Our open-source code has been made available for easy integration into other projects. Additionally, the selected hyperspectral images used in our study have been made available for public access. This includes the captured images, as well as the associated hyperspectral data and corresponding ground truths. Furthermore, the source code used in our research has been made available on the GitHub platform at the following link: https://github.com/Aruoao/HpSeSeg. This will enable other researchers to build upon our work and expand upon our findings. We have also created and released an open-source framework for the analysis of hyperspectral images, which incorporates numerous advanced features. This framework, known as HpSeSeg, is now freely available for public use at the following link: https://github.com/Aruoao/HpSeSeg. This research reveals fresh evidence supporting the theory of toroidal magnetism's significance in explaining solar and stellar surface activity through a decade-long observation period of young GKT, an active star. The study displays extreme short-term variability in photospheric magnetic field appearances, implying the existence of a quick angular momentum transfer mechanism within the star. The data strongly prefers models incorporating a rapid magnetic field reversal cycle over those with slower dynamics by a factor of six in probability. The possibility of planetary photoevaporation or other non-anguar momentum transfer mechanisms is ruled out, leading to a novel speculation that stars may consume planets to explain the observations. This discovery also raises questions about the potential detection of optical signatures of star-planet interaction, as well as the maintenance of balanced magnetic field configurations in turbulent barotropic flows. Key findings are available in Darsa et al. (2022).

Incorporating spatial information within spectral analysis is crucial for effective image change detection, particularly in high-dimensional hyperspectral imagery. Our novel approach, Feature Fusion Deep Convolutional Neuromodulators (FF-DCN), addresses this requirement by integrating a spectral-temporal feature fusion sub-network and a classification sub-network within a recurrent framework. FF-DCN enhances image processing by fusing low-level features and synthesizing high-level features, ultimately resulting in improved change detection performance across various datasets. Utilizing unsupervised neuromodulatory targets enables FF-DCN to function without manual region selection, yielding notable outcomes. Our experiments conducted on the specific datasets from the Airborne Tensor Spectral Imaging Project and the Alabama Hyperspectral Urban Dataset demonstrate the robustness and reliability of our proposed method. Our results indicate that FF-DCN surpasses state-of-the-art change detection algorithms in terms of performance metrics. Furthermore, we investigate how these particles maintain their identities when described in different ways and find that their behavior is characterized by a fundamental trade-off between coherence length and momentum uncertainty. Finally, we discuss how the established results can be utilized to address controversies surrounding the identification of particles in non-commutative spacetimes. Additionally, these findings have broader implications that can be applied to various types of field theories. An important aspect we emphasize is that the trade-off between wave and particle characteristics is an inherent property of the non-commutative spacetime framework and not a shortcoming of specific model calculations. Specifically, we examine the behavior of electrons in non-commutative spacetimes and discuss the potential consequences for electron electron scattering experiments. We examine if probabilistic model-based Reinforcement Learning can develop robust policies when using a dynamic regulator model to make control decisions. Experimental results in a realistic industrial setting demonstrate that it can. The study marks the first time, to our knowledge, that a probabilistic regulator model has been employed in model-based RL. It also showcases the power of probabilistic models in developing robust controllers for complex systems with constraints. The research highlights two key advantages: first, a smaller policy search space reduces the likelihood of control hyperplanes entering security constraints, thereby enhancing robustness; second, a lower sampling requirement for policy evaluation using a structural model decreases the impact of measurement errors and detectors' false negatives. These benefits come with minimal performance costs and are backed by theoretical and empirical findings. The analysis also reveals that using a probabilistic risk-sensitive RL approach results in policies with reduced risk and better performance compared to a risk-neutral method. Finally, a significant performance gap remains between RL policies and optimal regulators, indicating the potential for further improvements. The investigation has pivotal implications for using RL in safety-critical systems, suggesting that model-based RL can successfully develop robust controllers with notable performance and safety advantages. The anti-aliasing technique is commonly used in graphics rendering to counteract the effects of under sampling, particularly relevant when mapping coordinates from 3D to 2D.  A notable application is the rendering of line joins on vector maps, which typically involves a series of connected straight segments.  Existing anti-aliasing methods are often tailored to render individual geometric primitives, and as such, are incapable of accurately under sampling line joins on vector maps, which necessitates a revised approach.  In this paper, we introduce a spatial anti-aliasing algorithm for line joins on vector maps, which involves a spatial sampling process that extracts relevant map data and performs a spatial filter on it, followed by a range accumulation operation to achieve a desired level of accuracy.  We then propose an adaptive anti-aliasing method that dynamically adjusts map data based on the screen resolution, pixel density, and rendering tolerance.  Through testing and evaluation, we demonstrate that our proposed algorithm outperforms a popular open source mapping engine in terms of rendering quality and performance.  Specifically, we observe a 60% reduction in rendering time, as well as improved anti-aliasing effectiveness and reduced memory usage, ultimately enabling the seamless display of highly detailed vector maps on mobile devices.  We have successfully integrated the proposed algorithm into a ClippingMap-based mobile app, which has been validated through user studies.  A corresponding source code is available online for the sake of replication.  Additionally, we have submitted a design change suggestion to the maintainers of the OpenStreetMap Carto style language in light of our findings.  We have also made available a set of benchmarking datasets used to evaluate the anti-aliasing algorithm. We have also embedded two interactive visualizations that illustrate our anti-aliasing method at both a macro and micro level. This work examines certain types of $U(\frak h)$-free algebras, extending a concept initially explored by Kac and Sharpe. We investigate the properties of these algebras within two specific frameworks: Lie algebras of differential operators on a Riemann surface and the Virasoro and central extension, as well as on a circle. We establish that the Frobénius-Lotay-Vafaee algebras constitute a specific type of $U(\frak h)$-free structure and obtain new finite-dimensional realizations for these algebras. Furthermore, we analyze the locus in the Brieskorn-Greuel multivector field space where the structure is realizable and discover that this space exhibits an intricate, multi-component nature. We obtain results showing the realization of certain degenerate and nilpotent $U(\frak h)$-free algebras within the Lie algebra of the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a circle. Additionally, we demonstrate that the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a Riemann surface constitute a degenerate $U(\frak h)$-free structure and derive the Brieskorn-Greuel multivector field space and its multi-component locus. We discuss several fundamental questions regarding the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a Riemann surface that have yet to be resolved. Lastly, we examine the connection between the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a circle and a Riemann surface and derive key implications. We have also made contributions to the field by discovering certain relationships between the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a circle and a Riemann surface and the Monge-Antide Sitter constraint on a 3-manifold. This investigation provides new insights and asks a series of questions that we hope will be resolved in the future. It also reveals that certain degenerate $U(\frak h)$-free algebras have a connection to the formal type of Hamiltonian equations. We examine this connection and discuss how it may be utilized in the study of the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a circle and a Riemann surface. We also discuss how it may be utilized in the study of the Monge-Antide Sitter constraint on a 3-manifold. We derive key implications of this connection, and we hope that it will contribute to a greater understanding of the formal Hamiltonian vector fields on a circle and a Riemann surface and the Monge-Antide Sitter constraint on a 3-man

Social media monitoring, particularly through platforms like Twitter, enables
organizations and governments to gauge public opinion by analyzing sentiment
expressed towards brands, politicians, and other entities. As a widely used
indicator of public feeling, sentiment analysis is increasingly employed to
gain insight into global mood, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. We
have developed a basic, straightforward approach to sentiment analysis using
long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks, showcasing their effectiveness
in this application. Our results reveal that an LSTM structure comprising three
layers can achieve a high accuracy of 90% or higher in classifying the mood of
single tweets. Furthermore, we successfully integrated the use of word vector
models, specifically BERT and FastText, into our LSTM framework to optimize the
performance of the model. Our comprehensive experiment also involved the use of
enhanced datasets that capture the temporal dimension of public sentiment, as
well as two distinct mood targets: simple and complex. These findings serve as
a foundation for more intricate sentiment analysis models, such as those using
graph neural networks, as we explore alternative methods in a companion study. 
Finally, we present two novel applications of sentiment analysis to real-world
problems, including tracking the public mood throughout the year and
identifying correlations between aspects of service quality and the mood of
patrons of restaurants. Our study demonstrates that sentiment analysis can be
a valuable tool for enabling organizations to improve their non-core competencies
and ultimately drive their bottom line higher. Ultimately, we hope to see
systematic data-driven studies like this one spur the widespread adoption of
public mood analysis by businesses and governments seeking to refine their

We propose a novel hybrid model that integrates two distinct supervised learning techniques - naive Bayes and latent space models. Our approach involves predicting industry categories for unlisted companies by training two separate models. The naive Bayes model leverages historical data of listed companies to anticipate possible industries for unlisted companies, while the latent space model utilizes financial ratios and other company-specific information to generate a probability distribution over these industries. Additionally, we develop two auxiliary models that (1) extract key financial ratios from unlisted companies via k-means and (2) assign industry labels to companies based on their financial characteristics. By combining the probabilities from these two routes and incorporating auxiliary model outputs, the model yields an enhanced prediction of industry categories for unlisted companies. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our hybrid model, along with its accompanying auxiliary models, surpasses the performance of two existing techniques on both accuracy and semantic similarity metrics. Furthermore, we show that the model is capable of identifying the most relevant financial ratios for each industry and that the latent space model accurately represents the distribution of companies across different industries. Ultimately, we present a visual depiction of the model's internal structure along with an in-depth examination of its predictive performance. The study was motivated by a research inquiry into the most effective approach to predicting industry categories for unlisted companies and the optimal modeling techniques to accomplish this task. The underlying research data encompasses financial dataset EOD Financial Times, along with associated industry labels and relevant ratio information. The model was implemented over a 10-year period from 2011 to 2021. We performed 10 separate runs of the model, along with two baseline techniques, for every company in the dataset, yielding a total of 115,472 predictions. Additionally, we report outcomes for companies listed on the FTSE 100 index. The source code for the model is available at https://github.com/kleinerklug/HTP. Recent advances in Session-based Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) algorithms have successfully generated personalized item suggestions, outperforming traditional bandit-based methods. However, these breakthroughs have largely centered on the final item suggestion step, overlooking the enhanced understanding of interactive histories that can be gained through intermediate processing. To address this gap, a new framework, CSBRNN, has been proposed, which incorporates a contextualized item encoding module that interprets interactive histories at each step. Utilizing Candidate Rank Embeddings (CARE) to mitigate cold start issues rounded out the design. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated the effectiveness of CSBRNN compared to prominent baselines across two large-scale e-commerce datasets. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of distinct architectural choices was conducted to highlight the significance of intermediate processing in enhancing interactive histories. Ultimately, a two-stage recommendation approach was shown to yield superior suggestion accuracy and a notable increase of up to 15.5% in online conversion rates. The proposed technique, CSBRNN, has potential real-world applications and can serve as a complementary tool to support and augment existing recommendation systems with a particular focus on enhancing interactive histories and online conversion rates. The code for this research has been made publicly available at https://github.com/nphdang/CSBRNN. Additionally, the two datasets employed in this study have been sourced from https://competitions.dciu.io/index.php/competitions/3. This study introduces an original algorithm enabling a coordinated group of autonomous drones to identify and navigate around dynamic group structures composed of point clouds, analogous to bird flocks or school of fish. Unlike existing methods which rely on predefined trajectories or global models, our approach leverages a real-time image processing technique called point set registration to create a collaborative decision-making framework for the drones. This framework allows the autonomous vehicles to maintain formation, adjust to changes within the group structure, and avoid collisions with other vehicles or obstacles without requiring prior knowledge of the environment. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this method through both simulated and real-world experiments using a drone swarm equipped with RGB cameras. Results show that the algorithm achieves high registration accuracy, enabling the drones to adjust their flight path and maintain a consistent group structure at high speeds. Furthermore, their ability to adapt to shifting patterns and identify changing structures allows them to navigate complex environments effectively. Images and data collected during real-world testing validate the findings of the simulated experiments, showcasing the potential of this algorithm to solve complex problems in diverse domains such as insect-inspired robotics, autonomous transportation and environmental monitoring. This study focuses on examining patterns in editing behavior within Wikipedia's article pages to create an automated system for identifying and marking inappropriate content, such as off-topic material and false information. A novel representation technique allows for the accurate identification and modeling of individual hand objects within each frame, while a specialized network tracks the hands and their interactions across the sequence. The reconstruction quality is evaluated through a variety of metrics, including tracking accuracy, reconstruction quality, and user preferences. Our method also presents multiple challenging scenarios to illustrate its capabilities in tracking complex hand interactions, including synergetic movements of the hands and their interactions. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a different approach, focusing on geometric complexity that measures the shape of solutions represented in a given layer's feature space. Interestingly, multiple features of our model architecture, such as batch normalization, residual layers, and high-dimensional representations, contribute to controlling complexity naturally. Through thorough analysis and experiments, we demonstrate that natural regularizers can significantly reduce the complexity of models and improve their performance. Our findings are consistent across various domains, including classification, segmentation, and generation, and can be combined with other forms of complexity control, such as limiting the model's depth, to develop more efficient and effective training methods. The code for our research is publicly available at https://github.com/jaiser/complexity. Our study lays the foundation for a new understanding of complexity control in deep learning and showcases the importance of feature space geometry in shaping the shape of solutions. Additionally, our findings highlight the necessity to examine the used of chain rule and optimizer dynamics in future studies. Our work has implications beyond deep learning, and can be applied to other areas, such as dimensionality reduction and clustering. Our novel perspective on complexity control may lead to innovative ideas, and our experimental results illustrate the substantial performance enhancements that can be achieved through natural complexity control. Our research offers a practical solution to the long-standing issue of controlling complexity in deep learning models, and provides a practical guide for using our findings, titled 'The geometric complexity of deep learning, and how to harness it', which can be downloaded at https://jaiser.github.io/complexity/. Our study is the first to explore the geometric complexity of deep learning models explicitly. Our research provides a practical solution to the long-standing issue of controlling complexity in deep learning models, and offers a new perspective on complexity control that can be applied to various tasks and models. Our study is a significant contribution to the field, and can be applied to improve the performance of deep learning models significantly. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities. 
In contrast to previous RingCT-compatible DPoS schemes, Delegated RingCT effectively addresses privacy-related risks associated with public key exposure in consensus and mixing protocol vulnerabilities, as well as deterministic transaction generation. 
Furthermore, Delegated RingCT facilitates support for stealth addresses without compromising linkability, thus providing stronger anonymity guarantees for users transacting at will. 
A primary drawback of our approach is that it introduces code required for ring signature schemes, which may present computational overhead for low-power devices. 
Despite this limitation, we showcase our developed Delegated RingCT protocol and evidence of its effectiveness. 
In the future, this research could be adapted into evidence of knowledge protocols to provide even stronger anonymity guarantees. 
Lastly, our Delegated RingCT protocol presents a flexible framework that enables integration with diverse DPoS-based consensus mechanisms and RingCT-compatible schemes, thus presenting anonymity solutions for existing cryptocurrencies supporting DPoS. 
In particular, we propose an upgrade to Nano, a DPoS-based cryptocurrency that currently supports RingCT, to use Delegated RingCT for enhanced anonymity capabilities. 
We provide evidence and a prototype of this upgrad, which we subsequently analyse through benchmarking for maintainability and readability. 
Our results demonstrate that Delegated RingCT provides stronger anonymity guarantees compared to the current RingCT implementation in Nano, thus effectively addressing privacy risks for users transacting at will.

We introduce a new concept called space toughness for solving linear systems, which measures how difficult it is to solve certain systems of equations depending on their coefficient matrix properties. Unlike other tolerance metrics, space toughness assesses the hardness of each individual vector in the matrix and applies it uniformly to all vectors, making it both easier to evaluate and more robust. By developing a more straightforward analysis based on space toughness, we prove the stability of both the Conjugate Gradient and Stochastic Conjugate Gradient methods for solving linear systems, a result that is already known to be true with stricter tolerance metrics. We also adapt the space toughness concept to demonstrate the stability of the Stochastic Gradient Descent method for convex minimization problems. A significant advantage of using space toughness is that it allows us to set up a precise connection between the stability of iterative solvers and the properties of the system's augmented matrix, providing a clear way to determine if a particular solver will remain stable when faced with unexpected perturbations of its input data. Finally, we conduct an empirical investigation into the relationship between space toughness and actual solution time for various iterative solvers, and observe that there is a noticeable correlation between these two metrics, offering a potentially valuable prediction tool. We have created a public repository with accompanying code and further details at the website https://space-toughness.github.io/. Additionally, a more comprehensive version of this paper is available through arXiv at the link https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2202.05269. Despite its strategic importance, Hebrew's natural language processing capabilities have been hindered by a lack of high-quality, accurately annotated corpora. The development of UD Hebrew Treebanking and parsing initiatives has been hindered by issues of corpus ownership, web scraping limitations, and inconsistent annotations. Recently, initiatives have been restarted with enhanced resources: UD Hebrew Treebanking has released new versions of its treebank, and the Hebrew parsing task has been revived within the CoNDALE project. In addition to the revamp of UD Hebrew Treebanking, efforts have been made to create new, domain-specific corpora like Hebrew Financial News and Hebrew Cookbooks. These resources have allowed for the evaluation of various NLP models on tasks such as NER, Noun Phrase Identification, and dependency parsing. Notably, models have shown a high level of performance on tasks such as CoNLL-2019 NER and HN Noun Phrase Identification, but have struggled with dependency parsing due to complexities rooted in Hebrew's linguistic characteristics and the availability of training data. As a result, a significant gap in performance has been observed between state-of-the-art general models and those specifically crafted for Hebrew, highlighting the necessity of tailored models in addressing the linguistic challenges of this language. These newly developed resources have also enabled the exploration of various BERT-based models on Hebrew, including the evaluation of models transferred from English and others fine-tuned on Hebrew datasets, on tasks such as CoNLL-2019 NER and HN Noun Phrase Identification. We establish a dimension decrease principle for incompressible subsets of $\ell_p$. Given a finite-dimensional subspace $V$, and a constant $\delta>0$, if a bounded incompressible subset $A$ of $\ell_p$ meets the condition that for any non-zero scalar $\varepsilon$-isometry $T$ mapping from $V$ to $\ell_p$, the image $T(V)$ remains contained in $\delta A$, then $A$ can be expressed as the union of a countable collection of at most $2^{\frac{n}{p}}$ dimensional subspheres, each with a radius of $\delta$. Furthermore, under the same $\varepsilon$-isometry conditions, we find that a bounded incompressible subset $B$ of $\ell_p$ can be expressed as the union of a countable collection of at most $2^{\frac{n}{p}}$ dimensional subspheres, each with a radius of $\delta$. Consequently, we derive that a bounded incompressible subset $C$ of $\ell_p$ can be expressed as the union of a countable collection of at most $2^{\frac{n}{p}}$ dimensional subspheres. These results generalize the dimension decrease principle originally formulated for $\ell_1$ by P. Shtrihel and S. Vittler. Additionally, we define a new concept called 'local $Q$-isometry' for $\ell_p$ for $1<p<\infty$, and prove that a bounded incompressible subset $D$ of $\ell_p$ can be expressed as the union of a countable collection of at most $2^{\frac{n}{p}}$ dimensional subspheres. These results have been proven with the use of a novel technique called the 'dimension drop lemma'. This technique is based on a property of $\ell_p$ for $1<p<\infty$, which states that for any $\varepsilon$-isometry from a $n$-dimensional subspace to $\ell_p$, there exists a $t$-isometry from a $(n-1)$-dimensional subspace to $\ell_p$ for some $0<t<\epsilon$. This property is further analyzed in theorems 1.2 and 1.3 which provide conditions and consequences related to its occurrence. Also, a new criterion called the 'local $Q$-isometry criterion' which characterizes when this property can be utilized has been formulated.

Future-proof 5G networks require an intelligent, autonomous framework that can make data-driven decisions without human intervention. Key aspects of these management procedures include positioning 5G radio units, allocating network resources, and coordinating mobile terminal data paths. Our work is exemplified through a stable and sustainable network scenario where renewable energy sources feed a series of discrete green radio towers spanning various landscapes. We employ the concepts of auto-matized administration and digital twin(s) to efficiently optimize the placement of these radio units and accurately predict the long-term impact on electrical consumption, thereby identifying the most suitable locations for sustainable operation. Furthermore, our proposed framework dynamically adjusts 5G terminal data paths to minimize electrical consumption while ensuring that all mobile terminals maintain seamless connectivity at all times. This is effectively achieved through the use of an autonomous search mechanism operating within a simplified digital twin model of the green radio network. As a result, the electrical consumption of 5G networks is optimized, thereby preventing CO2 emissions into the atmosphere and aligning with the objectives of the Sustainable Communication Systems initiative. This research explores the feasibility of creating a neural voice model without access to labelled data or translation tools, relying solely on audio recordings of spoken sentences to generate new speech. By analyzing acoustic patterns within spoken data, this approach identifies units for synthesis. As human-like speech includes both phonetic and prosodic elements, and current neural models fall short in capturing the latter, a complementary algorithm is developed to extract melodic (rhythmic and syllable stress) information from acoustic units. Furthermore, a model learning objective called the Transposed Convergence of Proximity (TCP) has been devised to improve low-quality unit extraction by comparing and matching similar sequences. Experimental results for a given language show that this method surpasses baseline expectations in voice synthesis quality when evaluated against human listeners. Additionally, a relevant metric called Melodic Distortion has been proposed to quantify the difference in melodic elements between generated and reference speech. It has been observed that reducing melodic distortion yields improvements in voice synthesis quality. Consequently, a strategy called Melodic Refinement has been developed to correct the melodic structure of units extracted during the training process. When combined with TCP, this technique leads to significant improvements in voice synthesis quality. Consequently, a new system called ZEROSYN has been created, combining the principles of TCP, Melodic Refinement, and a supervised neural network for voice modeling. While initially intended for languages with untested voice data, this approach has also improved the quality of existing Chinese voice models, demonstrating its broad applicability. Moreover, ZEROSYN has successfully generated new speech with a degree of phonetic accuracy and voice quality comparable to human standards for a given language. Furthermore, analysis of generated speech reveals that phonetic errors often relate to corresponding tone errors. Consequently, a related algorithm has been developed to extract and represent tone units as well as to improve the accuracy of phonetic analysis. When integrated into the existing system, these new algorithms yield generated speech with enhanced voice quality and phonetic accuracy. Finally, a new neural voice model architecture called TAC-BELL has been devised, combining the previously proposed algorithms and components, as well as new ideas such as the extraction and representation of acoustic units, the Transposed Convergence of Proximity training objective, and the Melodic Refinement algorithm. It has been observed that this approach leads to voice synthesis quality ratings from human listeners that are superior to previously published standards. Consequently, TAC-BELL is rated the best available voice model for a given language. Moreover, related work has been undertaken to improve existing voice models

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by large problem dimensions. We've developed a multi-step optimization method involving separate convex optimization stages for a custom-designed nonlinear problem. Each optimization phase incorporates locally-tailored data-driven approximations to nonlinear constraints based on clear alternative formulations and a novel factorization approach for faster construction. The proposed technique is particularly suitable for optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion. Comprehensive simulation results validate its efficacy in a diverse set of scenarios, outperforming existing motion planning methods in terms of efficiency and scalability. Moreover, we've successfully demonstrated its practical application in generating feasible trajectories for a multi-limbed robot using a 3D printed prototype. Experimentation with varying problem sizes has shown the algorithm's scalability, with problem sizes that weren't feasible with previous methods becoming solvable. Lastly, data-driven model reductions have been found to substantially reduce processing times without incurring solution quality losses. This model was developed by considering key factors such as the shape of the cup, its movement caused by horizontal forces, and the influence of gravity. To analyze the movement of the coffee, we created equations that account for its rotation and the shift in its center of gravity due to sloshing. These equations were then applied to examine the phenomenon of sloshing and how it relates to the physical properties of the liquid and its container. We explored various scenarios, including the occurrence of sloshing and its potential consequences, such as spilling, and the effects of modifying the shape of the container to prevent sloshing. This study provides a mathematical framework for understanding the phenomenon of sloshing and how to mitigate it to prevent spills. It also includes a discussion on how to optimize the design of containers to reduce spills and splashes during transportation. We propose an approach for further research that involves numerical simulations to create an engineering guide for designing containers that minimize liquid spills and splashes. This framework can be applied not only to our study but also to other types of containers, such as those used for electronics transportation. We believe that our mathematical model can be a valuable tool in the development of more resilient packages for the safe transportation of sensitive equipment. Additionally, we acknowledge the relevance of this research to the field of engineering and package design and express our hope that our work will contribute to the development of innovative and reliable designs capable of withstanding the stresses of transportation. Lastly, we recognize the importance of our findings and how they can be applied to spark new ideas in package design. We envision that our research will inspire engineers to devise clever solutions to prevent damage to their products during transportation, such as using custom-shaped containers or specialized packaging materials. We are confident that our mathematical model will promote a more efficient use of resources, as it enables engineers to assess the effectiveness of different design alternatives before proceeding with production. We believe that our research will ultimately lead to greater economic efficiency through more rational design approaches. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to the development of a more sustainable environment by reducing the costs associated with product damage, which in turn will decrease the waste generated by undamaged products that are discarded due to transportation-related damage. We see this research as an opportunity to foster a more environmentally conscious design practice and promote the use of innovative, efficient designs that minimize damage and the resulting environmental impacts. In the context of machine learning, a network of autonomous agents works together to build a joint model by exchanging information through a coordinated communication process. Despite its potential for large groups, this cooperative approach has limitations due to the scope of its communication. A new challenge has emerged with the growing importance of ensuring model security and compliance with data protection regulations, which can be easily compromised even in relatively simple networks. Focusing on the particular case of Gaussian data, this research presents a robust cooperative learning method that protects against malicious outsiders while training on secure networks. By combining robustness and cooperation, this algorithm's communication requirements are minimal, allowing it to efficiently combine large datasets from multiple agents without compromising the overall model performance. A thorough evaluation against various baseline cooperative learning methods has shown that it consistently yields the best results, demonstrating the significant benefits of robustness against the costs of communication. A real-world test also confirmed that it effectively protects against potential data breaches in cooperative learning. Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which high-velocity protostellar jets form and influence surrounding low-velocity outflows was studied. These high-velocity jets are thought to be the initial low-density flows that develop during the early stages of protostar formation, eventually evolving into slower moving jets that are commonly observed. To investigate this relationship, we ran detailed numerical models of the protostar formation process. Our findings show that high-velocity jets can efficiently generate surrounding low-velocity outflows through a process of fluid advection. However, the rate at which this outflow expands and moves away from the protostar is largely dependent on various physical factors, including its rate of mass accumulation and boundary layer size. For example, an increase in mass accumulation by a factor of ten leads to an expansion of the outflow size from 100 astronomical units to 1,000 astronomical units. Additionally, changes in boundary layer size affect the rate at which the outflow expands but have little impact on its speed. Lastly, under certain conditions where the protostar formation process is slowed, the low-velocity outflow expands in a cuspidal shape rather than a cone, shaping the surrounding material into a concave envelope. Ultimately, high-velocity jets have the potential to significantly influence surrounding low-velocity outflows and are an essential component of the protostar formation process. Their interaction also provides a viable explanation for the varying shapes and dynamics of jets that have been observed during protostar formation. This research also confirms that high-velocity jets are an inevitable byproduct of the protostar formation process and can efficiently drive surrounding low-velocity outflows. Their contribution is most pronounced during the initial stages of protostar formation and becomes less significant as the protostar formation process advances. At this stage, high-velocity jets can no longer efficiently drive surrounding low-velocity outflows and become less important. In order to accurately study this process, models must account for the formation and evolution of high-velocity jets. Our simulation results demonstrate the potential for a positive feedback loop between high-velocity jets and low-velocity outflows, where the high-velocity jets aid the development of low-velocity jets, which in turn help to drive the high-velocity jets towards the protostar. This process has been observed in various protostar formation observations and is an essential component of the protostar formation theory. By deriving an analytical model and comparing it to numerical simulations, a detailed analysis is conducted to evaluate their characteristics. Specifically, the study examines how these resonances evolve over time, the impact of superimposed resonances, and the influence of perturbing forces. Additionally, it identifies reliable indicators to accurately predict resonant activation and provides statistical evidence to confirm its reliability. For complex objects, extracting category-level information from limited visual cues is crucial. In this research, we tackle the problem of perceiving category-level information for existing 3D objects by leveraging semantic keypoints. Specifically, we focus on estimating an object's pose and overall shape from partially observed keypoints on an image or point cloud. To achieve this, we develop two key contributions. Firstly, we define a novel geometric model that captures the intrinsic shape characteristics of an object relevant to its category. Secondly, we formulate a mathematical framework for determining the most optimal pose and shape representation that fits the given keypoints, accompanied by an efficient and robust optimization algorithm with a strong theoretical guarantee. Furthermore, we provide a framework for assessing the reliability of estimated poses and shapes by quantitatively analyzing their sensitivity to keypoint noise. Through experiments, we showcase the efficacy of our approach on various PASCAL3D+ objects by comparing it with explicit surface-based models, demonstrating improved generalizability and robustness on in-category poses and out-of-category poses. Additionally, our proposed method exhibits superior performance on novel object categories, point clouds, and keypoint noisy scenarios. The proposed approach is available on GitHub under the label "optcatper". For the one-parameter family of Cauchy distributions, deriving the mean and developing methods for the central limit theorem appears to be impossible. In this research, these challenges are overcome by first deriving a closed-form expression for the Cauchy probability function's second derivative, and subsequently using it to develop an exact method for estimating parameters based on sample squares. Building on this framework, this study also proposes a novel approach for constructing confidence intervals and squares for the Cauchy distribution using four distinct estimation methods, including the median absolute deviation-based method, the running trimmed mean, the running median, and an alternative approach (to be referred to as the OAM). Additionally, this investigation examines the performance of these proposed interval and square constructions for model selection, hypothesis testing, and forecasting in the context of rare events analysis. A series of numerical simulations demonstrate the efficiency of these new methods, and a real-world data example is also provided to illustrate their practical utility. A new statistical approach is developed for basket trials to assess the sample size required for identifying meaningful differences between treatment groups. This approach considers multiple subpopulations in a basket trial as separate clinical trials and uses Bayesian methods to calculate the required sample size, allowing information to be shared across these subtrial groups. The proposed method validates trial assumptions through Bayesian predictions, thereby accounting for uncertainties and relying on prior knowledge when available. The method has been shown to control type I errors for each subtrial group and to accurately detect meaningful differences when they exist. The performance of this approach is equivalent to that of a frequentist analysis combining data from all subgroups and maintains statistical power when subgroups are homogeneous. The method also enables simultaneous inference across multiple subgroups and facilitates Polychotomous Bayesian analysis. A numerical example and software implementation are provided to illustrate the approach. The findings suggest that it is beneficial to assess heterogeneity before determining the required sample size for a basket trial. The proposed method offers a reliable solution for such trials. To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in industry, advanced motion control systems must now be capable of auto-tuning for a wide range of applications without the need for manual adjustment. Traditional static auto-tuning methods fall short due to their failure to account for the unique characteristics of each individual system. This paper presents a innovative solution, leveraging linear parameter-varying (LPV) control techniques to develop a new auto-tuning approach. By incorporating an LPV sequential loop tightening algorithm derived from polyhedral robust control, this method is capable of automatically adjusting motion control systems to be both stable and highly precise without the need for manual calibration. Furthermore, the proposed LPV controller was found to outperform traditional controllers by a significant margin, with measured performance improvements of up to 40% in terms of tracking precision and 30% in terms of stability robustness. This research presents a groundbreaking solution for the automatic tuning of motion control systems, paving the way for increased efficiency and productivity in a wide range of industrial settings. We introduce a general framework, PRNet, for aligning partial point cloud views of the same object. Unlike existing methods, PRNet does not rely on a fully visible reference pose or complete 3D object models. It learns pose-invariant features and a canonical pose independently from a large dataset of aligned partial views. In both supervised and unsupervised settings, PRNet uses self-supervision from pairwise partial view alignments. We evaluate PRNet on three challenging datasets: partial pose, ego-centered pose, and full pose. Notably, PRNet achieves the top performance in the partial pose setting, and its unsupervised version performs similarly to supervised methods on the ego-centered and full pose datasets. The code for PRNet is available on GitHub at https://github.com/moabarker/PRNet.

The sparse annotations are then distributed across multiple segments by aligning image features with segment labels. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$. Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions on these operations to guarantee the norm-preserving property of $C_\varphi^{\ast}$ and $W_{\psi, \varphi}^{\ast}$ in relation to the given operations $C$ and $\psi$. It is also shown that under appropriate conditions, $W_{\psi, \varphi}$ can be expressed as a product of $C_\varphi$ and an additional operator for a particular choice of $\psi$. This study presents a comprehensive exploration into the properties of C-normal weighted composition operators within the context of the Hardy space $H^2$. As a result, this work is a significant extension of previous research by Koh and Ricker on the properties of $C$-normal composition operators. This particular research is a published finding by Ye and Su. The connection between this current research and the previously mentioned works by Koh and Ricker is established. This study presents a novel approach to addressing questions regarding the norm-preserving property of $C_\varphi^{\ast}$ and $W_{\psi, \varphi}^{\ast}$. Additionally, this work presents a new method of characterising the properties of $W_{\psi, \varphi}$. This information is then presented in a concise manner. As a result, this study can be expressed as a new version of the characterisation of $C$-normal operators presented in Theorems 3.16 and 3.17. This paper delves into the examination of p-core p'-sequences and their characteristics under modulo p. Notably, when p is 2, the investigation aligns with work by Kesten and Reid, yet the generalization to larger p reveals a distinct and complex phenomenon. Specifically, as p grows infinitely large, the probability that a randomly generated p-core p'-sequence, denoted as $\omega_n$, contains p-1 ones approaches 0. This outcome underlies a particular geometric configuration on a d-dimensional cube and is closely related to a specific graph walk starting at the origin $\mathbf{0}$ in $d$-dimensional space. This graph walk can be represented as the sum of $a_i$ where each $a_i$ corresponds to the $i$th element of a randomly generated vector $\mathbf{x}$ in a set of uniformly distributed vectors $\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{Z_p}^n\}$. Furthermore, when p is even, the probability that this sum falls within the range $[-1,1]$ simplifies to $\frac{p+1}{2p}$, yet for odd p, the probability that this sum lies within $[-\frac{p-1}{2},\frac{p-1}{2}]$ is estimated as $1-\frac{p-1}{p^2}$. Notably, this result shares a striking resemblance with the Euler-Mascheroni gamma function at an infinitely large p. Finally, the findings suggest that further generalizations to sequences containing more than two ones could yield highly intricate and intricate results. It is hypothesized that such a probability distribution could play a significant role in evaluating the correctness of conjectures in other mathematical problems. We calculate the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces V of finite dimension. This is based on developing a model for the circle action on the ungraded elliptic cohomology theory of V. Specifically, we demonstrate that for V of dimension 2n-1, its logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology ring is defined as the polynomial ring governed by the variables $x_0, \ldots, x_{2n-1}$. Furthermore, in this study, we also establish a model for the functors $R^{circle-equiv}(X;\ell)$. Here, X is a complex projective space of dimension 2n, and $\ell$ ranges over all positive integers, representing a logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology functor of level $\ell$. Our research investigates the impact of a sound ground surface on impact response in a system-bonded ground model, consisting of a mass-spring-damper supported by a ground model defined as a series of coupled springs. We found that the ground system's frequency response is influenced by the sound wave generated by an impact, but this influence diminishes as the impact energy increases. Additionally, the peak amplitude of the sound wave does not reach the maximum predicted value by the Rayleigh-Jeans law, which suggests a sound wave amplitude of $\sqrt{8kT\gamma}$ for high-energy impacts, where $k$ and $\gamma$ represent Boltzmann's constant and the specific heat ratio, respectively, and $T$ represents the temperature in Kelvin. We also observed that the time it takes for the sound wave to reach its maximum amplitude is longer for higher-frequency components and longer propagation distances. Furthermore, the peak frequency of the sound wave does not equate to the system's natural frequency but rather follows a resonant pattern in frequency response plots. These findings were obtained through numerical simulation using high-resolution images and a range of 1- to 256-fold spatial and temporal financing techniques. The simulated system exhibited a stable equilibrium with the ground wave amplitude decaying over time in experiments using a perfectly coupled system and the absence of scattering or absorption processes. Scattering processes were found to broaden the peak and reduce the peak amplitude by at least a factor of two, while absorption processes were found to cause a shift in the peak frequency and reduce the peak amplitude by at least a factor of two compared to a system without absorption processes. A theoretical model derived from the system's equations was found to accurately reproduce the numerical simulation results at both low and high energies. Furthermore, the theoretical model was verified against and compared to two other models, one based on Boltzmann's maximum entropy principle and another based on a quantum ground state approach. The outcome of this research may be useful in fields such as geophysics and astrophysics, spanning from seismic wave analysis to sound wave generation in space-time, with potential applications including earthquake detection, gravitational wave generation, and sound generation in stars. It also lays the groundwork for investigating the effects of sound waves on the free radiation field and non-equilibrium electromagnetic emission in the laboratory. A well-known theoretical demonstration of Bell nonlocality called the quantum circuit approach has a significant drawback: it only works with non-optimal correlations, which is a problem if you're trying to build a reliable device to prove this phenomenon in a real-world experiment. Our new approach uses a series of unitary transformations and output measurements to create Bell nonlocality without needing those tricky inequalities, and this method works with both optimal and non-optimal input states. Additionally, our approach has the advantage of being easily adaptable to real-world applications of this problem. We've also successfully implemented our idea on an experimental platform using optical circuits, which in turn proved the nonlocality of quantum states in this context. This finding has further connected quantum information principles to practical applications in quantum information processing. A key aspect of our experiment that verifies Bell nonlocality is the detection of four distinct post-click probabilities in our optical circuit setup, which not only surpass previous studies but also opens up new opportunities for quantitative Bell inequality violations in this context. Our discovery also has broader implications and could serve as a reliable resource for generating Bell inequality violations in diverse quantum communication applications. Lastly, our new method has enabled us to devise a more resilient quantum key distribution approach, which has the capability to successfully distribute secure keys under noisy conditions that would previously render quantum key distribution impossible. This breakthrough has significant practical implications and could potentially be employed in future research as a reliable method for generating secret keys in noisy environments. Lastly, our new methods have paved the way for an accurate conversion of secret key rates from any Bell inequality violation, which has profound theoretical implications and could be a valuable tool in future studies of quantum key distribution. This essay offers an examination of Leibniz's views on the calculus, presented through three distinct philosophical approaches.  The first theory, attributed to Calabi, reconstructs Leibniz's ideas within the inherent language of the physical world.  In contrast, the second framework, championed by Arthur, interprets Leibniz's concepts through a non-standard approach rooted in language.  Conversely, the third framework, defended by Wolff, seeks to capture Leibnizian calculus within the parameters of a fully-fledged non-quantitative metaphysics.  Throughout this essay, we will delve into each of these perspectives, before drawing upon recent research from the ontologies of Gurton Hyde and McKenna, to ultimately present an original critique of the third framework.  Upon this critical examination, we construct an argument that the first framework holds superior relevance to contemporary research in philosophy.  Furthermore, our study offers a novel interpretation of the dual approaches inherent in Leibnizian calculus, specifically that these approaches, often viewed as opposing notions, actually subsist in harmonious balance.  This balance is reflected in the fundamental principles underlying Leibnizian metaphysics, where the concepts of general and particular identities find equilibrium through the intersection of these principles.  In contrast, the third framework distorts this equilibrium, substituting a singular metaphysical view with the dual approaches, thus compromising the fundamental balance of Leibnizian calculus.  Ultimately, our defense of the first framework stems from our belief that the calculus itself remains the most authoritative expression of Leibnizian thought, and that any comprehensive metaphysical view must be derived from, and consistently informed by, this very calculus.  In consequence, the first framework emerges as the most suitable vehicle for disseminating Leibnizian ideas related to the calculus, and for facilitating a deeper comprehension of these concepts, particularly in relation to infinitesimal calculus.  Additionally, our study offers a novel distinction between 'first' and'second' reflections, where 'first' reflection signifies the fundamental examination of calculus as a fully-fledged non-quantitative metaphysics, and'second' reflection denotes the subsequent analysis and critique of this metaphysical structure, thereby reversing the traditional approach in the third framework.  In light of this, our study seeks to initiate a'second reflection' on Leibnizian calculus, specifically through the defense of the first framework and the presentation of a critical examination of the third framework. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. Furthermore, a theoretical model for isothermic expansion has been proposed, and the resulting calculations show quantitative agreement with experimental data. Additionally, using newly obtained parameters, internal energies, enthalpies, and Gibbs free energy expressions have been computed, and subsequently used to estimate enthalpy and free energy temperature dependencies. Finally, a fundamental relationship for alkali diatomic molecules has been derived which enables prediction of their rotational and vibrational energy characteristics. All obtained analytical expressions are straightforward, easy to calculate, and accurately quantify thermodynamic properties. These calculations are supported by comprehensive numerical simulations which demonstrate good agreement with experimental data. While some approximations have been introduced, they are justified by the fact that any further refinement would merely lead to numerical convergence with experimental results. Thus, this model can be utilized for accurate and reliable thermodynamic assessments in the group of alkali elements. Such analyses could be instrumental in resolving a number of outstanding problems in this field, such as identifying correct phase diagrams, developing accurate equations of state, and initiating a thermodynamic analysis of chemical reactions. Moreover, this work is a crucial step towards developing a theoretical framework for ionic thermodynamics in accordance with the principles of quantum mechanics and relativistic quantum field theory. All derived equations are incorporated into an openly accessible online database for alkaline elements (available at https://db-ion.ru/). Predicting time series data in complex systems, such as power and climate forecasting, often relies on intricate models that account for interdependent variables. A widely adopted approach, multidimensional time series prediction (MTP), seeks to forecast multiple time series variables simultaneously, considering their inherent connections. While deep learning models like recurrent neural networks and their variants have achieved notable performance in this context, they have critical limitations:  (i) they assume pre-existing connections between variables and (ii) their comprehensive architectures can lead to significant computational overhead and excessive trainable parameters. A novel adaptive graph convolutional network (AGCN) proposed in this study directly learns relationships between variables and mitigates the issues of pre-configured graphs, overly complex models, and excessive trainable parameters. Evaluations on open power and climate forecasting datasets demonstrate AGCN's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines, showcasing its potential for practical use in time series forecasting. The source code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbmanz/ADGCN. This study offers an innovative solution to the inherent challenges of time series forecasting with the adaptive graph convolutional network, providing a valuable tool for real-world application. Additionally, the employed methods can be utilized to improve the underlying data representations, thereby enhancing forecasting performance. Its suitability can be observed in the presented experimental results, where the adaptive graph convolutional network surpasses conventional models on diverse power and climate forecasting datasets. A notable observation from these experiments is that the magnitude of the adaptive parameters is relatively smaller than that of the non-adaptive parameters, while their direction is somewhat comparable. Hence, a plausible hypothesis is that optimizing these parameters may lead to enhanced model behavior. To validate this hypothesis, a novel training regimen was developed to favor the adaptive parameters and consequently the entire model. Consequently, the adaptive graph convolutional network exhibited even better performance than before, with a notable improvement in multidimensional time series forecasting scenarios. As a result, this approach is expected to be quite beneficial in practice. A valuable contribution of this study is also the creation of a multi-dimensional time series forecasting dataset based on adaptive graph convolutional networks. This resource, which is based on real-world data, includes variables with inter-dependent relationships and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbmanz/ADGCN. It can be utilized by the research community as a useful reference for comparable evaluations in the field of time series forecasting. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have largely been verified using laboratory-based techniques rather than on-sky data. A study has gathered a substantial dataset of on-sky measurements which can inform the improvement of atmospheric dispersion models. These on-sky measurements have been used to create detailed maps of atmospheric dispersion across different wavelengths and the results are presented in this paper. It outlines a new approach to characterizing the atmospheric dispersion using a control technique commonly employed in optics and introduces a novel model which integrates the effective refractive index of the atmosphere directly into a simple formula. This model can generate precise atmospheric dispersion models without the need for intricate and potentially misleading differential dispersion formulas. Furthermore, the on-sky dataset is publicly accessible and can be utilized by researchers to compare their models to actual on-sky measurements, ultimately aiding in the development of more accurate ADCs. It is anticipated that this work will contribute significantly to the improvement of telescopic imaging capabilities by providing on-sky validation of atmospheric dispersion models. Ultimately, these measurements will yield refined ADC designs that will minimize residual aberrations in the final images captured by ground-based telescopes. 

Note to Reader: In our initial paper on this subject (Boutin et al. 2022), we introduced the concept of utilizing on-sky measurements to optimize ADCs and proposed a novel approach to characterizing the atmospheric dispersion. This second paper expands upon that idea by presenting a publicly accessible dataset of on-sky measurements which can serve as a benchmark to evaluate the accuracy of ADC models. To address the issue of large models and their high computational costs under multiple instructor supervision, we propose the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) method. PILE works by first using multiple instructors' responses to create a logistic distribution for each student's answer. This is done by calculating the ensemble's logistic function for each student's answer. The top-performing model is then selected by iteratively adjusting the ensemble's confidence levels based on the teachers' feedback and updating the model weights until convergence is achieved. PILE does not require knowledge about the teachers' ratings and can train multiple models simultaneously with shared parameters. The approach offers notable improvements over current state-of-the-art techniques in both convergence speed and performance, with code available at https://github.com/jtimo44/pile. The best performer under the fair settings is the Converged PILE (CPILE) method. We evaluate the efficacy of our method using multiple publicly available datasets, including the AI2 dataset, the MultiInstructorDataset, and the comprehensive collection of science questions known as ScienceQA. This study examines the sparsest solution to a linear problem with a restricted coefficient sum and satisfies a set of linear equation constraints. Due to the non-convex nature of this problem, it's possible for multiple solutions with the same sparsity level to exist. Our research introduces a contnuous reformulation of the Basis Pursuit problem, enabling uniqueness analysis in specific structured measurement matrices. Unlike previous convex relaxations, this approach directly addresses the non-convex problem. Depending on the properties of the matrix, we derive both sufficient and necessary conditions for the uniqueness of the solution. This requires less computational resources and flexibility in matrix elements compared to previous methods. Our results demonstrate that unique solutions exist for homogeneous and rank-one measurement matrices under certain data acquisition scenarios. Furthermore, this approach proposes a candidate for the optimal solution and provides a numerical method to approximate it. Experimental results confirm the proposed solution's high quality compared to other methods. Additionally, our approach introduces an infinite-dimensional l1-minimization problem, which is a continuous analog of the Basis Pursuit problem. This framework can be applied to other problems with similar non-convex constraints and provides a general method for uniqueness analysis and solution approximation. The study also introduces continuous reformulations for Sparse Principal Component Analysis and the Greedy Basis Pursuit problem, confirming the efficacy of this approach for a wide range of applications. The proposed method is implemented in a publicly available Python package on GitHub. The study's findings are based on joint research with Alen Alizadeh, Sebastian Kurle, and Valentin Werner. The novel continuous reformulation of the Basis Pursuit problem and the accompanying theory and software constitute an significant contribution to the field and have not been previously reported. The study is scheduled for publication in the journal Mathematical Programming and has been previously presented at the 2021 Cambridge Optimization Conference. The present work is an extended version of the initial conference publication.
