P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison. Our compiler backend is paired with a resource simulator, allowing for forward processing of P4 programs and the analysis of implemented programs. A comprehensive validation was performed to ensure correct functionality and identify areas for improvement in existing P4 programs. Furthermore, multiple mapping algorithms were implemented and tested on real P4 programs, demonstrating significant potential improvements. Interestingly, our results show that simply reordering the instructions in a program can substantially reduce its resource usage, underlining the complexity of the mapping problem. Ultimately, our open-source compiler backend provides a flexible framework for testing, evaluating, and refining different mapping algorithms and instruction sets. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/p416-compiler/p416-compiler-backend. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have inaccurate vector projections, which may lead to further complications such as convection error and spurious currents in flow simulations. In this study, we introduce two linear scalar transport equations that help correct these inaccuracies, specifically for quadrilateral elements, and propose a corresponding correction strategy for the momentum equation. The feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed correction approach are substantiated through numerical experiments on various test cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the implementation of the correction strategy for quadrilateral elements also improves the accuracy of the corresponding highest-order and triangular Raviart-Thomas elements, specifically when the underlying triangular or quadrilateral meshes are arbitrarily deformed. Additionally, we provide numerical validations of the proposed correction approach for both static and dynamic momentum conservation methods. The outcomes of these numerical evaluations confirm that the proposed correction approach yields superior accuracy for quadrilateral elements, and even improves the performance of the corresponding higher-order and triangular elements. As a result, this correction approach can be utilized as a reliable and efficient fundamental building block for developing more accurate numerical algorithms based on the standard finite element methods. The proposed correction strategy can be easily adapted for use in both static and dynamic momentum conservation methods, and its implementation details are freely accessible on the GitGub repository: https://github.com/epfl-mme-course-619/tree/main/transport-correction. Additionally, the associated Python classes for the conservative and adaptive finite element framework, CADCHeleF, that encompass the proposed correction approach have been documented in the UQ4FluidMechanics wiki: https://wiki.epfl.ch/ucfm/wiki/index.php/FEs_for_Momentum_Equation_with_CADCHeleF. The proposed correction strategy can be generalized and applied to various other finite element discretization schemes that are widely used in fluid dynamics, such as the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, for which the details of the implementation are freely accessible on the GitGub repository: https://github.com/epfl-mme-course-619/tree/main/NS-correction. Similarly, the proposed correction approach can also be employed for analyzing and simulating magnetohydrodynamics, for which the details of the implementation are freely accessible on the GitGub repository: https://github.com/epfl-mme-course-619/tree/main/MHD-correction.

In the field of signal processing, continuous-time estimation problems are often resolved through the optimization of a cost function that integrates past measurements. It can be formulated as a differential problem, which is analyzed in this paper to develop an efficient algorithm. By applying standard techniques to a related functional, we reformulate the optimization as a positive sum involving continuous time Runge-Kutta approximations. Consequently, we propose the Continuous-Stage Runge-Kutta (CSRK) algorithm. We demonstrate its convergence and evaluate its performance in a numerical study compared to established methods. Notably, CSRK offers a flexible framework that can incorporate various discretization techniques, alongside an inherent property of yielding lower error rates than conventional methods. Furthermore, we illustrate the implementation of CSRK through two significant use cases, namely, vehicle location estimation using cellular network cell IDs and vehicle speed estimation using accelerometer data. These examples not only showcase the performance of CSRK but also highlight its potential applications in vehicle tracking. Additionally, CSRK has vast potential in other vehicle tracking scenarios and various other signal processing applications. Lastly, due to the state-dependent nature of CSRK, it is capable of achieving a superior order of convergence compared to previous methods, effectively making it an advanced solution. Therefore, CSRK presents a high-order, state-dependent algorithm that can successfully solve complex signal processing problems. Lastly, the source code associated with this research has been publicly released at a designated repository for public use, which includes the necessary code to replicate the study's results and extend the CSRK algorithm to various applications. Specifically, the repository contains the necessary code to reproduce the figures and results, notably, by reproducing the performance of CSRK and traditional methods under the same experimental conditions, it was observed that CSRK offers significantly improved estimation results compared to conventional methods. This has been meticulously documented and made available for the benefit of the signal processing community. Additionally, the algorithm's code is openly accessible on GitHub for the convenience of researchers and engineers working on vehicle tracking and other signal processing-related tasks. Moreover, a detailed tutorial has been included in the code repository to facilitate seamless integration and use of the CSRK algorithm in a wide array of applications. This encompasses a step-by-step guide on implementing CSRK and is complemented by a collection of pre-written code examples that demonstrate its performance in various use cases. This has been designed to foster the widespread adoption of CSRK among the signal processing community. Lastly, the code has been used to replicate the study's results and showcase the improved performance of CSRK in several vehicle tracking applications.

Human activity recognition (HAR) is a significant task in numerous real-world applications such as healthcare, retail, and logistics. This study focuses on recognizing activities through video recordings. Our primary contribution is the development of a novel hierarchical attention network (HAN) for HAR. This model comprises two interconnected components: the local feature network and the global feature network. The local feature network extracts motion and non-motion features from videos, while the global feature network aggregates information across videos. Notably, our HAN incorporates an attention mechanism at both the local and global levels to optimize feature extraction and aggregation. As such, our model is capable of extracting key information from videos, effectively adapting to activities with high movement frequencies and better aggregating information for complex activities. Through evaluations on three public activity datasets, we demonstrate that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques by achieving substantial gains in recognition performance. Specifically, on the NTU-RGB+D-120KE dataset, our model achieves an overall accuracy of 97.7% for 120 kinematics, surpassing the second-best method by 3.9%. Furthermore, on the CrossUSB and PsTechUSB datasets, our model exhibits average accuracy increases of 4.3% and 2.5%, respectively. All evaluation code and datasets are available for reproduction of results on this website. Additionally, our model has been deployed in activity recognition applications with 10% fewer parameters than comparable models for HAR. As such, our model offers an efficient and optimized solution for adaptive activity recognition. Furthermore, comprehensive experiments were conducted to analyze the behavior and efficiency of our model. Notably, our model exhibits exceptional generalization capabilities, as evidenced by our loss curves and generated feature maps. As such, our model serves as an efficient and generalized solution for activity recognition tasks. Lastly, the efficiency of our model was further validated through hardware implementations on an NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU, where we observed a performance boost of 2.2x for cross-activity recognition on this dataset. The earliest period of the Universe's history, from the Big Bang to the emergence of the first stars, remains largely unknown due to a lack of data and theoretical limitations. The most detailed calculations available today rely on computer simulations, such as the cosmological particle-in-cell code called ENZO. This code was used to simulate the Universe's evolution between redshifts 150 to -1, and the results are reported here. The simulations assume an early Universe composition with neutrinos, photons, and dark matter, and use a sophisticated sub-grid model for star formation and metal enrichment. Two different models based on the initial fluctuations in density are examined: one with simple spherical formation and another with more complex formation sites. The findings include the average rates of star formation, the average masses of forming stars, the average ages of stars at specific metal levels, and the overall mass of all formed stars. These data are then compared, analyzed, and put to use in two proposed methods for estimating the Universe's expansion rate, particularly its critical value for forming stable star particles. This research marks the first attempt to estimate these parameters using a detailed simulation of star formation, and the findings suggest a critical value for the Universe's expansion rate that is in close agreement with other predictive methods. The output of these simulations, along with the critical values for the Universe's expansion rate, has been made publicly available. Additionally, the researchers have developed an online tool for estimating the Universe's expansion rate based on the earliest star formation. Cybersecurity attacks on IoT devices are increasing, and can be traced back to faulty IP cameras which make it easy for attackers to gain unauthorized access. To mitigate this issue, we developed NBcoded, a unique assault detection system using a Naive Bayes model and Deep Neural Network for classifying malicious network behavior. NBcoded detects unusual traffic patterns and identifies system anomalies, specifically tailored for resource constrained IoT devices. By integrating a binary encoder, we successfully reduced the memory requirements of the model, and verified its effectiveness using the KDD99 benchmark dataset and IP camera traffic data. The results showed that NBcoded achieved remarkable accuracy, recall, precision and F1-score values of 99.9%, 99.9%, 99.9% and 99.9% respectively for the KDD99 dataset, and 97.94%, 97.67%, 97.80% and 97.37% for the IP camera traffic data. Additionally, we computed the energy and model size overhead of NBcoded, and found that its naive bayes model achieved a substantial reduction of 24.79% and 67.69% in these metrics respectively, making it an efficient detection method for IoT devices. Finally, our analysis revealed that NBcoded outperformed other classical and deep learning-based detection methods in terms of classification performance. The source code of NBcoded is available at https://github.com/abdelrahmanomran/NBcoded. This project has several significant knowledge gaps that contribute to its innovation: (1) we developed a detection method specifically tailored for IoT devices based on naive bayes model, (2) NAcoded makes the hard decoding of binary labels possible without the need for additional memory, (3) NBcoded achieves a notable reduction in the memory requirements of the model while maintaining high accuracy. These key innovations make NBcoded a pioneering technique in the field of assault detection. Additionally, we found that NBcoded has several practical applications in various detection tasks such as network intrusion detection, and NBcoded can potentially be employed in a wide range of scenarios where resource constrained IoT devices need to detect unusual traffic patterns or anomalies. The underlying mechanism can be attributed to the channelization of waves during multiple scattering processes. In this study, we present various theoretical models that quantify power deposition inside and outside of the billiard. The models rely on eigenchannels formed by wave functions following scattering. The results indicate a strong correlation between power deposition and channel number. The findings suggest that power deposition is more likely to occur near the billiard boundary due to the scattering-induced concentration effect. Additionally, we derive and experimentally validate a universal formula governing the average power deposition ratio inside to outside the billiard. The research provides a foundation for its application and extension to other quantum many-body systems. The approach can also be adapted for studying the thermalization of classical waves in random media. Recent studies conducted at Royal Observatory in Edinburgh used the CALIFA project to examine spiral arms in galaxies and their relationship with spiral structure, velocity dispersion, and star formation rates. Researchers identified a far-reaching spiral arm in the relatively quiet Seyfert galaxy NGC 109, located approximately 67 million light-years from Earth. This far-reaching spiral arm is remarkably similar to another spiral arm in the galaxy NGC 109's twin, NGC 747. Through photometric analysis along spiral arms in multiple galaxies, a far-reaching spiral arm was detected in four additional galaxies. This far-reaching spiral arm was found to be most prevalent in relatively quiet galaxies and those with high stellar masses. However, it was not found in galaxies with extremely high stellar masses or those characterized by intense star formation. Further examination of ten spiral arms in six galaxies, including visual and velocity maps, confirmed that far-reaching spiral arms are typically compressed and characterized by high velocity dispersion. These findings are consistent with models that suggest spiral arms are dynamic and moving features. Researchers hypothesize that far-reaching spiral arms are temporarily existing spiral arm structures formed through a process known as "resonant interaction," where a brief, intense spiral arm structure can persist for millions of years. This theory is consistent with observations of spiral arm fragmentation and the presence of relatively old young star clusters in these arms. Furthermore, it's evident that far-reaching spiral arms are primarily compressed due to the galaxy's central black hole's influence, particularly in the case of NGC 109 where a far-reaching spiral arm passes through the galaxy's very dense, spiral arm core where a supermassive black hole is located. This compression was found to be the strongest in galaxies with relatively weak star formation, leading to the formation of dense star clusters. Data suggest a relationship between the spiral arm's velocity dispersion and the galaxy's central black hole's influence, with a far-reaching spiral arm's presence in galaxies being a signature of a relatively massive central black hole. This research provides evidence of a link between spiral arms and bar structures and reveals that a spiral arm's morphology is influenced by both a spiral potential and velocity dispersion, as well as a central bar and active galactic nucleus. It's also possible that a central bar drives a spiral arm's compression but a central black hole's influence predominates in these cases. A well-established principle in optimization lies in the crossover effect, where combining optimal parents preserves optimal solutions. However, this concept's practical application is contested when optimizing complex, real-world problems using multi-objective optimization or solving a single problem with multiple optimal solutions. In such scenarios, the prevalence and effectiveness of the crossover effect remain unclear and require further investigation. Our research focuses on this knowledge gap by examining the cognitive processes and mathematical foundations of multi-objective optimization and multi-optima problems. Through comprehensive analysis and case studies with various optimization domains, including self-organizing systems and evolutionary algorithms, we demonstrate the rarity of the crossover effect in these scenarios. Our findings contrast with the widespread assumption underlying many artificial life and optimization algorithms. Ultimately, our research calls for a more nuanced understanding and potentially replaces the fundamental principle of the crossover effect with a more skeptical approach. A possible alternative hypothesis is proposed, stating that no universal optimality preservation through crossover exists for any domain. Our study contributes to three distinct areas - multi-objective optimization, multi-optima problems, and optimization theory - and paves the way for further research on multi-objective optimization, proposing three potential directions for future investigation. Additionally, our analysis identifies several intriguing open problems and challenges, along with their implications for the future development of optimization theories and techniques. By critically examining the current knowledge and results, our research aims to facilitate a more accurate and skeptical reasoning in multi-objective optimization and multi-optima problems, thereby promoting a more robust and transferable body of work in artificial life and optimization. A companion document is available that includes detailed algorithmic and mathematical results, as well as comprehensive experimental analysis. It also features an extensive bibliography on optimization that has not been critically evaluated in this study. This resource is part of a larger research endeavor that has produced a series of position papers on artificial life and optimization, promoting a more skeptical and accurate reasoning in these fields. The researched antenna has potential applications in various wide beamwidth antenna systems including vehicular mm-wave communication. Meta-analyses that investigate the relationships between multiple outcomes in the same study are becoming more common, yet statistical methods to analyze such data are limited. Existing approaches often make unrealistic assumptions about homogeneity across studies or rely on approximate solutions. To address these shortcomings, we have developed new methods that include a novel superpopulation model allowing for heterogeneous within-study correlation. Our approach utilizes cluster-robust estimation to analyze the relationships between outcomes while accounting for study-level effects and within-study residual variance. Simulation data suggest our methods perform well, and we apply them to a real-world dataset analyzing the correlation between cognitive and motor impairments in schizophrenia. Our results reveal significant positive relationships between these outcomes, and further analysis indicates the observed correlations are largely driven by a small number of highly productive studies. Our full technical description is available online at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.1101/2020.12.23.421664. Additionally, the relevant R code can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/jbrechinger/cormeta. Our work is currently in revision for publication in Psychosomatic Medicine. If you would like to access the preprint or reproduce the results, please contact the corresponding author. We are also happy to provide updates on the publication status. We discovered that our proposed approach performs comparably or better in several other scenarios such as combining large-scale meta-analyses and performing meta-regression analyses. These additional findings are not included in the original submission but are briefly described here for transparency. We found that our superpopulation model and associated cluster-robust estimators have broader applications than initially demonstrated. Specifically, we found that our model and estimators perform well even when there is no within-study residual correlation, and we provide intuition for this observation through simulation data. We also discovered that our approach can be extended to perform meta-regression analyses, and we found that our estimators often perform better or comparable to existing alternatives in these scenarios. Lastly, we found that our proposed approach can be adapted to accommodate not only continuous but also binary outcomes by leveraging the concepts of Y-consistency and pseudo-residuals. These additional findings are briefly described here for transparency. We plan to revise our work extensively to include these new insights and applications in a future submission. Investigating the source of radiation emitted by uniformly accelerated and static observers in the Hawking/Unruh process is crucial for understanding its physical mechanisms. When an accelerated observer detects the emitted radiation, it is generally considered that the source is the accelerated charge itself, which is supported by both the "physics of particles in a force field" approach and "quantum fluctuations" theory. However, there's a critical missing link in both theories: how and when the charge acquires its partner, the virtual particle, before pair disruption. This acquisition, from quantum fluctuations, is the fundamental source of radiation emitted by the accelerated observer. The absence of this particle is misrepresented in both theories as particle disappearance at the horizon or "unbounded occupation number," which is not actually zero but unmeasurable. This finding reveals that the emitted radiation originates from the accelerated charge's partner, the virtual particle, which is part of a larger picture than previously thought. Consequently, the notions of "virtual" and "unbounded occupation number" should be replaced with "real" and "finite," which is particularly evident when examining radiation emitted by statically expanding charges. This correction brings both theories into closer alignment with one another. Moreover, the emitted radiation's direction and spectrum can be explained by a simple charge-motion model, which further reinforces this correction. Finally, this model's results can also shed new light on the black hole scenario. The key difference between uniformly accelerated and static charges lies in their emission patterns only when an accelerated charge crosses the event horizon, which is primarily a spatial separation issue rather than a temporal one. This finding indicates that the point of no return is actually a meaningful point of reference for understanding radiation emission. The concepts of "outside" and "inside" spaces can be misinterpreted if the emission process's timing is misjudged. Consequently, the notion that the emission process occurs solely "outside" the horizon is inherently correct. This understanding can also shed new light on the point of no return in the black hole context. Additionally, the unrestrained occupation number at the horizon might be seen as a residual effect of unbounded charge distance, which is particularly evident in the static charge scenario with infinite distance. This possibility can also apply to the black hole scenario. Lastly, this corrected picture can also shed new insight on the pair's emission at the horizon in the black hole context. It promises a broader understanding and deeper interpretation of quantum mechanics, particularly the concept of vacuum states, which was initially proposed by Dirac and has since been expanded upon by Wheeler and DeWitt

In the 20th century, mathematical attempts to predict the long-term behavior of the Three-Body Problem yielded limited results. Consequently, astronomers discovered numerous exotic binary and ternary star systems, prompting the development of statistical models to explain their existence. One such model proposed by C. Bennett and O. Steel (Theoretical Astrophysics, 2006) suggests that most short-period binaries originate from a 1:1 resonance, where a passing star disrupts a pre-existing binary system. This model also predicts the binary star's velocity at the time of disruption and the resulting velocity of the ejected star. In an effort to verify their theory, researchers aimed to determine the binary star's velocity at the time of disruption using data from a sample of 47 short-period binaries. By analyzing the data, it was found that the velocity at the time of disruption is consistent with the statistical model, supporting their claims. Additionally, the analysis yielded a precision of 14% for the velocity at the time of disruption, and a 21 arcsec error margin for the 2pi phi velocity, with the possibility of further refinement using more extensive data. Furthermore, the statistical model facilitates the estimation of binary star system parameters, including the binary star's radius, and the mean and distribution of its eccentricity. Ultimately, the findings of this study facilitate the pursuit of a more in-depth examination of the Three-Body Problem, including a comprehensive analysis of the Rosetta mission's trajectory. The proposed approach is poised to become a standard tool in the study of exotic star systems and potentially applied to a broad range of astrophysical phenomena. Additionally, the polarized intensity in the western direction of the remnant is higher than in the east, suggesting that the electron density is higher in the western portion due to the shock interaction with the nearby molecular cloud. In 1942, Erdos posed a problem by querying the minimum size of an $n$-element subset of the natural numbers, taken so that the sum of any two elements from the subset differs from any other subset element. Erdos even provided a general upper limit for this query, estimating that the subset size should be within the range of $2^{n-N}$, where $N$ represents an arbitrarily large and fixed constant. Researchers have since found that subsets of size $2^{n-m}$ satisfy this condition, with the difference being that the sum of any two elements in these subsets may not necessarily be a member compared to a third element. Building on this, we present modified versions of Erdos' problem in three forms. Firstly, we investigate the minimum size required for a subset to ensure that the sum of any three elements is unique. Secondly, we aim to determine the minimum subset size guaranteeing that the sums of any two elements are distinct. Finally, we seek to identify the minimum subset size ensuring that all its element triples have one and only one pair-wise sum. Additionally, we offer answers to these questions for specific exponents and provide new upper limits on the known lower bounds from the original problem by Erdos. The sound speed in dense stellar matter is a crucial component for ensuring a compact star's stability and admissibility as per the Cauchy-Schwartz and maximum pressure conditions in the theorem. Applying these constraints to various nuclear energy density functionals reveals that approximately one-third of them violate these conditions in neutron star matter, with a significant portion of these cases being instances where the sound speed squared in dense matter does not undergo a minimum or even has a flat minimum. Furthermore, our research focuses on dense stellar matter composed of neutrons, protons, and various exotic particles such as kaons, hyperons, quarks, and strange quarks. In our analysis, the admissibility of nuclear energy density functionals is extended to neutron star matter with various exotic components and to various two-fingerprints conditions related to the speed of sound. The results show that many functionals fail to fulfill these additional conditions. The study also examines the admissibility of nuclear energy density functionals in various star types, such as those with strangeness, comprising of neuts, protons, and strange quarks, and in stars undergoing various phases, including quark, neutron, and kaon stars with strangeness. The research reveals that numerous functionals cannot adequately describe the various phases of compact stars with strangeness. The theoretical framework used here can be utilized to extract information about the unknown density-dependent properties of the nucleons by analyzing mass and radius data from compact stars with strangeness. The research demonstrates that numerous low and high-density nuclear energy density functionals cannot simultaneously fulfill Cauchy-Schwartz and maximum pressure conditions in various star types, resulting in a significant discrepancy between predicted masses and the actually measured mass of the PSR J0740+6620 pulsar. The study identifies vast possible density ranges of the incompressibility and symmetry energy and highlights the significant impact of the quark phase on sound speed properties and nuclear energy density functionals. The research also suggests that the speed of sound in dense stellar matter should be a smooth and monotonic function of density. The theoretical framework developed here can be utilized to extract the density-dependent properties of the nucleons by analyzing mass and radius data from compact stars with various components and phases. The research will facilitate future research on nuclear energy density functionals with strangeness and compact stars. The results can be used to analyze various compact star types, resulting in new insights and constraints on their properties. The research paves the way for further studies on nuclear energy density functionals, with a focus on dense stellar matter

We examine a specific model featuring a dilated quantum system composed of two interacting oscillators, one of which is coupled to a thermal bath represented by Bose-Einstein distribution. We look at how the reduced dynamics of the other oscillator, following a sudden separation, impacts its quantum state across the entire Fock space. Focusing on a particular regime characterized by weak coupling and high temperatures, we find that the final state can be either a pure two-photon coherent state or a specific mixture of odd-parity states, dependent on the initial conditions and the energy released during the separation process. Specifically, a specific initial condition leads to a perfect two-photon coherent state as the sole outcome, while other initial conditions result in a specific mixture of odd-parity states. We develop a new mathematical approach based on the Jaynes-Cummings model to analyze these results and provide a framework for understanding the effects of compression and energy loss on the quantum state of a single oscillator following a sudden separation. Additionally, we outline the implications of these findings for the measurement of energy correlations following a sudden separation. Our study offers a framework for exploring the effects of external influences on dilated quantum systems and their subsystems, providing insight into the enduring physical consequences of quantum processes like black holes and compact iftar objects. Our work also lays the groundwork for a broader quantum phenomenon known as the Unruh effect. The findings of our study can be applied to various contexts, such as superfluid ultracold Bose fields, and we suggest an experiment using such a system to measure specific odd-parity coherent states. Furthermore, we outline potential pathways for scaling down our model to utilize quantum information in smaller systems and emerging technologies. During certain types of fluid dynamics, such as rainfall impacting a puddle, highly distorted interfaces occur due to the interaction of multiple fluid phases. The geometry of these distorted interfaces, which are often too complex for standard representation methods like level sets or signed distances, contains vital information for predicting physical phenomena. We propose utilizing a surface skeleton model to characterize the intricate geometry of multiphase interfaces and demonstrate its applicability to two-dimensional and three-dimensional fluid dynamics scenarios. The skeleton transformation produces a sparse, high-level representation of the interface geometry, which enables efficient computation of morphological quantities such as branch lengths and branch splits. We show that this approach enables the accurate computation of morphological statistics from simulated data in two-dimensional scenarios and enables real-time visualizations of three-dimensional interfaces with high fidelity. The implementation details are available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/dskeeler/skeletify. The interface geometry tool is referred to as skeletify in this repository. The technique has potential applications for various other distortion-prone interfaces, such as a jet penetrating a surface or a droplet splitting into multiple fragments. The resulting skeletal representations could provide valuable insights for free surface flow characterization and feature extraction. The code is based on the level set method for tracking multiple fluid phases. The figures in this work depict skeletal representations for (a) a jet penetrating a wall in a jetting flow; (b) a droplet splitting into multiple fragments; and (c) a vortex ring generating an offset interface. The figures in this work also depict skeletal representations for (d) a vortex ring at various stages of creation and evolution; (e) a surface with pores; (f) a solid body with an embedded pore; and (g) a droplet merging with a pool. The figures in this work also depict skeletal representations for (h) a jet penetrating a wall in a jetting flow with an embedded air bubble and (i) a vortex ring generating an offset interface with an embedded air bubble. The proposed approach provides a general, applicable method for high-level representation of distorted interfaces and has potential applications in various fields. The technique has potential applications for predicting physical phenomena related to highly distorted interfaces in fluid dynamics. The interface geometry tool is based on the surface skeleton model and is capable of characterizing the intricate geometry of multiphase interfaces. The technique has potential applications for data analysis and feature extraction in free surface flow characterization. Researchers discovered that the MS2 bacteriophage, a virus that infects E. coli bacteria, exhibits unique and complex behavior when treated with certain chemicals that break down its outer protein coating. This phenomenon was initially observed with simple light-microscopic observations, revealing that the virus particles rotate spontaneously due to inherent physical properties. Employing both physical modeling and high-speed video microscopy, the research reveals that these virus particles maintain overall stability despite external influences, displaying characteristics similar to a torque-free gyroscope in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, the model developed facilitated the prediction and explanation of two critical observations: the specific conditions under which the virus rotates, and the specific angle at which the virus preferentially orients itself when rotated in a controlled environment. This work, bridging physics and biology, uncovers the underlying physical mechanisms governing the behavior of these virus particles, shedding light on potential biomolecular systems exhibiting similar phenomena. Lastly, the research discusses the connection between this physical model and the inherent stability of the virus particle's structure, the capsid. This study may pave the way for the utilization of physical models in the analysis of numerous biological entities exhibiting complex and intricate behavior. The research mentioned above was referenced in a recent review article by Johnson and Brooks, where the virus's behavior was connected to prions and the proposal of creating a 'hall of fame' for misfolded proteins. Additionally, the research has contributed to the emerging field of virophysics, where virus particles are being utilized as simplified models for the study of the behavior and characteristics of macromolecules. The research has far-reaching implications and recommendations for the field of structural biology. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies, which make up 11% of the S galaxies, have distinct characteristics including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates. U galaxies predominantly have spiral arms oriented 90 degrees with respect to their warp, and their spiral and arm features are more fragmented compared to S galaxies. Our data also show that U galaxies have a higher rate of tidal disturbances and a higher central mass-to-light ratio than S galaxies. Notably, U galaxies tend to be more frequent in galaxy clusters and superclusters. Following a phenomenon similar to jellyfish star formation, U galaxies experience increased star formation along their curved edges. Unlike S galaxies, U galaxies do not display this increase in star formation. Our findings suggest that tidal forces, likely caused by a massive forefather galaxy, are responsible for the unique spiral orientation and the massive galaxy cluster concentration of U galaxies. This led to the proposal of two main theories: the 'fish' becomes a 'jellyfish' or the 'jellyfish' becomes a 'fish'. Our research provides new insights into the complex and dynamic nature of galactic evolution. Our research also reveals that U galaxies are more likely to be associated with large galaxy clusters and have distinct star formation characteristics. Additionally, we found no evidence to support the abundance of U galaxies in isolated systems. Instead, we observed a sharp increase in U galaxies within a galaxy cluster and supercluster comparison. This led us to the key discovery that galaxy clusters may play a crucial role in shaping galactic disks through tidal forces, ultimately leading to unique spiral arm formations and massive galaxy transformations. Our research lays the groundwork for future studies on galactic evolution and the intricate processes governing the dynamic lives of galaxies. To further explore our findings, we gathered over 1,000 unique U galaxies from various catalogues and conducted new observations using e.g. Gemini, MaNGA, and photometric catalogues. Our research further reveals that tidal interactions are a dominant factor in the formation and evolution of galactic disks. To further establish the connection between galaxy clusters and the unique spiral arm formations, we analyzed numerous galactic disks in superclusters and supergroups. Our research indicates that major tidal interactions are required to break down galactic stability, ultimately leading to unique spiral arm formations and massive galaxy transformations. To further disentangle the complex evolution of galactic disks, we conducted new observations and analyzed massive galaxies and galaxy clusters

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, this research has implications for understanding the behavior of the solution to the Dirichlet problem for the Laplacian on these manifolds and its converse. We have also provided an example that confirms a specific critical dimension threshold for this type of manifold. Furthermore, this research can be extended to analyze the behavior of the gradient of a harmonic function in this context, yielding another significant finding. Lastly, this research can be adapted to examine the configuration space of a particular type of particle, thereby providing a geometric interpretation of its moments. The presence of these chiral phonons is caused by the inversion symmetry breaking within the cubic structure. Using a technique called density functional perturbation theory, researchers calculated the dynamic atomic positions and phonon properties. Notably, the calculated results matched experimental findings from x-ray scattering experiments. What is more, the researchers discovered that the chiral nature of the phonons can be influenced by an applied electric field. This influence, however, diminishes at room temperature due to the presence of phonon-electron coupling and temperature-dependent phonon dissipation. Finally, the researchers found that the chiral phonon frequency, although sensitive to temperature, remains non-temperature-dependent. This is consistent with the idea that the chiral phonon is not affected by temperature-dependent mechanisms in these materials. Lastly, potential applications and future research directions have been identified. We calculate the non-adiabatic Born effective load in several three-dimensional metals. The Drude weight is also determined for each metal and we find that the Born effective load is indeed proportional to it, as expected from an adiabatic treatment. However, the proportionality constant varies with the type of Born effective load considered (conventional or quasi-adiabatic/adiabatic). Furthermore, the Drude weight is found to be insensitive to ultraviolet cutoff effects within a reasonable range. Moreover, quasi-adiabatic and adiabatic Born effective loads converge quickly as the ultraviolet cutoff distance increases and perform similarly to the conventional load for low-frequency and long-distance comparisons. All calculations are done using a simple Debye model for the density of states. The ratio of the conventional Born effective load to the Drude weight is presented for a range of metals across several rows of the periodic table and we find that it decreases roughly linearly with the row number. This result, along with previous observations, suggests a general (not just next-nearest-neighbor) linear relationship between the conventional Born effective load and the Drude weight for any metal, as long as the density of states is described by a Debye model. We examine the extension of this characteristic to nonlinear effects, leading to the discovery of a novel phenomenon. A time-reversal-symmetric electric current arises in response to a magnetization gradient, independently of its spatial gradient's direction. Moreover, a typical scenario is found where the magnetization responds to a constant voltage, giving rise to a covariant Witten effect. By considering a gap opened by a Higgs mode in a topological insulator with a half-integer quantum Hall effect, we find that the emerging local critical indices exhibit consistency with the established theories on both the electrical and thermal responses. Consequently, the observed behavior in this critical scenario exhibits a complete correspondence with the three-dimensional quantum critical points characterized by a noncompacted spatial structure. The obtained results are in accordance with the proposed universality classes in the field. A proposal for an experimental detection of the nonlinear magnetoelectric influence is also presented. Lastly, the found relationships are anticipated to be applicable not only to other types of topological insulators but also to a diverse range of other systems exhibiting a topological response in their dynamics. We provide a proven sound and complete definition for the intrinsic semantics of the random lambda calculus. By integrating a sequence-valued semantics derived from Bierman and Krishnaswamy's abstract machines, our definition encompasses the fundamental properties of the random lambda calculus. Furthermore, we derive a corresponding relational semantics, allowing for the precise description of the calculus's high-level properties, including strong may-test and probabilistic termination. To confirm the correctness of our development, we formally establish a strong connection between the relational semantics and the internal consistency of the effects monad that underlies the random lambda calculus's type theory. As a significant consequence, we demonstrate that the monad is internally consistent, since we prove that the relational semantics of the unit and composition operations accurately reflect the algebraic laws of the effects monads. Moreover, our result implies that the monad is compatible with the Forth and Hyland-Ong lifting techniques. Following a similar approach, we define and justify the semantics for the probabilistic and dependent type theories of Wadler and the bandera group, as well as for the P- and Q-monads. As an alternative, we also provide a Curry-style composition theorem for the relational semantics of the random lambda calculus, as well as for probabilistic dependent type theories. Furthermore, our paper includes a series of related open problems and conjectures. Finally, the entire development has been implemented in Coq and made publicly available at https://plott.github.io/quantific/quantific coq/.html. The project has also been announced on the POPLMark list as the "quantific" challenge. The results in this paper have been announced first at TPHC 2019 and were subsequently further developed and refined through interactions with the type-theory community. In software development, designers utilize various techniques to visualize their thoughts and overcome creation obstacles, with design discussion documents serving as a valuable tool to document their reasoning and solutions. Natural language extraction methods can streamline the process of applying design decisions to implementation, but current approaches yield inconsistent results due to the novel nature of design documentation and limited availability of relevant research. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing an innovative technique to summarize design discussions and conclude new discussion topics implicitly present within the content. The proposed method achieves superior outcomes in Conclusion Stability, demonstrating robust conclusions and flexible applications that can be adapted for different design documentation types. The results show that this approach outperforms existing natural language processing techniques, with further analysis highlighting the benefits and potential applications of this technique in design documentation extraction. The findings and findings' implications are presented in detail. The source code for this approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AzherSh/dde and the model's pre-trained data can be accessed at https://azher.sh/dde. Experimental data is available on Dropbox at https://dropbox.com/home/AzherSh.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter. It posits that these phenomena arise from the coherence and persistence of cosmic vacuum states following inflation. Specifically, dark energy stems from the initial conditions of space-time, dark matter results from the interaction between free particles and the matrix-like holographic structure of the universe, and gravity emerges as a retro-causal effect stemming from the unstable Higgs-Goldstone state. Furthermore, this theory predicts the universe should exhibit spherical symmetry, and offers potential explanations for cosmic anomalies such as the distribution of large galaxy clusters and the discrepancy between observed and predicted temperatures in the cosmic microwave background. It also proposes that black holes are transient phenomena and that entropic forces play a role in the universe's evolution. Ultimately, this theory suggests that the fundamental laws governing the universe are quadratic, and that the universe's complexity arises from the interplay between quantum fluctuations and the meta-stable Higgs-Goldstone state. As such, this theory predicts that the fundamental laws governing the universe should exhibit symmetry at very small scales and that the speed of light may not be constant in the vacuum state. However, the theory requires further development to accurately predict the gravitational force between small objects. This study focuses on the area of imitation learning, specifically tackling tasks where an agent is unable to receive instructions because the instructions would require an understanding of the expert's perspective, expertise that can't be obtained. We present a novel approach, 'MIMO,' where an agent learns to mimic various behaviors by observing multiple experts working on distinct tasks. Unlike traditional expert demonstration methods, MIMO doesn't involve the expert's actions but instead relies on the observations from each expert. We test this approach with three practical scenarios: 1) crossing roads for self-driving vehicles, 2) cooking tasks in a kitchen, and 3) navigating through forest paths. MIMO successfully applies to these tasks and others without needing task-specific algorithms, expert-specific modeling, or reinforcement learning. MIMO's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art performance in these scenarios, indicating its efficiency and effectiveness. We also investigate MIMO's capacity to generalize between tasks and note that its success is largely driven by the expert behaviors being consistent within each task. We hope MIMO can serve as a basic framework for addressing imitation learning challenges that require an outsider's perspective. Current state-of-the-art neural automatic speech recognition and translation systems heavily rely on large amounts of carefully annotated data. Yet, it's uncommon to have access to such precision, especially for lesser-resourced languages, due to the time-consuming and resource-intensive annotation process. This paper proposes a pioneering approach, called MEDA, which leverages unannotated speech data to create training data with minimal effort. MEDA relies on the listener's ability to provide basic quality feedback to improve speech translation, without needing complex external tools. It achieves this through a multi-task model trained on pairs of speech, translation, and quality assessment. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify a single garment's incompatibility with an outfit. To address this limitation, we introduce VICTOR, the Visual Incompatibility Transformer, capable of accurately identifying a single garment's incompatibility. VICTOR's multi-modal architecture combines a fashion-specific image-learning capability, attained through contrastive pre-training on a massive fashion dataset, and a fast Transformer encoder that processes input images as a whole. By leveraging the full image content, VICTor captures a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of incompatibility, resulting in significantly improved performance compared to traditional classification methods and even outperforms text-based generation methods in certain scenarios. Experimental outcomes also demonstrate that with minimal fine-tuning, the pre-trained model can generate compatible suggestions for an incomplete outfit, saving computation and potentially incorporating other forms of input (e.g., user preferences). The full code and demo are available on GitHub at https://github.com/stevejpang/VICTOR. We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces using the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the original and transformed surfaces interact in specific geometric and analytic terms. Additionally, we explore examples of compact isothermic surfaces with this particular quadratic differential and determine the resulting transformed surfaces in each case. Lastly, we conjecture that certain properties of the original surface imply analogous characteristics of the transformed surface. However, this conjecture holds true only for a specific limited set of surface configurations. On the other hand, we demonstrate that a particular known surface - specifically a compact surface known as the Chow surface - undergoes a generalized Calapso transformation. Importantly, this finding resolves an previously open question regarding a particular isothermic surface configuration. Moreover, our analysis also yields insights into generalized Darboux and Calapso transformations across multiple surface types. This review focuses on estimating a nonparametric conditional expectation function, which an application-oriented reader may find beneficial. The review is organized such that the initial sections introduce the essential estimation methods and assess their efficiency, before moving on to examine the automatic selection of key parameters like the degree of the polynomial and the size of the neighborhood in a weighted least-squares framework. The latter involves a thorough examination of the theoretical underpinnings, followed by a discussion of practical implementation issues. The review concludes with a examination of other important topics not covered in the initial sections. The underlying assumption is that the reader has a basic understanding of the essential concepts in nonparametric statistics, as well as standard estimation methods like least-squares and bootstrap methods. This review does not delve into the specific practical challenges associated with estimating nonparametric conditional expectation functions, as these challenges have been extensively covered in other reviews focused on practical implementation.

The consideration of temporal elements in knowledge graph embeddings has not been thoroughly explored, despite the importance of time in real-world scenarios. This research focuses on developing models for predicting relationships in temporal knowledge graphs. Initially, we thoroughly examined the concepts of time awareness models and evaluated their applications in link prediction tasks. This analysis led us to realize that non-time awareness models can also be effective in tackling link prediction challenges for a significant portion of existing knowledge graphs. Consequently, we propose the use of static models, comprising approximately 50% of the knowledge graph's relationships, as an affordable solution for addressing link prediction in large-scale graphs. This approach is outperformed by time-aware models on a smaller dataset but shows more promising results on a larger scale, also offering comparable performance to models that incorporate additional side information. This discovery indicates that static models can be an affordable and efficient solution for large-scale knowledge graph embedding tasks. The findings of this study can provide insights for developers and researchers on the suitability of static models for link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs. The proposed models, along with evaluation results and code, are available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbq-learn/StaticKG. This repository also includes a detailed tutorial on using static models for temporal knowledge graph embedding. Additionally, the generated models can be found on the knowledge graph embedding server at https://kgeshub.org/. (From https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.00309)

Assuming a perturbing force acts on the fluid that causes it to move, we calculate the fluid's velocity and pressure gradients using fourth-order partial differential equations. Given that the fluid exhibits small deviations from an ideal state, we are able to simplify these equations and obtain an approximation of the fluid's movement under the influence of the perturbing force. This model is validated by comparing its results to numerical data obtained through direct simulation of the fluid's movement using more complex equations. Additionally, we analyze the effects of varying parameters on the fluid's movement and examine the significance of viscosity in the context of this problem. Our analysis also reveals that the assumption of a neutral surface has a non-negligible effect on the results, and that this assumption is not valid in certain real-world scenarios where the assumption of a neutral surface is not met. Furthermore, we observe that the dynamic interaction between the fluid and the solid surface plays a crucial role in the fluid's movement, and that the idealized model of a neutral surface is unable to capture this dynamic interaction. This analysis confirms that the assumption of a neutral surface is a valid one under certain conditions, but that it is not a reliable assumption in all cases. Lastly, we estimate the time it will take for a solid object to come into contact with a solid surface in a scenario where the assumption of a neutral surface is not met, and find that the time it takes for this to occur is on the order of the hydrodynamic timescale. Deep reinforcement learning has achieved significant success in numerous areas, but its applications in computer vision are still limited, particularly for tasks that require precise object localization. A fundamental challenge lies in training a reliable agent that can effectively utilize visual cues from a complex and dynamic visual environment. To address this issue, agents tend to focus excessively on minor variations when the amount of available data is limited, which leads to overfitting. This is analogous to the information-theoretic concept of mutual information upper bound (MIB). Based on this insight, a novel method referred to as MIBRL is proposed, which integrates the information-theoretic concept of mutual information upper bound (MIB) and maximum entropy estimation (ME) into deep Q-learning. The ME component encourages the agent to discover and learn the underlying statistical relationships in the visual environment, while the ME component enforces the independence between visual features and actions. As a by-product, this approach can generate high-quality and informative visual features that can be utilized for various computer vision tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques for vision-based reinforcement learning tasks that require precise object localization. Furthermore, the generated visual features exhibit superior performance in various computer vision tasks. A detailed analysis is provided to explain the underlying mechanisms and how the proposed method achieves better performance compared to existing techniques. A smooth quadric of dimension $n>1$ can be represented by a finite sequence of positive integers $(d_1,\ldots,d_k)$, where each integer $d_i$ is greater than or equal to two, and the sum of the squares of these integers is equal to the sum of the squares of the first $2\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ positive integers plus one. The concept of topological insulators has piqued the interest of both theoretical mathematicians and physicists due to its distinctive characteristics and potential for groundbreaking applications in quantum technology. This briefing delves into the increasing significance of topological insulators, their classification through both numerical and theoretical approaches, and highlights various examples of defective systems, incorporating both experimental and theoretical results from the field. This presentation aims to bridge the gap between numerical and theoretical methodologies, illustrating how advanced mathematical techniques can be utilized to predict and interpret anomalous transport properties observed in defective systems using the Z2 topological invariant. Furthermore, we examine a hypothetical 2D quantum spin Hall system featuring a defect, calculated the dynamic Green's function via the Kubo formula, and found its spectral density to be in direct proportion to the topological invariant $
u$ for both bulk and defective systems. This correlation confirms the predictive capability of the topological invariant $
u$ in determining transport properties, thereby validating the practical application of the invariant $
u$ in interpreting anomalous transport phenomena in defective systems. Lastly, we propose an approach for extending the invariant $
u$ to systems featuring extended, non-local quasiparticle properties by utilising spectral Z2 projections, thereby providing a comprehensive mathematical framework for topological insulators that incorporates both defects and non-local effects. This approach is anticipated to contribute significantly to the development of quantum technologies due to its potential in predicting transport properties at the edge of topological insulators. Ultimately, we conclude by outlining potential future research avenues originating from the complex interplay between topology, defects, and quantum transport phenomena. A collaborative robot's ability to perform tasks efficiently relies heavily on its ability to do physical work together with a human. When humans and robots share a common frame of reference for their collaborative manipulability tasks, it's known as conforming manipulability frameworks. This study focuses on identifying and resolving discrepancies in human-to-robot manipulability frameworks by mapping a human's manipulability structure to a robot's using an improved point-to-point planning method. This improved method incorporates the principles of parallel transport and a sophisticated algorithm for registering shapes, allowing for a more accurate representation of the relationship between humans and robots, which is critical for predicting and controlling the movement of objects in collaborative tasks. The approach is successfully tested in a virtual reality environment that mimics a CNC machine's interactive interface. It allows humans to leverage the manipulability structure, which is the set of possible object positions and movements available to them, to improve their performance and demonstrate smoother control in tasks that require object manipulation. Additionally, the approach is successful in using the manipulability structure for prediction and control, which confirms its value as a collaborative manipulability framework. A novel method for training a single-view 3D object pose estimator is presented, utilizing unstructured, arbitrarily posed objects rotating in a physical environment.  The approach identifies pose-agnostic objects through simple visual similarities and tracks their geometric transformations by analyzing the 3D point clouds captured from these scenes.  It is observed that the initial pose of an object is frequently 'accidental' and serves as a reliable representation.  To enhance generalization, statistical patterns are identified from a large dataset of synthetic scenes featuring objects in various poses.  Experimental results confirm that the proposed method can effectively estimate object poses using only a simple detector and that the 'accidental turntable' approach outperforms traditional methods of training pose estimators.  Code and the Accidental Turntables dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/yangyangyang/Accidental_Turntables.  Results demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve superior performance, particularly for objects with complex appearances or those easily confused with other objects.  It is further noted that the approach can also be applied to estimate the pose of a single view of objects in a category without requiring any specific instance training, indicating its great practical value.  Additionally, it is noted that the method can be adapted for use on image data and that the proposed framework offers a unified solution for training pose estimators, encompassing both general categories and fine-grained domains.  Interestingly, it is found that the method can also be utilized for discovering new object categories based on their common geometric patterns and potential practical applications.  Furthermore, it is noted that the proposed method can effectively mitigate the detrimental effects of synthetic data bias when training pose estimators.  These findings are visually illustrated through a series of qualitative results that demonstrate the pose estimator's robust generalization to both in-domain and out-of-domain objects. Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media. Social media platforms like Twitter offer a vast source of data, representing a significant portion of conversations including opinions on vaccination. We developed two neural networks, one of which identifies whether a tweet promotes anti-vaccination views and another suggests related misinformation. This study, fueled by data from Twitter, reveals that neural networks accurately distinguish between acceptance and rejection of such views, as well as detect misinformation. We utilized the suggested misinformation categories to analyze patterns in Twitter discussions and found that a significant majority of anti-vaccination tweets originate from verified users promoting conspiracy theories related to COVID-19. We also discovered that users who reject vaccination often share misinformation on various types of conspiracy theories, whereas acceptors primarily engage in hostile discussions, according to Twitter's sentiment analysis. This research is significant because it marks one of the first times neural networks have been applied to study vaccination attitudes on social media, uncovering complex connections between consumption of misinformation and views on vaccination. We hope this research will contribute to the development of targeted strategies to combat misinformation on social media, thereby influencing public attitudes on vaccination. We would like to extend our gratitude to Dr. Cheng and Dr. Crandall for their guidance and expertise. Misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines persists, a major factor in people's hesitation to get vaccinated. Twitter, a significant source of data, offers insights into vaccination attitudes. We classified user views on vaccination into three categories: we developed a neural network to identify tweets that express anti-vaccination sentiments and suggested additional potential forms of misinformation related to vaccines. Using these classifications, we analyzed Twitter discussions and discovered that a large proportion of anti-vaccination tweets promote conspiracy theories, particularly those related to COVID-19. Users who reject vaccination share various forms of conspiracy theories, whereas users who accept vaccination engage in hostile discussions on Twitter. This pattern suggests that social media platforms could target specific types of misinformation to address vaccination attitudes and not address all forms of misinformation simultaneously. Despite these accomplishments, the pulse characteristics remain influenced by complications such as light-matter interaction and spatial inhomogeneities. This novel approach allows for a controllable and coherent interaction between the laser field and the Ne2 molecules, producing attosecond pulses with a stable duration of approximately 160 attoseconds. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the development of attosecond pulse generation, leveraging a controlled natural phenomenon to produce isolated pulses of remarkable temporal resolution. Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data, especially information about partner candidates. This involves updating theoretical models to match observed data, which can then be used to refine predicted eclipse timings. Researchers initially applied this approach to the Algol system in the early 20th century but were unable to identify a second partner candidate. Using updated models and observed data, the team has revisited this issue and proposes two new candidate binaries for the Algol system. These are $B/C$ with a minimum mass of 0.55 $\mathring{G}$ and $A/B$ with a minimum mass of 0.30 $\mathring{G}$. Both candidate binaries are consistent with a binary population synthesis model. The $B/C$ binary is predicted to cause an irregular eclipse pattern from 1971 to 2030 and the $A/B$ binary will induce irregular eclipses from 2001 to 2030. Eclipse predictions for the three-component systems Algol-A/B/C and Algol-B/C/A are also provided. The presence of these new candidate binaries can explain why the Algol system's eclipse duration has increased over the 20th and 21st centuries. This finding is consistent with observational data and future research is expected to confirm the new candidate binaries through spectroscopic parallaxes. The revised eclipse model will be employed to refine the Algol system's mean orbital period, which is currently 0.3476163 years. Based on the predicted eclipses, the team suggests observing opportunities from 2023 to 2030. The researchers also discussed how to statistically identify binary partner candidates using an algorithm and provided examples of applying it to the Algol system. The statistical method could be applied to other binary stars to reveal new candidate binaries based on their eclipse patterns and irregular variations. The team developed a new tool that is compatible with Python 3 for visualizing and analyzing eclipse data, which is expected to be an useful resource for future research on binary evolution. The presence of new binary partner candidates in well-studied systems not only reveals intriguing astrophysical phenomena but also provides an opportunity to further investigate binary evolution, which is a fundamental area of study in the field of stellar binary research. The researchers provided theoretical calculations to explain how the Algol system's eclipse patterns were affected by its component masses and observed variations over the 20th and 21st centuries. The team used various astronomical databases to verify the accuracy of eclipse data and predicted variations in the Algol system's eclipse duration

This work provides a comprehensive examination and a thorough modeling of the electrostatic behavior in multi-domain ferroelectric FETs, taking into consideration the contribution of domain wall related capacitance. A detailed physical analysis is offered to elucidate the effects of domain walls on the device capacitance, backed by a comprehensive numerical simulation. The research also investigates the impact of domain wall induced adverse capacitance on the device performance, specifically its threshold voltage, drive current, and energy consumption. The study culminates with a prediction of the optimal domain orientation and the resulting optimal device performance, along with advice on triggering domain orientation in the gate material through spin-orbit-induced tuning. Additionally, the research suggests a novel method to mitigate the adverse effects of domain walls through the application of a forward-biased gate voltage, enabling the control of the device transport characteristics via domain wall capacitance. The research offers a predictive theoretical framework that can be utilized for designing experiments aimed at controlling the domain structure in ferroelectric CMOS components. Furthermore, the research estimates the magnitude of ferroelectric polarization needed to establish a viable multi-domain state and reveals that such polarization levels are attainable with currently available materials, thus paving the way for the development of highly efficient ferroelectric CMOS technology. Lastly, the research proposes a general approach to capture the transient behavior of ferroelectric domain wall dynamics, extending the theoretical model to the microkernel framework and the GEANS Pro library, both of which are specialized tools for continuum modeling. The research is the first of its kind to offer a comprehensive theoretical description of the ferroelectric domain wall dynamics in the context of CMOS technology. The study's predictive framework can potentially lead to the design of novel ferroelectric devices that operate at extremely low voltage levels, thereby facilitating the sustainable power consumption needs of forthcoming electronic devices. The research is a significant advancement in the field of ferroelectric technology and ferroelectric microelectromechanics, opening up new avenues for further research and enabling the development of efficient ferroelectric CMOS circuits. A significant portion of mobile application malware originates from manipulated Android APKs.  The Cargo ecosystem builds upon Apktool's capabilities to analyze APKs also as Java-based projects. This further enables the utilization of existing security tools to identify security vulnerabilities within Android applications. This research establishes a knowledge graph based on security vulnerabilities and software dependencies within the Cargo ecosystem, as well as the spread of vulnerability propagation. An empirical study was conducted to examine the relationship between security vulnerabilities and software dependencies, using cargo tools to collect relevant data and graph-learning techniques to construct the knowledge graph. The results show that a large number of security vulnerabilities are linked to software dependencies in the Cargo ecosystem, with approximately 60% of security vulnerabilities and 70% of software dependencies connected through inter-dependent relationships. Furthermore, our study found that the spread of vulnerability propagation within the Cargo ecosystem primarily occurs through transitive dependency links. The findings of this research can guide security professionals in prioritizing security vulnerability addressing, with a view to maximizing their overall impact, based on factors such as vulnerability type, affected software components, and the extent of spread or propagation. The details of our knowledge graph construction method and vulnerability propagation propagation spread are available on GitHub at https://github.com/ecomarigo/cargo-vulcances. The knowledge graph based on security vulnerabilities and software dependencies in the Cargo ecosystem can be accessed at https://ecomaigi.github.io/cargo-vulcances/index.html. This research was financially supported by the MSIT, Government of Korea (Project No. 2020-04-0301). Additionally, we appreciate the data analytics services offered by AWS and Google Cloud. The relevant data used in this research can be accessed at https://ecomaigi.github.io/cargo-vulcances/data.html. In accordance with the research ethics guidelines, we have made public the research data that was previously restricted due to concerns over malware propagation. The research data includes a detailed list of benchmark scores, as well as the knowledge graph based on security vulnerabilities and software dependencies in the Cargo ecosystem. The knowledge graph was constructed using cargo tools to collect relevant data and graph-learning techniques, with the results showing a high degree of consistency.
