The SHARK project involves the development of an advanced hadron spectrometer system consisting of multiple detectors, including calorimeters, tracker systems, and particle identification devices, to form an all-in-one large-scale detector system. This comprehensive detector will serve two primary purposes - hadron physics research with its high-intensity beams at the FAIR facility and super-proton-decay experiments at deep-underground facilities like the LNGS, as well as a multi-purpose detector for the SPS at CERN and SHARK will also be utilized in connection with the MOON project at the FAIR facility for detecting astrophysical neutrinos, and at the FAIR and SPS for observing various secondary particles resulting from cosmic ray interactions with air, and at deep-underground locations for detecting proton and antiproton cosmic rays. Furthermore, SHARK will also serves as a forerunner for future large-scale hadron experiment projects such as the SEVEN experiment at the FAIR and SNOMAD at the SPS, as well as for detector systems in future deep-underground neutrino detection projects like the DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande experiments. Hence, the SHARK project is a pioneering initiative that is pertinent to ongoing and future research activities in hadron physics research with its wide-ranging applications at various experimental facilities. Following an extensive design and R&D work-over a period of 18 months involving 23 researchers from Russian and European organizations, comprehensive designs and prototypes of SHARK's various sub-systems were developed and presented at a Workshop organized by the JINR in Dubna on the 4th of July 2019. We shall present here the outcome of this work and also report on the response it garnered from the international hadron physics community during the mentioned Workshop. This note serves as a summary of the SHARK project and will be presented at various international hadron physics conferences throughout 2019 and 2020. Moreover, the project website with detailed information about SHARK is under development and is expected to be launched in the near future at the address http://shark.jinr Blondin.org. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered. Our examination notes that even with the correction for polyatomic effects, carbon's measured reaction rates do not match the calculated values predicted by conventional computational models. Consequently, these models are unreliable for predicting reaction rates at lower energy levels. It is contended that an alternative method, the Trojan horse method, holds great potential for resolving long-standing discrepancies in measurement versus calculation. However, further refinement of this technique is required, particularly regarding its handling of polyatomic effects and high-energy data, and both experimental and theoretical experts must collaborate to achieve this goal. Finally, the update to the latest microscopically-based fusion computational model, known as Couped, is discussed. This model seamlessly integrates the angular momentum and collective motion frameworks, and when combined with the corrected $\alpha$-cluster wave functions, can accurately account for observed fusion trends. The revised model is capable of predicting reaction rates at energy levels as low as 0.08 MeV, and has been validated through a comparative analysis with carbon-carbon fusion data. Furthermore, the model's ability to predict fusion rates for larger nuclei is explored. When adjusted for polyatomic effects, the predicted reaction rates for the relevant isotopes ${}^{13}{\rm N}$ and ${}^{16}{\rm O}$ align with experimental measurements. Lastly, an approach to eliminating the lingering issue of non-fusion yields is proposed, and potential future research directions are outlined. A crucial element in understanding the evolution and formation of planets is the detailed chemical composition and thus the structure, as evident from the diverse range of known exoplanets.  The focus is placed on metal-poor stars with habitable zone planets, especially low-mass ones, as their extremely low temperatures could facilitate water retention. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become the preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI). Recent research suggests that leveraging CSI can yield more accurate location estimates compared to conventional RSS methods. Nevertheless, the performance of CSI-based models heavily relies on sufficiently abundant training data. Unfortunately, gathering sufficient CSI data is often impractical due to the computational expense associated with collecting CSI data for each individual sample. To overcome this challenge, a novel attention-based CSI-based localization model is proposed. By utilizing a attention mechanism to selectively optimize the CSI data used for training and testing, this method can effectively enhance performance while reducing the requirement for training data. The proposed model was evaluated using real CSI data collected in an indoor setting and demonstrated improved localization accuracy across various indoor locations with both abundant and limited training data. Furthermore, the model was found to outperform rival CSI-based localization methods. Source code for this work is available at https://github.com/PU-EE-EE/AttentionLearnableCSI. The recent advancements in data-driven methods have significantly altered the traditional approach to scientific research, now commonly referred to as 'Scientific Machine Learning.' This subfield utilizes machine learning techniques to analyze large datasets, producing numerous probability density functions that describe various scientific parameters. However, the assessment of uncertainty associated with these predictions remains a major challenge. To address this issue, a comprehensive framework has been developed that systematizes the comparison of uncertainty measures and their evaluation in scientific contexts. This framework consists of three primary components: a hierarchical structure that categorizes uncertainty measures; a metric that evaluates their effectiveness; and a reporting standard that facilitates transparent and clear communication of these measures. Through an application to existing research on radii estimation, our approach highlights several benefits, including streamlined evaluation processes and increased clarity in scientific presentations. Furthermore, our uncertainty assessment framework can be adapted for use in various research domains beyond our test case. Lastly, our research stresses the importance of well-defined and accessible evaluation methodologies that enable the objective assessment of existing models to facilitate scientific progress and informed decision-making in areas like machine learning applications in combinatorial biology. This research will be publicly available upon publication. We invite the research community to contribute to, quote, and build upon our work. We particularly call upon researchers in the area of prediction and uncertainty quantification to contribute their specific expertise in addressing the methodology's proposed hierarchical structure. We foresee the development of novel approaches and the incorporation of our framework in various research domains, such as structure refinement and protein function prediction. To facilitate this, we are releasing the code for our research, including the uncertainty assessment framework and the metric evaluation metric, at a publicly accessible repository under the terms of the CC0 dedication. We will continue to maintain and expand upon this resource, which can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/uncle-bonnet/uncertainty_meter. Through our findings, we determine that teachers can effectively utilize local insights to impart valuable knowledge to students if the underlying model's layer structure exhibits gradual complexity gradation. We demonstrate this through two primary findings. Firstly, we observe that layer-wise parameter initialization serves as an accurate predictor of student performance in robust learning. Secondly, we note that teachers can enhance student robustness by focusing on local student-tutor pairs where the tutor's layer structure significantly differs from the student's corresponding layer. These contributions expand upon existing research by revealing the utility of local tutors in robust learning and also pave the way for the development of sophisticated learning environments that are more resilient to adversarial attacks. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the coolest Y dwarfs. Moreover, the object possesses color indices of W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 about 1.6 mag bluer than a typical Y dwarf. New data collected from WISE, Spitzer, and HST for parallax measurement have determined a close distance of $16.3^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ parsecs and a substantial transverse velocity of $207.4{\pm}15.9$ km/s. The calculated J, W2, and ch2 absolute magnitudes align with the coolest Y dwarfs despite W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 indices being distinct. Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor brown dwarf and possibly the initial member of a binary system consisting of two Y dwarfs, discovered merely because the brighter companion is dominating the WISE detection. Further observation is needed to confirm the object's characteristics and explore possibilities for follow-up studies in the most distant celestial regions of the sky. The object in question, named "The Mishap", earned this nickname due to its unexpected and mysterious identity. The research for more objects like this is essential to enhance our comprehension of the object's nature and expand our knowledge of the object's demographic, ultimately shedding light on the object's uncertain classification. This process is akin to matching a theoretical model to data in fitting techniques. Specifically, we use NNLL DGLAP theory paired with FONLL-like parton distribution functions to achieve a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, we incorporate pole mass parton distribution functions and a novel scheme for matching them to the running mass, yielding predictable outcomes. We also developed a new code, ` evolvePP`, to facilitate the evolution of parton distribution functions and fragmentation functions at the NNLL accuracy with a fixed-order alpha_s behavior. This code can be utilized for various applications such as parton-to-resonance-to-parton transitions with improved accuracy. We demonstrate the precision of `evolvePP` by comparing it to `FONLL-GRV`, 'HERWIG++', and 'QCDPOT', showcasing its high agreement with these tools. Various methods for estimating star formation rates exist but have not been consistently compared, resulting in a lack of knowledge about their overall reliability. By comparing different techniques using a limited yet controlled set of data, a study concludes that the brackett-$\gamma$ line serves as the most trustworthy indicator of star formation rates derived through spectrum emission fitting. Furthermore, the study determines that stellar mass-derived star formation rates have limited correlation with those inferred from brackett-$\gamma$ or other strong emission lines like H$\alpha$ and [OIII] at 5007 Angstroms. On the other hand, SFRs derived from far-infrared luminosity have a respectable correlation with those inferred from brackett-$\gamma$. Furthermore, the study finds that the hydrogen recombination line-based star formation rates present a more accurate representation of the physical processes involved when compared to line-driven wind model-predicted rates. Last but not least, the study suggests multiple possible causes for the observed discrepancies between predicted and observed SFRs, including the suppression of star formation in extreme wind-emitting systems and the insufficient modeling of gas dynamics in the current cosmological code simulations. As such, further research is needed to develop a more comprehensive model for the prediction of SFRs that takes into consideration both star formation and gas outflows. These subgroups originate from a broader structure known as a braided endomorphism semigroup, specifically a type $II$ braided subgroup. Our research focuses on the elements of this semigroup, which are represented through a higher-level mathematical construct called a fusion matrix. This paper delves into the underlying algebraic patterns within the semigroup by examining regional modules of a more fundamental quantum group and its associated representation, referred to as type $II$ global subgroups. We identify distinct structural elements within these modules and establish a general mathematical framework to characterize the braided module structure of a type $II$ quantum subgroup. This framework allows us to analyze and generalize a previously reported phenomenon in which the fusion matrix of a global subgroup $\mathcal{Q}_{(n)}$ consists of two distinct square blocks for $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_N)$ with $N\geq 3$. This result implies that the fusion matrix of a type $II$ quantum subgroup is comprised of square blocks if and only if its base subgroups have this property. This study addresses the MMath challenge, focusing on accurately detecting handwritten mathematical expressions from text data captured by various sensors. The research involves two key components: (1) Handwriting System Identification (HSI) and (2) Mathematical Expression Detection (MED). For HSI, a multi-classifier approach incorporating sensor features and deep learning-based models is proposed, with notable performance from a combination of sensor-based and deep learning-based classifiers. For MED, two approaches are presented: (a) using deep learning-based methods similar to MMath 2018 and (b) integrating spatial information into a model designed by Jiang et al. Both methods of MED yield satisfactory results, with significant improvements in certain configurations. The overall framework demonstrates effectiveness in MMath 2019, with our approach matching or surpassing the official baseline proposed by Jiang et al. in three out of four settings. Furthermore, our study reports state-of-the-art performance in two configurations and comparable performance in the remaining two configurations. Notably, our deep learning-based MED and HSI methods demonstrate a high level of similarity with those of the top three officially proposed methods by Jiang et al., with our approach even surpassing theirs in three out of four configurations. The proposed technique successfully identifies the used writing instrument in all cases, detects mathematical expressions with high precision, and outperforms the baseline in three out of four scenarios. Moreover, our deep learning-based MED and HSI methods exhibit a high level of similarity with those of the top three officially proposed methods by Jiang et al., with our approach even surpassing theirs in three out of four configurations. Deep multimodal learning using K-fan-based deep learning (KL) has gained significant advancements recently. Despite improvements, several fundamental challenges persist with existing multimodal deep learning models, including (1) the lack of a unified theoretical framework for deep multimodal learning, (2) the limited ability of models to learn and represent complex data, and (3) the difficulty in evaluating classification performance efficiently. A new K-fan deep learning model is proposed to address these challenges by providing a unified theoretical framework for deep multimodal learning. It learns shared representations using a shared hidden layer with optimized weights, and has multiple independent output layers with unique weights for each modality. Additionally, the model incorporates feature learning, shared representations, and a low-rank multi-modal learning component to learn unbalanced multimodal data efficiently. A new learning algorithm for the model, L1-KL, is also developed based on the model's unique hidden layer with the L1-norm constraint. Experimental evaluations of the model demonstrate its effectiveness on 29 balanced datasets and 13 unbalanced datasets across various classification tasks. It achieved superior or comparable performance compared to 30 prominent deep multimodal learning models, and required significantly reduced computational resources, evaluating classification performance using only a small subset of data instead of the entire dataset. The model's performance is remarkable, and it has surpassed many deep multimodal learning models even with evaluation classification performance optimization. The study also validated the model's efficacy on open-access dataset collections and real-world application datasets, and provided comprehensive analysis of the model's performance and its implications on deep multimodal learning research. A dataset with detailed information on the model and its evaluation is available for public access at https://github.com/alimomoh/K-fan_MM_Learning. L1-KL is an extendable deep multimodal learning model, and the study's findings can be generalized to other deep multimodal learning models using K-fan deep learning. The model's unique hidden layer with the L1-norm constraint can be integrated into existing deep multimodal learning models to improve their performance and efficiency. The study offers a new perspective on deep multimodal learning based on K-fan deep learning, and can be applied to other areas of machine learning and pattern analysis. The globally pervasive messaging app, WhatsApp, has become integral to information dissemination in numerous countries. However, its robust features have facilitated the rapid spread of misinformation. In an effort to combat this issue, WhatsApp introduced limitations on the number of people to whom a single message can be forwarded. In this study, we analyze the impact of this change in India, a country heavily reliant on WhatsApp. Our research reveals an intriguing reduction in the frequency of forwarded messages. To gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, we developed and released two open-source tools that enable users to send messages to WhatsApp numbers. Our analysis suggests the limitations have primarily affected groups targeted by misinformation, while participants who previously engaged in such practices continue to do so undeterred. Conversely, users who primarily engage in personal conversations are largely unaffected. Interestingly, our model shows that WhatsApp's measures have reduced the reach of every type of forwarded message, except those containing one or two unique words. Furthermore, our analysis suggests the limitations have decreased the transmission rate of information across long-distance social connections and significantly limited the reach of information to higher-ranking social network nodes. In terms of user behavior, our study reveals that Eswaran's theory on social network analysis holds promise in explaining how users respond to WhatsApp's changes. Our findings demonstrate the value of combining social graph-based user modeling with quantitative social network analysis to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how users behave under different economic and social conditions and how they respond to external interventions, such as the limitations implemented by WhatsApp. Our research provides actionable insights for other tech companies looking to address the problem of misinformation via similar features and offers a framework for evaluating the impact of such interventions. Moreover, our study serves as a cumulative contribution that could be applied to various domains beyond misinformation. The open-source tools enabling users to interact with WhatsApp users are available for public use at https://github.com/razorbridge/whatsapp-bot/tree/main/whatsapp_forwarder. Our code for data collection is available at https://github.com/razorbridge/razorbridge/tree/main/instagram_and_whatsapp_project. Our website, https://razorbridge.com/, offers additional information on our methods and findings. Additionally, the figures mentioned in this paper can be accessed at https://razorbridge.com/publications. Our research has been detailed in a working paper, https://razorbridge.com/publications/2022-01-609. This paper has been presented at the 2022 ACM Conference on Online Social Networks and the 2022 IEEE Conference on Information Science and Engineering.

Empirical analysis and simulations based on a detailed model of international asset management reveal that an innovative investment approach does, in fact, capture existing clients, but only under specific conditions does it lead to a decline in revenue for the established strategy. Ultimately, our findings suggest that incumbent tactics should remain open to new ideas, as they can generate significant benefits. We also provide guidelines for both managers and researchers on navigating similar market dynamics in the real world. Furthermore, our study contributes to the body of knowledge on cross-sectional approaches and agent-based models in finance. The empirical portion of our research focuses on the German asset management sector and incorporates a comprehensive network that maps the relationships between fund managers and their competitors. The simulation-based analysis of our model was conducted over a 10-year period (2009-2018) utilizing data from Thomson Reuters' Global Financials database. Additionally, we developed an agent-based model that simulates the behavior of independent decision-making agents in a stylized financial system. Our study follows a two-step approach, combining both empirical and simulation-based methods. First, we analyzed existing revenue patterns and the impact of an new tactic on a established strategies. We employed cross-entropy technique to estimate the likelihood of one strategy being preferred over another. Subsequently, we tested these findings using a detailed simulation-based model that incorporates a complex network of financially interconnected entities. Ultimately, our study connects the empirical analysis of a specific financial sector to a more abstract model of complex financial interactions. Throughout our research, we sought to maintain objectivity by minimizing the influence of any personal opinions on our findings. Additionally, our study verifies the robustness of our results by employing a range of techniques. We tested our findings by changing key variables such as the degree of competition and the structure of the financial sector to see if our results would hold under these different conditions. Furthermore, our study is characterized by a high level of contextualization as we examined the specific financial sector of German asset management while also developing a more abstract model of complex financial interactions. We propose an idea for creating a highly controlled interface between a ferromagnetic insulator and a superconductor. This proposal involves depositing a thin layer of a Satisferromagnetic compound, specifically PdDc, on a surface coated with a thin film of MoSi2. This specific combination features a well-matched lattice structure and possesses unique properties due to their proximity. Our theoretical models, utilizing a Hubbard model with Raman interaction, indicate that the interface between these materials exhibits long-range spin waves with exceptionally low energy, and that these energy levels can be significantly altered by applying an external voltage. Our study shows that a voltage of approximately 0.5V can create a barrier blocking these low-energy magnons, and that this magnon barrier can be toggled by changing the voltage to 0V. This system has the potential to be incorporated into qubit systems for an enhanced performance. Due to the versatility in materials, these properties can be observed in various other configurations as well. This research offers a new mechanism for controlling spin waves and has potential applications in the development of quantum devices and superconductor-based processors. Additionally, the employed method involves presenting model data through graphically engaging visualizations that facilitate intuitive understanding, and the associated analysis provides a framework for investigating the spin wave properties in Satisferromagnetic insulators. Our study opens the door for further research on the spin wave properties at the interface of superconductor and ferromagnetic insulators with inherent electric gating capabilities. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Overall, our findings imply that local news can play a crucial role in raising public awareness about the pandemic but also highlight potential shortcomings and biases in coverage that may exacerbate existing social inequalities during the pandemic. Based on these findings, our study offers several practical suggestions to enhance pandemic coverage and promote equitable dissemination of information to vulnerable populations. This research has significant practical implications for scientists, policymakers, and local news outlets seeking to design and disseminate effective COVID communication strategies targeted at specific groups within a community. Moreover, our study's analytical framework can be applied to other public health crises and various demographic contexts to develop targeted approaches for local news outlets, vulnerable populations, and relevant policymakers. Such an approach could potentially inform initiatives by non-profit organizations, government agencies, local health departments, and news organizations to develop effective strategies for pandemic communication that are tailored to the specific needs of different communities. It can also aid researchers and scientists in their efforts to design and disseminate pandemic messages that are targeted, accurate, and reach vulnerable populations who may not have access to reliable information due to barriers like limited English proficiency, a lack of internet connectivity, or inadequate access to social media and other digital platforms. Furthermore, our study's findings can empower local news outlets to reflect more adequately on their pandemic coverage, thereby enhancing their journalistic credibility and promoting equity in the dissemination of information to diverse communities. Lastly, our study's results can aid policymakers at federal, state, and local levels in their efforts to develop effective communication strategies that are grounded in a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between local news coverage, regional COVID cases and deaths, and the distinct characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. By leveraging these insights, policymakers can work more effectively with local news organizations to raise public awareness about the pandemic and ultimately help to mitigate its severe impacts on individuals and communities nationwide. We employ a dynamic neural network called the attention model to investigate the developmental sequence of basic addition skills. By incorporating learned contextual memory into a standard recurrent neural network, such as a GRU model, we enable the network to retain previously acquired knowledge. Initially, we train a sophisticated three-part attention mechanism - similar to that described in the guide by Ye at al. (2019) - on a dataset of intricate math problem-solving procedures. The findings indicate that the attention mechanism is primarily utilized in the initial stages of training to accumulate 'tools', with subsequent stages characterised by the attention mechanism's decrease as expertise is acquired. We then modify this system to better mimic the sequential acquisition of mathematical knowledge by initially training on basic addition skills and gradually exposing it to more complex operations like'subtraction as the opposite of addition'. Notably, we discover that the attention mechanism's behaviour changes significantly in response to the updated training data. More intriguingly, when we initialise the contextual memory with random data, we observe that the attention mechanism is able to recognise and group related mathematical operations together. Furthermore, we find that the attention mechanism's behaviour varies according to the complexity of the mathematical operations. Ultimately, we conclude that the attention mechanism is capable of modelling the progression of expert-level mathematical knowledge and that the contextual memory plays a vital role in this process. We provide a detailed analysis of the attention mechanism's behaviour at various points during training. Furthermore, we experiment with training the attention mechanism on additional mathematical operations such as multiplication and division, and find that it is able to learn these skills as well. The code for these experiments is publicly available on GitHub. The findings of these experiments have led to the development of a mathematical knowledge framework, which we plan to develop further in the future. We believe that the attention mechanism offers an appealing explanation for the sequential acquisition of expert-level mathematical knowledge and holds promise for the automated generation of mathematical procedures. In the future, we intend to expand on this work by exploring the attention mechanism's behaviour for a broader range of tasks and examining the relationship between expert-level mathematical knowledge and real-world reasoning abilities. The research has significant potential to advance our understanding of how expert-level mathematical knowledge is acquired and generated, which could lead to the development of more effective machine learning algorithms for a range of applications. The research has far-reaching implications for the field of artificial intelligence and machine learning, particularly in the domain of mathematical knowledge, where it has the potential to revolutionise the way that artificial intelligence generates mathematical procedures. A new approach is proposed for creating historical price charts that take into account transaction time sequences and feedback from future transactions. Unlike conventional methods, this concept dissolves the linear structure of the Cartesian coordinate system by combining time with the log of price, resulting in a two-dimensional space. The introduction of a metric that measures the similarity between price movements in different regions enables the development of directional market time-series data. Statistical analysis of this data has revealed that its distribution is uniform, whereas autocorrelation has been significantly reduced through the application of an autoregressive model. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated by comparing it with previous strategies for predicting the S&P 500 index using machine learning models, with impressive improvements achieved. Specifically, a long-term forecast made on February 1st, 2020, accurately predicted the low point of the S&P 500 index on March 23rd, 2020, and the current trend is being used to make forecasts until June 2023. The concept of this directional data is further extended to multiple markets, allowing for the detection of coinciding market signals. The theory behind this approach can be found in the author's previous research regarding price movement direction, which has a theoretical foundation known as the Theory of Market Behavior. The underlying idea is that the future contains more information than the past, which is a fundamental principle in quantum physics referred to as the principle of forward direction. This study aims to provide a tangible representation of this idea through the notion of "kicking into the future". The findings presented here can be considered a precursor to an advanced trading system known as "price distance", which is also described in the author's previous research. A simplified trading system based on directional data has yielded notable profit gains, as detailed in the provided documents. The integration of the Theory of Market Behavior and directional market data has the potential to significantly enhance our understanding of market dynamics. The proposed concept can be used to develop a comprehensive framework for creating market time-series data that incorporates feedback from the future, which is a novel feature. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent data tampering and safeguard user privacy across multiple communication cycles. Specifically, clients utilize twin neural networks to process data while the server employs a robust neural network designed to recover the original client data after network transmission. Additionally, the server implements twin neural networks to accurately classify incoming data and detect potential attacks from clients. Notably, this approach involves minimal computational overhead and no privacy information is disclosed to the server or third parties. Finally, experimental evaluations confirm that FLVoogd effectively prevents data breaches and protects user privacy across various applications. Planets similar to Earth that orbit close to their stars are crucial to analyze if they possess conditions or characteristics necessary for life to exist. Since the surface temperature of a planet is determined by its star's brightness and the state of its atmosphere, distinguishing between supersonic and subsonic atmospheres is a key factor in identifying a given planet's suitable conditions. By comparing the characteristics of tiny particles that absorb light in a calm vs. active atmosphere, scientists can identify whether a planet's atmosphere is peaceful or turbulent. Unfortunately, our current understanding of how particles in a peaceful atmosphere change is limited because the processes that influence them are still largely unknown. Conversely, it is known that active atmospheres are heavily influenced by the release of chemicals such as CO and NH3. As a result, planets with more soluble gases like CO2 are likely to have calmer atmospheres, while those without (like H2) are likely to have turbulent atmospheres. Recent observations of 15 temperate exoplanets have shown that about half of those without soluble gases have calmer atmospheres, which is unusual and suggests that other factors must be at play. In this research, we examined the potential for a new characteristic to identify a peaceful vs. active atmosphere by comparing how two chemical reactions release CO and NH3 in an atmosphere near their triple points. The models suggest that this characteristic, or transition, is more pronounced in atmospheres without soluble gases and is more likely to be detected in spectra taken near the star's brightest point. Analyzing this feature in existing data from the MOONS survey reveals that 9 out of 15 planets with this characteristic show signs of a calmer atmosphere, which is consistent with our expectations. Additionally, 5 of these planets do not exhibit the expected signature of a peaceful atmosphere, which could be the result of turbulent atmospheres or unaccounted factors. Ultimately, further studies using deeper surveys are needed to confirm whether a given temperate exoplanet's atmosphere is peaceful or active. However, it is already clear that a particular type of atmosphere is more prevalent among planets without soluble gases, which was initially unexpected and calls for a reevaluation of the role of soluble gases in calmer atmospheres. Lastly, it is also possible to distinguish between active and turbulent atmospheres by looking for specific signs of chemical equilibrium in spectra taken near the star's brightest point. Inspired by brain neuroscience, spiking neural networks have the potential to replace traditional deep neural networks, particularly for resource-constrained devices such as hardware-efficient AI computers. However, unlike deep neural networks, SNNs face significant challenges due to their limited update frequency and data availability, preventing them from learning complex models like convolutional neural networks efficiently. Our research introduces a pioneering approach for sequence-based SNN learning of binary classification models using temporal backpropagation through time. This method enables spiking neural networks to learn complex models with high accuracy similar to deep neural networks, while also being more biologically realistic than previous methods. Our results show that high data update rates and prolonged training times are necessary for successful spiking neural network training, revealing a significant discrepancy from deep neural network learning processes. Additionally, our findings indicate that the temporal backpropagation through time technique is only effective for models with short spatio-temporal memory and certain non-linear data distributions. Our research lays the foundation for further exploration into the learning capabilities of spiking neural networks and their applications on hardware-efficient AI computers. A significant aspect of our research remains to be the reduction of spike arrival gaps, followed by the exploration of other learning algorithms such as spike-rate-dependent learning and the incorporation of biological short-term synaptic plasticity. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, verifying the precision of these expansions poses a significant challenge because the original equations are inherently complex and involve uncertain factors. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a reliable method to confirm the accuracy of these expansions by comparing them with the original equations. In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach to validate the precision of these expansions by comparing them with the original equations. This approach utilizes the inherent properties of the original equations to confirm accuracy. In addition, we developed a universally applicable method to confirm accuracy that can be applied to a broad range of equations, including those governing fluid flow. Notably, this method does not rely on the underlying assumptions of the original equations and can be applied to both conservative and non-conservative equations. Furthermore, we utilized this approach to confirm the accuracy of several generalized polynomial chaos expansions, including GPC-LES and GPC-LES with stabilization. These results demonstrate that the framework of these methods can effectively analyze the precision of these models. In particular, we confirmed the precision of GPC-LES and GPC-LES with stabilization by comparing them with the continuous equations of the fluid flow. These results provide a theoretical foundation for the development of the methods and can be utilized to improve the accuracy of these models in the future. Additionally, we utilized the confirmed accuracy of these models to derive explicit models that can effectively analyze the precision of these models. Notably, these models were developed from the precise versions of the generalized polynomial chaos expansions. The increasing complexity of modern large-scale systems has given rise to a significant challenge: monitoring millions of data streams in real-time to identify sudden changes and isolate anomalies in high-dimensional data sets. Our approach tackles this obstacle by developing an advanced algorithm that learns automatically from example sub-systems to recognize shifts in real-time, thus facilitating timely anomaly detection and mitigation. Building on a novel adaptive change detection algorithm, we integrate it with a data analysis method to extract meaningful patterns from unlabelled data sets, thereby enabling high-performance detection and isolation of anomalies in high-dimensional data streams. Comprehensive experimental studies conducted on multiple data sets reveal that our approach surpasses established alternatives by delivering superior detection and isolation performance along with significantly lower computational complexity, thus paving the way for real-world applications. For example, our methodology has potential to monitor massive networks, such as those employed in large industrial settings, for enabling real-time anomaly detection and avoidance. Additionally, it can be utilized for monitoring massive biomedical data sets for early disease detection and intervention purposes. Our work provides a premier solution for performing real-time anomaly detection and isolation in high-dimensional data streams. Additionally, it provides a pioneering approach for designing real-time biometric anomaly detection systems with high accuracy and high-dimensional data streams. Finally, it offers a novel algorithm for identifying and isolating massive dimensional data sets in real-time.

Document analysis, a visually rich field, demands considerable time and money to set up a labeling process. To overcome this challenge, we investigate the capabilities of a low-cost, semi-supised learning method that relies on minimal, high-quality labeled data. This approach leverages a large, unlabeled dataset to calculate data distribution and a smaller labeled set to train a model using a targeted loss function. Our experiments in extracting text from invoices demonstrate that semi-supervised learning can significantly reduce data labeling costs without compromising extraction accuracy. With 128 labeled data points, our method matches the performance of fully supervised learning with 20,000 labels. Furthermore, we analyze the labeling costs of 8 different dataset scales and find that semi-supervised learning reduces costs proportionally. With the unlabeled dataset being the primary factor, we explore strategies to enhance performance under the same conditions. This study examines how a dynamic system with interconnected elements behaves over time. By generating random networks with a fixed number of nodes, it's discovered that their activity tends to be irregular, with periods of high and low activity separated by sudden increases. It's found that this irregular pattern is similar to phenomena like stock market fluctuations and the sleep-wake cycles of natural systems. Despite the variability, the total amount of interaction within these networks tends to remain consistent. However, in cases where the nodes' connections are highly uniform, the total interaction can occasionally drop below a certain threshold, indicating a failure to engage in sufficient interaction. This research identifies two key factors that influence the failure to engage in sufficient interaction: the density of the nodes' connections and the differences in their behavior. It's discovered that in highly uniform, dense networks, the failure to engage in sufficient interaction is more likely to occur and the nodes' behavior is more closely synchronized. This research contributes to our understanding of dynamic systems' behavior and has implications for maintaining diversity in natural and artificial systems designed to exhibit complex behaviors. It also suggests new methods for managing these systems, such as the maintenance of diverse ecosystems to prevent widespread insect outbreaks. Additionally, it has potential applications for tackling challenges in computer science, such as boosting search engine results by promoting diversity of information. Furthermore, it has implications for neuroscientific research, such as the regulation of sleep patterns to prevent the failure of entire brain regions to communicate effectively. Lastly, it has potential applications for tackling technical issues in distributed computing, such as the failure of multiple processes to accomplish a task due to a lack of communication. In general, this research can be applied to any dynamic system where the interaction between elements is crucial to its functioning and stability. It provides a theoretical basis for understanding these systems' behavior and has been validated through numerical simulations as well as by analyzing real-world data on coupled neurophysiological systems during sleep. Consequently, it has broad theoretical and practical implications. A key challenge in developing the most effective dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) is enhancing the negativity, indicating a measure of a DTR's ability to restrict its application to suboptimal policies. We tackle this issue via a Bayesian approach that utilizes Q-learning to create a Bayesian network that represents the patient population's diverse patterns of treatment and reward collection. By constructing an ensemble of DTRs with high negative Q-values and implementing a decaying acceptance rate in Bayesian sampling, we optimize negativity. The proposed method is validated through a real-world study of a patient population receiving treatment for acute myocardial infarction. The results indicate that the generated DTRs are competitive with the state-of-the-art policies, including IMRT, Q-IRT, and OT. Additionally, we show that the optimized negativity significantly improves the overall quality of the DTRs. Due to the diversity of the patient population, a single DTR is insufficient; thus, we organize the learned policies into a personalizable library, enabling each patient to be assigned a tailored DTR based on their distinct treatment and reward patterns. The code is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/jianjunhuang1988/BayOptDTR. We investigate the phenomenon of superconductivity in a 2D electronic system, characterized by a smooth topological band. Through application of the Sanjev-Young exact model, we develop an exact solution for its phonon-mediated effective electron interaction. This exact interaction serves as a reliable starting point for analyzing electron correlations. Utilizing mean-field theory, we demonstrate the emergence of superconductivity when the system's Fermi surface is enclosed by the topological band's gap. Notably, the Cooper pairing exhibits a long-range order characterized by wave vectors equivalent to those seen in topological band theory, specifically the reciprocal space points where the band's topological character is most pronounced. Furthermore, the underlying electronic nature of these special points is reflected in the correlation function's non-local structure. Additionally, the exact solution allows for a thorough examination of the pairing symmetry, revealing that the pairing wave function retains the complex structure observed in 2D systems with broken time-reversal symmetry, even when the system's symmetry is unbroken. Finally, based on an analytic calculation of the Bonn-Mangano diagram within the Sanjev-Young exact model, we find that the critical interaction strength for superconductivity is directly proportional to the system's topological band's curvature at the gap's inner point. This discovery provides a previously unreported topological mechanism for the emergence of superconductivity in such a 2D system. The topological band curvature also plays a crucial role in determining the system's Meissner effect, as well as its superconducting gap structure and size. The exact solutions obtained here provide a comprehensive understanding of these phenomena, paving the way for a potential observation of such a superconducting phase in 2D electron gases hosted on substrate materials featuring a smooth topological band. Specifically, graphene is an exemplary case that can be studied in an experimental setting. However, another potential candidate is a 2D ruthenium clathrate compound exhibiting an electron-rich topological band. Although this material exhibits strong electron-phonon coupling, the topological band's inherent dynamics plays a critical role in its superconducting properties as observed at low temperatures. By comparing these observations with the theoretical results, we can gain a deeper understanding of the system's phase diagram and evaluate the relative importance of electron-phonon and electron-electron coupling in its superconducting properties. Lastly, the interplay between these coupling mechanisms may provide a pathway for further theoretical and experimental investigation and could potentially reveal novel phenomena beyond the scope of the current study

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches have been utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of equal proportions, latent Dirichlet allocation, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, and applying continuous data methods to the marginal probabilities of species presence. Our study compares these clustering methods using simulated and real-world data across multiple indicators. Our findings suggest that the application of traditional continuous data clustering methods to the marginal probabilities yields the most consistent and accurate results for presence-absence data. These findings show a high level of consistency with previously established findings in the field. Additionally, our study highlights the superiority of the latent mixture model that assumes equal proportions among others in the context of our comparative analysis. Our research further reveals that the applied hierarchical clustering method often produces tree structures whose branches hold significant interpretative value. Our analysis also explores the impact of sampling rate, sample size, and data dimensionality on the proposed approach and suggests that the number of zero entries in the data has a substantial influence amount. Our study ultimately demonstrates the effectiveness of the latent mixture model approach, along with hierarchical clustering, in the analysis of presence-absence data. These methods can be effectively applied to data from diverse research domains such as ecology, medicine, and linguistics. It appears that combining statistical and machine learning techniques along with theoretical insights into presence-absence data can significantly enhance our understanding of this data type. Our findings also emphasize the practical value of the proposed approach in practical applications and recommend the topmost approach for analysts to utilize in their work. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 NLP Task on Identifying Offensive Tweets aimed to determine the most effective approach to identifying abusive language online by comparing various combinations of machine learning algorithms and advanced NLP models. The quotient $\mathbb{Z}/P$ is defined as the set of remainders when any given integer is divided by a palindromic number. Similarly, let $N$ denote the ensemble of non-palindromic numbers, and define the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/N$ as the set of remainders when any given integer is divided by a non-palindromic number. It has been observed that the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/P$ yields even, non-palindromic numbers and the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/N$ results in odd, palindromic numbers. In this context, we prove that the quotients $\mathbb{Z}/(P^2N)$, $\mathbb{Z}/(2P^2N)$, and $\mathbb{Z}/(4PN)$ produce sequences of consecutive, full or near-full sets of integers from 0 to 2^k-1 for a sufficiently large k, where P is a palindromic number greater than 2. We then extend our findings to the more general case of quotients $\mathbb{Z}/(f(N)P^2N)$. It is noteworthy that our work has successfully generalized and consolidated various results presented at the Arithmetic of Palindromic Numbers workshop held at the Mathematical Institute of the University of Alabama in March 2018. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves complex mathematical models and non-convex optimization techniques. These methods often rely on restrictive assumptions and conventional gradient-based optimization methods, which can be impractical and computationally expensive. A more recent approach involves a variational framework that combines data-driven and model-based components with an optimized fusion process. However, this framework has several key limitations, including a fixed and predetermined data set, a fixed number of sources, and a fixed level of noise. In an attempt to address these limitations, a new variational framework is proposed in this study. The new model goes beyond traditional optimization methods by incorporating a data-driven component derived from deep learning methods called the variational network (VarNet). This breakthrough results in several significant advantages, including a more naturally occurring fusion process, the ability to use prior knowledge through variational Bayesian inference, the ability to utilize various priors on images, and joint sensor denoising and material decomposition capabilities. Experimental findings on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the proposed framework's capability to produce accurate results with minimal artifacts. Additionally, the proposed framework is shown to integrate VarNet effectively and produce high-quality denoised images with reduced artifacts on experimental data. The code for this research is publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/Niu20050216/Multi-Energy-CT-reconstruction. Also, the reconstructed images can be found at the following link: https://github.com/Niu20050216/Multi-Energy-CT-reconstruction/tree/main/RECONSTRUCTIONS. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific hurdle is encountered in deciphering the contents of Early Commercial Catalogs (ECC), which are centuries-old advertisements characterized by lengthy texts, diverse scripts, and a mix of numerical values. In contrast to standard handwritten text, these catalogs often contain numerical values not found in typical handwritten text. The current project addresses this obstacle by making use of the advancements in Visual Language Representation (VLR) for generating synthetic datasets from minimal resource pairs, thereby bypassing the need for extensive annotation. Nevertheless, synthetic data production poses two distinct challenges: 1) it is essential to obtain synthetic data samples that are close to real examples, thereby ensuring a smooth transition between synthetic and actual data, and 2) the synthetic data training process should prioritize the acquisition of relevant data samples swiftly. A potential solution to this challenge is presented in the form of the Vibro_HTR dataset, which comprises images of numerical values, and an end-to-end pipeline designed to demonstrate the synthetic data production process for low-resource HTR scenarios. The proposed approach is evaluated and compared over multiple benchmarks, including the widely used IHST dataset. In addition to outperforming competing methods in terms of synthetic data production, our solution also exhibits superior performance when it comes to achieving the highest possible accuracy rates on real-world datasets. This work presents a completely integrated temperature sensor, fabricated using 0.18$\mu$m eFlash process technology. A digital geometric spanner of a set of points in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space is a subset of digital line segments connecting the points, which approximates the original Euclidean metric with a specific distortion value for all pairs of points. Here, digital line segments are defined as containing only grid points, and the distortion value for a spanner is the maximum ratio of Euclidean distances to digital distances between all point pairs. We study digital spanners in Euclidean spaces of dimensions 2, 3, and 4, and establish upper bounds on the number of digital line segments needed to achieve a given distortion value for any set of points with a specific size. These upper bounds rely on a novel application of a technique called the Halton sequence for generating low-quality uniform coverings in Euclidean spaces. We also present an algorithm for generating digital line segments of the sparsest possible weight while approximating the Euclidean metric within a specified distortion value, and as input size increases, the number of line segments grows as the square of the logarithm of the number of points. The technique used here includes a novel digital analog of the Lipton-Spigel bound for sparse coverings in Euclidean spaces. The presented results are also independent of the underlying metric space's dimension. While large language models have achieved impressive results in continuum creation, they often generate unhelpful or irrelevant content, especially in tasks that require creating multiple sequential items.  There are two main issues with existing continuum models: 1) they generate poorly defined outputs that require additional interpretation, and 2) they fail to create coherent sequences of content.  To address these challenges, we introduce the Stable Creator, a novel fine-tuning technique for continuum models that improves the quality and coherence of generated content by refining the model's understanding of semantic direction.  The Stable Creator employs two novel approaches: 1) the assessment of semantic definitions, which helps the model align its internal representations with external standards, and 2) the distribution regularization of created content, which prevents the model from producing highly similar outputs.  To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we developed a comprehensive framework consisting of five diverse creative tasks that require producing sequential content and multiple levels of semantic definition precision.  Experimental results have shown that the Stable Creator is a highly successful method for developing coherent and high-quality creative sequences across all tested tasks.  Additionally, the Stable Creator's flexibility allows it to be effectively applied to various types of continuum models, as well as different content creation tasks.  You can find the code to reproduce the results of this work at https://github.com/csauvi/The-Stable-Creator.  Furthermore, a demo video showcasing the performance of the Stable Creator is available at https://youtu.be/8U6Hm5T1OEI.  Overall, the stable creator offers a practical solution to the problems of content creation, particularly to the challenges of producing coherent sequential content and interpreting the semantics of the generated content accurately.  To showcase its real-world potential, we presented three creative scenarios for each of the tested tasks, and demonstrated the stable creator's capabilities in an actual creative environment.  You can find these examples in the document "The-Stable-Creator-Creation-Examples.pdf" in the project repository.  To better capture the diversity of the content, we also introduced two novel evaluation metrics for continuous creation, called Comprehensive Coherence and Comprehensive Novelty. This project focuses on developing a mark elimination method, an essential concept in reversible concealment, utilizing Bayesian neural networks (BNNs). In concealment studies, an object's presence is allowed, and then its mark is eliminated without affecting its detection status. Most existing methods are non-reversible and fail to meet this requirement. Our novel approach leverages BNNs to analyze the mark elimination process from multiple perspectives. Firstly, we employ a predictive network to assess the reliability of eliminated marks. Secondly, we use a generation network within an optimization framework to create marks that can reverse the elimination process. Finally, we analyze the network's internal state to gain insights into its prediction or generation capabilities. Our BNNs-based method achieves state-of-the-art performance in object detection and mark preservation, and successfully enables the reversal of mark elimination. The proposed method is platform-independent and can be applied across various domains. Its code will be publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/zzz-zyx/BNN_Mark_Elimination. Additionally, a demo video has been uploaded to YouTube: https://youtu.be/6Bp1t1SC0kQ. Experimental findings demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed strategy, and the study suggests several potential future research directions. The major contributors of this project are Zhiyuan Xu, Rui Zhang, and Jianzhang Yao. If $J/\psi$ decays into invisible particles, it could take a significant amount of branching ratio, potentially up to $10^{-4}$ or higher. In this scenario, our research indicates that such a decay would have far-reaching implications for models of neutrino and dark matter that involve the neutrinos or dark particles communicating with the Higgs or photons. Specifically, if the invisible particles weigh less than approximately 35 MeV, a $J/\psi$ branching ratio of $10^{-4}$ or higher would necessitate that the neutrino or dark particle mass lies within the neutrino or dark matter sensitivity range of current experiments, forcing a reevaluation of the effective field theories based on this new physics constraint. Our research also constrains certain types of dark matter models, such as the vector-like and scalar-like models, yielding more stringent limits than those derived from direct detection and XENON1T, as well as certain types of neutrino models, such as the type-I seesaw model, assuming an energy threshold of 100 MeV for neutrino production. In contrast, invisible decays of $\psi(2S)$ might offer more tolerable physical consequences. It is suggested that the investigation into the invisible decays of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ could serve as a valuable sensitivity criterion for the effective field theories based on neutrino and dark matter interactions. Furthermore, our research proposes the establishment of a new experimental limit on the invisible decay branching ratio of $\psi(2S)$ that could be realized using the SHiP experiment. If the experiment at SHiP exploits the $\psi(2S)$ data with 5 times $10^{20}$ integrated luminosity, it could set a limit of $10^{-5}$ on the invisible decay branching ratio. Based on our research, it is also indicated that the experiment at BEPCII with 5.5 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity and 2-4 GeV $e^+e^-$ beam energy could provide a limit of $10^{-4}$ on the invisible decay branching ratio. It is suggested that the experiment at BEPCII should focus on an energy range of 2-4 GeV for an in-depth exploration into the invisible decays of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$. It is anticipated that the experiment at BEPCII could offer either a limit or actual observation of the invisible decays of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$.

Researchers have studied human perception of visual patterns by analyzing recognized shapes and their transformations. This is based on the idea that stable forms are inherently associated with specific geometric configurations that remain unchanged under various distortions. To investigate this concept further, we examined minimal films, which are the least complex dynamic environments containing recognizable shapes and their evolutions. Our analysis revealed that these environments comprise simple tracks with a singular point and at most one singular axis. Human subjects demonstrated consistent recognition of the underlying geometric configurations across different minimal films. Interestingly, the internal structure of these films varied greatly, even for films with the same recognized pattern. This finding indicates that dynamic settings can also be used to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying processes of shape recognition. Additionally, we observed that the patterns observed in human recognition correspond to the intrinsic groups of the surfaces associated with these films. This prompted us to propose a corresponding grouping process for shape recognition, which is robust against certain types of distortions and can be used to generate new dynamic settings containing the same recognized shapes. Furthermore, we analyzed the computational complexity of this grouping process and found that it is related to the parameters of the setting. Specifically, we observed that recognizing geometric patterns in certain dynamic settings is a NP-complete problem. This is in contrast to settings with trivial groups, such as those containing non-singular planes, for which recognition is a polynomially solvable problem. Our study provides a new mathematical framework for dynamic shape recognition and highlights the intrinsic connections between geometric patterns, their dynamic environments, and the underlying groups that facilitate human perception. This leads to the research question of how these patterns can be applied to develop more robust and dynamic computer vision systems. To pursue this goal, we developed a new algorithm for dynamic setting recognition, which is an extension of the state-of-the-art method for static settings. This algorithm is highly flexible and allows for the recognition of geometric patterns in various types of dynamic settings. Specifically, we tested the algorithm on settings with geometric patterns derived from motion trajectories and found that it achieves high accuracy rates, especially for settings with simple topologies. Our study provides a new perspective on shape recognition that takes into account dynamic patterns and the underlying groups, which is essential for the development of more advanced computer vision systems. Additionally, we observed that dynamic settings can be used to generate new instances of the geometric patterns through a process called homotopy. This is in addition to the existing methods for generating new instances through heterotopy. To validate the approach, they conducted rigorous experiments and analyses on standard blur datasets and demonstrated a notable improvement in its performance. The work presents a detailed comparison of the method against current state-of-the-art techniques, showcasing its potential applications and areas of influence. Our research strengthens this notion by showing that any graph with t colors contains a complete graph of size t and a complete graph of size t+1. This result is achieved through the construction of near-colorful graphs, where every subgraph with t colors is also complete. Alternatively, proof can be done by combining existing proofs of Hadwiger's Conjecture for t=4 and t=5, demonstrating that the complete graph property is hereditary for 4- and 5-chromatic graphs. Our work also yields an easier proof of Halberstam's Conjecture regarding the distribution of prime residues in arithmetic progressions. Moreover, our method can be adapted to prove a more general case of Hadwiger's Conjecture for 5-color graphs with additional edge weight constraints. This approach also yields an alternative proof of a theorem by Moshinsky and an analogous result by Gower, Moshinsky, and Wolf. Lastly, our research presents a new lower bound for the Tur\'an's fourth problem. These findings provide evidence supporting Hadwiger's Conjecture and Turan's fourth problem. The key concept in our research is the notion of near-colorful graphs and its related properties in the context of Turan's fourth problem. The framework is further validated through various experiments and real-world data analysis. This study provides a precise estimate for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the nonlinear $p$-Laplace operator. The research focuses on a specific problem involving a bounded $C^{1,1}$-domain in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with a smooth boundary, and selects two real, nontrivial functions as part of the eigenvalue problem. The selected functions satisfy specific regularity conditions and an nonlinear Lipschitz condition. The first eigenvalue is closely related to an extremal value, and this study establishes a precise estimate for this extremal value through a combination of functional and monotonicity argument techniques. The estimate is specifically expressed in terms of the Hausdorff dimension of the boundary $\Gamma$. The results of this study generalize the existing findings of Kouchnir and Vazquez, and can be applied to a broader range of problems involving nonlinear anisotropic maximum principles and polyharmonic equations. A notable operation within CPT involves union and intersection over sets defined by recursive queries. Researchers have long theorized that if a particular graph containing recursive structures, specifically OBGP, were to be completable by a path, it would lead to a proven containment of CPT within PTIME. This paper presents a new, simpler CPT-based algorithm for complementing OBGP, thereby validating the initially hypothesized relationship between CPT and PTIME complexity. Additionally, the paper establishes that SJC (Symmetric Circuit), a well-studied problem since the 80's, can be solved using a CPT-based approach, thus being complete in PTIME. Moreover, the paper presents an algorithm for determining whether a di-graph contains an even-length Hamiltonian path, an problem which has been solvable in PTIME but only definable through auxiliary sets within CPT. These findings confirm that CPT can effectively capture the essence of PTIME complexity. Most current virtual machines, including the Java Runtime Environment, undergo runtime setup in their start-up phase, consuming a substantial amount of time. Specifically, the process is notoriously slow in JVMs, with some evaluations indicating that it takes around 50-100 milliseconds. Several factors contribute to this slowness. Notably, JVMs delay optimizing certain costly compiler phases until the runtime stage, effectively shifting these expenses to later. Even with incremental compilation, the source code of top-level applications, including the main class of a Java application, remains unoptimized until runtime. This unoptimized state persists until all classes required for the application have been compiled, necessitating a new optimization phase for each additional class. This research investigates a novel approach called "specializing runtime setup space" at compile-time. In this model, each application has its own dedicated compile-time area for runtime setup, eliminating the need for shared runtime resources and enabling concurrent compilation of multiple applications. Our findings confirm that this specialized space not only prevents sharing of runtime resources but also includes unoptimized classes in the compile-time area of each application. Consequently, we observe an unexpected phenomenon where the time it takes to launch an application is sometimes faster when multiple applications are running concurrently compared to when only one is running alone. This phenomenon arises because the time it takes for other applications to initialize is subtracted from the total initialization time of the target application. Our proposed model consists of two complementary strategies. The first strategy involves adjusting the compile-time area for specializing runtime resources to minimize runtime overheads. Our second strategy includes a predictive model to estimate the compile-time area needed for optimizing multi-threaded applications, which in turn enables the optimal distribution of unoptimized classes across applications to minimize their collective runtime overhead. Both strategies are demonstrated using an experimental framework based on the MojoPortal wiki-platform consisting of 458 Java classes and totaling 415 KB. Our results show that the predictive model is more efficient than other available methods, including random and round-robin approaches, in distributing classes between applications to minimize their joint runtime overhead. Furthermore, we have developed a compiler extension for the JVM called CEP, which allows us to optimize the startup time of applications by limiting the number of classes that can be initialized on the fly. Our experiments using the same MojoPortal wiki-platform reveal that the compiler extension can achieve remarkable gains, with a particular configuration producing a startup time that is nearly 3 orders of magnitude faster than the baseline JVM. Unfortunately, developing a BERT-like model for low-resource languages can be impractical due to the need for large datasets and computational power. An alternative approach, model agnostic cross-lingual transfer, enables the use of a BERT model from a resource-rich language to perform tasks on a low-resource language, thereby alleviating the aforementioned limitations. However, existing methods rely on task and word level alignments which can be unreliable and require additional annotations. Consequently, this increases the overall computational expense and infrastructure requirements. In response to these challenges, we introduce Neural Task Representations as Weak Guidance (NTR-WG), an model agnostic transfer framework that utilizes neural task representations as weak guidance and exploits the probability distributions of shared words between two languages to perform cross-lingual task transfer. Unlike existing methods, NTR-WG makes no assumptions about word and task similarities and does not require any additional annotations. We evaluate NTR-WG on BERT-based cross-lingual sentiment classification and achieve notable improvements, showcasing its efficacy and best practices for cross-lingual transfer using neural task representations. In this paper, we examine the behavior of square-integrable function values of Dirac operators on n-dimensional Euclidean space. A novel approach is taken in establishing a theorem that quantifies the magnitude of these function values within any subset of n-dimensional Euclidean space. This theorem has implications in Clifford analysis, allowing for the derivation of a major eigenfunction estimate. Furthermore, this estimate is critical in the formulation of a hypothesis concerning the minimum number of distinct balls required to contain the zero set of any homogeneous monogenic polynomial of degree m. This hypothesis, referred to as the Three Balls Conjecture for homogeneous polynomials of degree m, is confirmed in this paper for all m ≤ 17. Importantly, this result is achieved without relying on specific assumptions regarding symmetry in the polynomial's properties. Additionally, this paper expands on existing findings from [7,8], which had focused on the specific case of symmetric polynomials. Consequently, a corollary to the hypothesis's statement can be deduced for square-integrable function values of Dirac operators, providing a precise upper limit on the minimum number of required balls for a given degree m. This corollary remains partially unsolved and paves the way for a potential resolution of the original hypothesis's statement. Finally, this paper's methods are a combination of those initially presented in [7,8] and newly introduced techniques based on a backward Fourier transform selection principle. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions, specifically highlighting the potential for further generalization of its methods and a more comprehensive exploration of the polynomial's symmetry properties. We examine a family of one-dimensional complex dynamical systems, generating code-based models known as heterochaos baker maps. These maps exhibit anomalous behavior under typical definitions of entropy accessibility when combined with two distinct transitive driving systems. We identify and analyze a one-parameter family of invariant measures achieving maximal entropy for the driven system. Notably, as entropy accessibility benchmarks are compromised, we observe that our entropology framework allows these maximal entropy measures to emerge, even though they cannot be reached through a natural entropy approximation method. Furthermore, our results reveal a critical mechanism for the breakdown of entropy accessibility: a previously unrecognized phenomenon, where two invariant measures of the driven system become indistinguishable under sufficient chaos in the driving system. We establish conditions for the existence of these maximal entropy measures in two specific cases and provide numerical data for additional examples. Additionally, we show that one of these measures corresponds to the Chirikov standard map's maximal entropy measure, previously studied in a related publication. Lastly, we propose possible connections to other one-dimensional systems and discuss potential generalizations to multi-dimensional systems. Numerical software associated with this study is available at https://github.com/ReinhardWinterhoff/heterochaos_baker_maps. WN struggles to generate signals longer than its context window, and even in shorter signals, its efficiency severely deteriorates as the number of output values increases. To overcome these limitations, we have developed QPNet with two distinct innovations. Firstly, we have introduced pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural networks (CNet), a new type of neural network that adapts its output size based on pitch, in contrast to previous fixed-sized networks. Secondly, we have incorporated the average pitch prediction (AP) algorithm to calculate the pitch of the target audio prior to generation. Both the CNet and AP algorithms were previously proposed by X. Gong et al. in a different context, but have now been integrated into WN. The resulting QPNet shows significant improvements over WN and even surpasses state-of-the-art models in generating long quasi-periodic signals of up to 256 frames.
