The search for Earth-like planets in the habitable zone around other stars must consider how magnetic activity affects the spectral characteristics observed in high-precision radial velocity measurements. Using data from the HARPS-N 3.6-year dataset, which includes solar observations with a high signal-to noise ratio, we analyzed the relationship between magnetic activity and spectral features. We found that coronal heating affects spectral activity and identified two new activity indicators, $\log F_8$ and $\log F_{14}$, which are more stable than traditional indicators like $\log R'_\sun$. These stable indicators provide insight into the long-term magnetic activity and degeneracy of observations, which is particularly important for smaller datasets or weaker signals from other planets. We applied these indicators to test the reliability of radial velocity signals from other planets, including $\epsilon$ Eri, which has been linked to $\log R'_\sun$ but shows conflicting results with $\log F_{14}$. This highlights the potential of these indicators to improve bio-habitability research and explore the habitable zone for other Earth-like planets. Additionally, these indicators enhanced the detection and statistical analysis of the radial velocity signal from b Barnard's star, which is the largest ever recorded. These findings contribute to the goal of accurately observing solar-like activity and its influence on other planetary systems observed through HARPS-N and future instruments, like ESPRESSO. We have shown that coronal heating effects can be effectively reduced by utilizing $\log F_8$ and $\log F_{14}$ activity indicators in observational data, even with noisy signals from other planets. These indicators have demonstrated their value in the analysis of the habitable zone around other stars and will likely be useful in observing other solar-like systems, particularly those with weaker activity and exotic planets in the habitable zone. Lastly, these indicators provide insights that are essential for correctly interpreting future observations of other planetary systems with available data. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our approach involves swapping the typical electrode-vortex interaction for one where the electrode itself acts as a vortex. This modification enables us to utilize the Prouty-Schwinger model, which incorporates Ohmic dissipation, to analyze our findings. Within this context, our model's results indicate that the high temperature non-zero-energy peak is significantly affected by the high temperature limit of the Eliashberg function $\Gamma_{E}(0)$. Furthermore, we observed that the ratio of the low to high temperature values of the Eliashberg function, $\Gamma_{E}(T)/\Gamma_{E}(0)$, is minimal when the transport threshold meets the superconducting gap, and that this ratio's behavior in the high temperature limit is primarily influenced by the high temperature expansion of the Eliashberg function. Our model's predictions have been tested against numerical solutions obtained from the Prouty-Schwinger model and the physical mechanisms underpinning these phenomena have been explained. Our analysis suggests that the low-temperature upshift of the Eliashberg function is caused by weakly coupled vortex states, while the high-temperature region is characterized by the presence of quasi-particles. Additionally, we observed that the cross-over phenomenon in the Eliashberg function can be attributed to the transition from quasi-particles to condensed Majorana particles. Consequently, our results indicate that the zero-energy peak should exhibit two distinct regimes based on the temperature, namely a non-Majorana like behavior at low temperatures and a Majorana like behavior at high temperatures. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that the presence of a zero-energy peak should not be solely attributed to the condensation of Majorana particles due to the influence of non-Majorana related peaks that can mimic the behavior of the Majorana peak across various temperature ranges. To verify our theoretical model, we propose an experimental design that utilizes a two-resistive-contact point contact device where one contact acts as a vortex and the other as a normal electrode. This setup allows for the utilization of a low temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy apparatus in conjunction with a cryogenic magnetic field. Furthermore, our model's predictions indicate that the same device can be utilized to test non-Majorana like behavior in various superconducting 3D, 2D, and one-dimensional systems. Specifically, our analysis suggests the examination of a zero-energy peak in a photo-doped silicon surface covered in amorphous ErSi1-xGex

The theory of shadows constitutes an essential branch of bicategorical combinatorial geometry, encompassing the development of the shadow formulation for posets, manifold covers, and more broadly, polytopes and sterile posets. What underpins the success of the shadow formula? Through a series of case studies, we argue that the markability of a poset serves as the critical underlying factor in explaining its efficacy. Markability can be defined as the ability of a poset's marks to function as individual 'characters' where each mark generates a partition of the poset's elements, and the theory of marks includes a established framework for analyzing them. In this context, bicategories serve as the theoretical foundation, permitting the marks to be regarded as objects of a bicategory, and their connectivity by order relationships translating to equivalence relations between these objects. Crucially, we demonstrate that the poset's marks constitute a subposet that is necessarily sterile, and therefore, extensible to polytopes, manifolds, and other smooth covers of their faces. Additionally, we introduce the concept of $\mathscr{C}$-marks, allowing for the marks of a poset or polytope to be regarded as objects of a bicategory $\mathscr{C}$, and show that this poset or polytope is markable if and only if these $\mathscr{C}$-marks form a subposet that is sterile and relatively markable. Furthermore, we establish that markability in polytopes can be expressed through the existence of a faithful markable cover, and demonstrate the markability of intricate structures, including Coxeter posets, omnium posets, face posets of polytopes, and more. The theory of marks that we apply is an extension of its topological analog (Goussarov, Shumakovych, and Silovs work in progress) and encompasses the development of marks for polytopes and their faces. Lastly, we propose an intriguing conjecture concerning marks and their relationship to the polytope's face numbers. A type of geometric hypergraph, known as k-holes, is introduced, where for a given positive integer k, it represents a collection of k or fewer points such that their convex span covers the entire convex hull. This concept is further explored through the establishment of a theorem relating to the formation of geometric hypergraphs from point sets in 2D space. While these systems learn from extensive data, their core mechanisms remain opaque, necessitating good user interface design and clear explanations to foster trust. From a requirements engineering perspective, the development of transparent and understandable AI systems poses significant challenges. To address this issue, the current approach focuses on collecting and documenting requirements for explainable AI systems. Nevertheless, little research has been conducted on the overall explainability requirements for these systems. The survey's results reveal that stakeholders consider key explainability requirements for AI systems to be comprehensive, easily understandable, and consistent. Our findings contribute to the existing body of research on explainability requirements and suggest practical applications for the requirements engineering community. This study presents a new dataset, UniToPatho, consisting of 13,414 histological frames originating from 102 whole-mount specimens and labeled by 12 expert UniTo and UniTo- affiliated pathologists. This large, extensively annotated dataset addresses some of the existing limitations by including various types of lesions, numerous labeled areas, and being based on whole-mount specimens. The UniToPatho dataset is designed to enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based techniques for classification (adenoma, hyperplasia, normal tissue, carcinoma, serrata-type lesions) and abnormality grading (levels 1, 2, or 3). The dataset is accessible at https://www.tochigai.unito.it/unitoPatho/ and can be utilized by the deep learning community to develop and refine methods for colorectal polyp classification and adenoma grading. Airborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images are commonly utilized in various remote sensing applications due to their capability to provide high-resolution imagery in harsh environments and numerous benefits, including enhanced target resolution, increased flexibility in data collection, and reduced operational costs. Nevertheless, the data collection process is often hindered by malfunctions and limitations. Consequently, the acquired data is frequently plagued by noise, shadows, and other forms of degradation. This paper proposes an innovative deep generative model called the hierarchical MrSARP model, which is a modified version of the SWAP model. The MrSARP model comprises two interconnected components: the complex prior and the complex approximation. The complex prior is responsible for generating synthetic SAR images, while the complex approximation is trained to generate synthetic data from real SAR images. Through a series of optimized operations, the model is capable of leveraging the complexity of the prior distribution to facilitate SAR image enhancement by decomposing the degraded image into synthetic noise and image components. Moreover, the model employs a directed graph and stochastic node values to simulate noise and simulate synthetic data from the prior distribution. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model in enhancing the quality of degraded images. Furthermore, comparisons with four prominent baseline methods, including data-driven, learning-based approaches, reveal that the proposed model outperforms the competing methods in terms of performance and image enhancement. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of varying noise levels on the performance of the MrSARP model and discovers that the model is capable of producing enhanced images at both low and high noise levels. Notably, the model is capable of leveraging the complexity of the prior distribution to facilitate SAR image enhancement, which is a notable advancement in the field. The proposed model's source code is publicly available on GitHub for the sake of transparency and facilitating replication. Furthermore, the study provides a detailed tutorial on training and testing the model for the benefit of remote sensing researchers. Supplemental materials, including image datasets and the model's source code, can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/yang-remote-sensing/MrSARP. Additionally, the study demonstrates the potential of the proposed model in a variety of remote sensing applications. For example, the study showcases enhanced images produced by the MrSARP model in a diverse environment, which highlights the model's capability to produce high-quality results in a wide range of scenarios. In conclusion, the proposed MrSARP model has been successfully tested and validated through extensive experiments and real-world applications, which have consistently shown its superiority over competing methods. We've adapted the Q-learning algorithm to continue learning for an unlimited duration of time. The traditional Q-learning algorithm updates action values based on the average long-term reward after combining short-term rewards with the value of taking a specific action in a given state. However, this approach can lead to biased estimates when dropped frame and the time interval between frames vary, which is the case in our work focusing on motion data. To rectify this issue, we've developed a new update rule for action values, incorporating a novel concept we call the "discounting sum of visits" – a measure of visiting frequency combined with a discounting factor. The mathematical underpinnings of our algorithm ensure its convergence to an optimal policy. Moreover, we've tested our algorithm in a real-world application involving human walking data and observed it to be superior to existing methods. Furthermore, we've established a relationship between our updated action values and the long-term rewards, which is referred to as the "expression rule". The expression rule presents an alternative approach for updating action values, which can be utilized instead of the original update rule; however, it demands additional computational expense and may not be applicable to all situations due to potential memory issues. Lastly, we've presented a way to reduce memory consumption and demonstrate the feasibility of applying the expression rule in a more limited sense, thereby facilitating the use of q-learning for continuous duration. The presentation follows this structure: related work is introduced in Section 1, the algorithm is explained in Section 2, empirical evaluations are covered in Section 3, theoretical justifications are provided in Section 4, and lastly, we conclude in Section 5. Moreover, a demonstration of the algorithm's efficacy using motion data is available at this link: https://yunyang.github.io/continuous-q-learning/. Our method employs spine rectification, which aligns adjacent vertebral bodies, and uses anatomically-moderated optimization to select the most suitable vertebrae based on logically connected and experimentally verified rules. It consistently outperformed three leading vertebrae localization deep learning models, demonstrating superior performance with the Cox penalty, a measure used in medical radiology. Our method is adaptable to diverse medical conditions, radiological findings, and imaging modalities, with the added benefit of explaining its reasoning for easier validation and interpretation. It can also enable more accurate computer-assisted spinal disorder diagnosis and surgical planning by accounting for anatomical variations. A fundamental approach in stochastic thermodynamics utilizes a duality relationship between stochastic processes and statistical mechanics. This framework is applied to a broad category of nonlinear Markov processes that can be represented on a finite state space. We have derived mathematical expressions for the limiting fluctuations of various thermodynamic properties, such as heat and work, under two standard normalization conditions. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its adherence to gauge invariance - the ability to isolate unique flux characteristics regardless of arbitrary time unit selection. The introduction of a new method allows for the derivation of normalized fluctuation expressions that are consistent with Euclidean rotation invariance. This fundamental understanding forms the basis for a broader generalization in a follow-up publication. There, we will directly calculate normalized flux distributions using a path-integral technique. This generalization will be applicable to a broader range of nonlinear Markov processes even with infinite-dimensional state spaces. Furthermore, we will derive an on-demand measure of heat and work that is not only path-dependent but also shows a thermodynamic free energy profile with sub-Ohmic decay properties. This result will reveal an explicit power law for the decay of the specific heat and confirm the existence of a infinite set of detailed balance conditions for all conceivable driving forces that can be applied to the system. This understanding will be translated to various driven dissipative systems such as driven harmonic oscillators, driven spin systems and biomolecular motors. Moreover, we will describe how our approach in the realm of stochastic thermodynamics can be used to derive an effective quantum action for the driven oscillators, which is applicable at both the classical and quantum levels. This action will display an underlying duality symmetry. At the quantum level, this action will also show a loop equation similarity with the one that governs quantum gravity. This duality symmetry will be seen to give rise to duality relationships between various driving forces such as angular momentum, driving force and thermal energy. Finally, we will introduce an on-demand measure of thermodynamic driving force in terms of a fictitious Pauli matrix that governs the dynamics of a two-level system coupled to a heat bath. This driving force will be shown to have a nonlinear relation with the usual driving force and will lead to a probe method for identifying the thermodynamic driving force in any generic two-state system. This method will be applied and tested in a variety of concrete examples such as the Kibble-Zurek mechanism for quantum phase transitions, the Brownian motor in arbitrary dimensions and the quantum harmonic oscillator. The discovery of exoplanets with diverse properties has led to the advancement of studies in planetary science, particularly in observing transiting planets using ground-based telescopes. This process has been proven for the hot Jupiter K2-22 b by combining photometry and spectroscopy utilizing the Large Binocular Telescope. Conducting a detailed analysis of the planet's 2015 transit observed through the Multi-Object Double Spectrograph, researchers detected dust particles with sizes exceeding 1-2 micrometers forming a ring around K2-22 b. Estimates suggest the planet loses 3.2 x 10^10 grams per orbit, equivalent to a mass loss rate 5.5 years after its initial discovery. This research is the first to document a planet losing mass due to dust particles outside the Solar System and these results imply a planet with properties similar to Jupiter constantly losing mass in a circumbinary system. This study further expands our understanding of a planetary process that can affect the long-term future of a planet's equilibrium, particularly for small to large planets like K2-22 b. We establish a coherence condition for the milnor fiber of a hypersurface singularity in a specific context: when the degeneration family coexists with a family of smooth surfaces. This condition has two significant implications: it proves that the milnor fiber is a coherent category, and it also implies that the solution to the holomorphic implicit function problem has a partial moduli flatness property. Our investigation is motivated by a combination of theorems from the works of V. Goresky and F. MacPherson, as well as M. Leclercq and J. Seade. Furthermore, we derive a topological invariant that measures the complexity of the degeneration family, and demonstrate its equivalence to another known invariant previously discussed in the works of J. M\"oller-Kimiecki, J. M\"oller, and J. Seade. Additionally, we propose a conjecture regarding the milnor fiber's geometric structure, as well as the ultimate solution to the degeneration family's moduli flatness problem. My interpretation of the Galileo affair contradicts the conventional view that science suffered at the hands of religious intolerance.  Instead, I believe that Galileo's supporters viewed his scientific methods as a threat to their philosophical ideals, which emphasized the importance of clear and distinct ideas.  His opponents, who were more pragmatic and open-minded, preferred a quieter scientific approach that did not challenge their social status.  This clash of values ultimately led to the condemnation of the Galileo affair.  Furthermore, I observe that the successful integration of mathematics into scientific inquiry during the scientific revolution laid the groundwork for a modern, mathematical world view, which was heavily influenced by the scientific methods employed by Galileo and his supporters.  This modern mathematical world view continues to dominate contemporary science, despite ongoing qualms about using mathematics to describe the physical universe.  Finally, I suggest that the scientific revolution was not a singular event but rather one of several 17th-century revolts against traditional knowledge, which were accompanied by the creation of a diverse range of new world views.  These included a non-Epicurean atomic world view and a non-Aristotelian natural world view, both of which were developed by thinkers who were not necessarily associated with the mathematical world view.  Lastly, I note that the rise of the mathematical world view was not a inevitability, and an alternative, non-mathematical world view could have emerged as the dominant perspective, which would have prevented the Galileo affair from becoming a pivotal event in the history of science.  This understanding allows us to reevaluate the significance of the scientific revolution in general and the Galileo affair in particular.  Additionally, it inspires a revised interpretation of the nature of scientific progress, which may be applicable to other fields beyond science, and encourages a more cautious approach to predicting the future of scientific development.  Finally, I suggest that the incorporation of an empirically informed historical understanding of scientific progress could serve as a counterbalance to a predictive model based on statistical analysis of past data.  This could have significant implications for contemporary science and technology, which may be shaped by a modern mathematical world view that continues to dominate the scientific revolution's legacy.  This, in turn, raises intriguing questions about how the scientific revolution's mathematical world view has influenced the development of science and technology over the past four centuries.  Ultimately, I observe that the incorporation of a non-mathematical world view could still shed new light on numerous, previously unresolved issues in the history and philosophy of science. We propose a unique application where a human trainer guides a human apprentice in learning a new skill by providing feedback, even if the trainer has no expertise in the subject themselves.  We call this application Amanuensis.  In the context of computer programming, the trainer acts as an apprentice's mentor, helping them achieve mastery through collective effort.  Our system revolves around a shared screen and enables diverse forms of interaction, including voice, gesture, and direct input.  We have conducted three successful experiments in the programming domain, demonstrating that even a trainer with no particular expertise can effectively aid an inexperienced programmer in learning new skills.  Our results indicate that this unique human collaboration can lead to notable outcomes.  In particular, we found that the trainer's involvement can even benefit themselves, leading to new insights and utilizing existing knowledge in innovative ways.  You can find the detailed report on our experiments and findings at https://tinyurl.com/ProgrammerTrainer.  We aim to make Amanuensis a versatile tool, applicable in a wide range of educational settings beyond just programming.  Our current research is centered at https://amanuensis.net.  We invite you to visit, explore, and engage with this application.  It serves as an open-source platform for testing the boundaries of this unique human collaboration method.  In the spirit of Amanuensis, we hope to learn from your experiences and achieve success together.  You can follow our project on Twitter @Amanuensis and look for us on other social media platforms using the #Amanuensis hashtag.  We are constantly seeking new collaboration opportunities and would love to hear from you!  In particular, we are looking for trainers with unique, lesser-known skills and expertise.  If you fit this description, please get in touch with us at hello@amanuensis.net.  We are committed to equity, diversity, and inclusion in our research and strive to build a diverse community of trainers, spanning various backgrounds and skill sets.  We look forward to learning from each other and achieving great things, one training session at a time.
